IN DARKNESS. BY FLOREECR EARLE COATES. I will be still; The terror drawing nigh Shall startle from my lips no coward cry; Nay, though the night my deadliest dread:fulfil, I will be still. For oh! I know, Though suffering ho;:rs delay, Yet to Eternity they piss away, Carrying something onward as they flow, Outlasting woe! Yes, something won; The harvest of our tears— Something unfading, plucked from fading years Something to blossom on beyond the sun. From Sorrow won. The agony, So hopeless now of balm, Shall sleep at last, in light as pure and calm As that wherewitn the stars look down on thee, Gethsemane.
..—Etarper's Magazine.

Smith: "My wife wants a new dress every day in the year."—Jones "She must be awful extravagant Does She get it ?"—Smith : "No; that's the reason she is com- pelled to want it." Mrs. Christopher Cross: "This is a pretty time of. night for you to come home."—Mr. Chris. Cross: m' dear. Ain't come home vet- Jes' called t' shay y' needn't sit up f' me to-night.." Laziness grows on people; it begins in cobwebs and ends in iron chains. The more work one has to do in the world, the more he is able to accomplish, for he ' learns to economise his time. A little boy went to his first tea-party when four years and three months old. Upon his hostess asking him how be liked his tea, he replied, "It is very nice, but it tastes very much of the water." The Spartans were not allowed to combat often with the same enemy. IThey wished not to inure these to battle; and if their enemies revolted frequently, they were accustomed to exterminate them. Ate ANNenoex OF WOHDSWORTIT.—Just before reaching Rougha or Rough How Brioge, had we been hereon a certain day nigh fifty years ago, we should have seen the Whitehaven mail come round the corner, crash into a pony-chaise, with two middle-aged men in it, have seen the pony-chaise. occupants and all, fly over—or rather through—the wall, and have heard one of the gentlemen pick himself up and say, in a solemn way, "I shall have this matter thoroughly investigated." We should have heard David Johnson, the driver—pale as death, and pulling up sharp and looking over his shoulder—say, "Good God! its Muster Wadswuth." And, had we been in the Keswick Market Place that night, and asked whether Mr. Wordsworth was much hurt, we should have heard David say, "No, air. thank Heaven for that, sir! But I never heard a body's tongue swear gladlier though, for I thowt we'd kilt the poit"—Corakill Maya- sine. AN UNFXPECT/O1 ViSlTOß.—Strange noises came from the direction of the front door of No. 9,803, South Park. avenue. The second fiat is occupied by Mr. and Mrs. John Fowler and their son William. The family had just retired. The strange noises grew louder. " Burglars !" whisperer] Mrs. Fowler with a shudder. "Nonsense," replied Mr. Fowler, "no burglar would belfool enough to make such a racket as that." Mr. Fowler got up and lighted the gas in the hall. Presently Mrs. Fowler heard him say: "%Vell, I never." When the gas blazed up Mr. Fowler was amazed to see standing on the stairs, just below the first turn, a large Texas steer, with the back-yard gate on one horn and the front hall hat-tree on the other. The steer looked at Mr. Fowler and Mr. Fowler looked at the steer. The steer seemed to have no explanation to offer 03 to why he should call at that hour of the night. So Mr. Fowler inquired: "What do yoN want here? This is no china shop." The steer dropped the back-yard gate and shock the hat-tree at Mr. Fowler. Then he pawed up a yard or two of stair c irpet and bellowed in a rich baritone voice that awoke everybody in the block. The steer climbed a step or two higher. "Shno," said Mr. Fowler, waving the front flap of his nightgown at the animal; "Shoo, scat! Get out, you're not wanted." But the steer only pawed up another yard of carpet and shook the hat. tree at Mr. Fowler. The steer, having recovered his wind, had made up his mind to COMP up those steps at a jump. Mr. Fowler got inside and shut the door barely in time. The animal knocked, but as refused admit- tance. Then he hung the hat-tree on the door-knob, pawbd up some new carpets. bellowed sonorously, and started up the stairs to the third flat. Meantime quite a crowd of neighbours hail gathered in front of the hause. Presently a couple of men in slouch hats and spurs, with coils of rope in their hands, came up. "Seen anything of a strange steer?" they inquired. "You'll find him up Stairs in that house," said a bystander.- The cowboys dashed up the stairs. They had a rope round his horns in a jiffy, and he came down humbly enough.—Chicago Tribune.

SHAKtiPFRTAN METAPRO—RS.—For a finely expres- sive metaphor, so common that we use it 'without any thonsht of its full sign) ficance, what have we better than the words of Enobarbus on the beauty of the Queen of Egypt, "it beggared all description" ("Antony and • Cleopatra," ii. 2) ? We still beg our friends not "to stand on ceremony" ("Julius Caesar," ii. 2) ; a hopeless pursuit. is still popularly describsd as "a wild-goose chase" ("Romeo and Joliet," ii. 4) ; and if we seek to give a vivid picture of a lingering disease we cannot well improve upon the time-honoured "death by inches" (" Coriolanus," v. 4). When men comfort themselves with the immediate success of a new enterprise, some croaker is sure to stfggest, even at the risk of "dashing their spirits a little" ("Othello," iii. 3), that " 'tis but early days" (" Troilus and Cressida" iv. 1) for con- gratulation. Most of us in the course of our lives are called upon "to dance attendance" ("Richard iii. 7) on "some privileged man" (" Troilus and Cressida." ii. 3). and both students and reviewers find it sometimes a difficult matter to "grasp their author's drift" (ibid.. iii. 3). Not being so bellicose as our ancestors, we are well satisfied with the "weak piping time of peace" (" Richard 111.. i. 1), and have no desire to become "food for powder" (" Henry 1V.," Part 1. iv. 2). Even when we are "out at elbow" ("Measure for Measure," H. 1), we still like to have plenty of " elbow-room " ("King John," v. 7). "Tittle-tattling" (" Winter's Tale," iv. 2) has always been condemned; we are fortunate if we do not number among our acquaintance one of whom it may be said, as of Wolsey. that "no man's pie is freed from his ambitious finger" (" Henry VIII." 1. 1). When a school has "broke up" ("Henry 1V.," Part 2, iv. 2), the pleasant experience will now and again force itself upon us of being "eaten out of house and home" (ibid., ii. 1), and of finding everything left "at six and . seven" (Richard II.," ii. 2). Two old enemies meeting will" embrace the occasion" ("Merchant of Venice," i. 1), to "pluck a crow together" ("Comedy of Errors," 1) ;'it is well if we can simply some seductive beverage in which they may "drink down all unkindness" '"Merry Wives of Windsor," i. 1).--I1aciaillan's Maga- zine. :Wrirrrisn's Rinsomos POENS.—One of the poems which is less read now than it used to be, but which is typical of Whittier's genius, is the dramatic episode in early Quakerism, in which Barclay of Ury (father of the Apologist Barclay) was insulted and mobbed in his own city of Aberdeen. After picturing the scene, how the Laird rode up the "streets of Aberdeen," with a furious mob beside him, jeered at, flouted, and cursed by those who had been dependents or servants; how the troop of soldiers came riding by "with broadswords swinging," and how they proposed to-- Ride him down, Push him, prick him, through the town, Drive the Quaker coward, when one of them, an old comrade of Urv's lord,-came with "ready weapon bare" to help him, but that aid is refused by Barclay, who avows that he can stiffer. "Give me joy that in His name :can bear, with patient frame, All these vain ones offer; While for them He suffered long. Shall I answer wrong with wrong, Stvfling with the scoffer?" And so, as "towards the Tolbooth prison" the old ' soldier goes to bear through iron gates poor disciples "preach of Christ arisen," the fine moral is drawn that he is happy whose inward ear is consoled by angel comfortings, and, when the faggots of hatred burn, can discern glimpses through the smoke "of the goad here- after." There are others of this Class of picturesque and denominational poems, possibly the best being that en- titled "The Quaker Alumni," a poem read at a Friends' school anniversary, a verse of which may be quoted, in which Berkeley, Hopkins. and Charming are described as three shades walking Rhode Island— One holy name bearing, no longer they need Credentials of piety. and passwords of creed; The new song they sing has a threefold accord. " And they own one baptism, one faith, and one Lord. and in one of the hymns that he has written for the use , of others—the " Hymn for the Opening of Thomas ::ltarro King's House of Worship."as the Quaker poet phrases it —he echoes a little the words, for that hymn ends with the hope that, in time to be, a sweeter song shall be heard, when "one faith, one hope, one love," together restore "the seamless robe that Jesus wore." And be- fore passing away from this class of Whittier's poems, reference should be made to that noble tribute to John Sturge— Thanks for the good man's beautiful example. Who in the vilest saw Some sacred crypt or altar of a temple, Still vocal with God's law. —The Quiver, for Noternber—preen Volume. The opening meeting of the Warrington Parish Church Temperance Society was held in the National School, Church-st„ on Monday evening, when there was a good attendance. The chair was occupied by The Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis), who said that he first of all wanted to explain his own views on the question of temperance. He took theaair at a large meeting of the Warrington Temperance Federation the other evening, and he-said that the object of the meeting was a very good one, and a very great one indeed. So, without inquiring very closely into it. or looking teo narrowly at it, he felt it his duty as Rector to take the chair. He wanted them clearly to understand thnt he was not a total abstainer himself. He had been a total abstainer, and he might become one again, but at present he did take sometimes beer and sometimes wine. At the meeting referred to, some things were said which he did not agree with, but he felt that he was there as chairman and that he might be looked upon as being perfectly impartial in the matter. It was not for him to criticise everything said. He Was there simply to take the chair and to advance a very great and very good cause. But be had a very great objection to extravagant language, and he fe.t very strongly indeed upon that point. He could quite understand men speakingstrongly when they considered the evil consequences of drunkenness. He did not, however, agree with anyone who thought that it was as wrong to take a little as it was to take a great deal too much. He did not like to hear strong language used with regard to the brewers, because until he could seethat the beer traffic was in itself an iniquit- ous trade, he could not say a word against the brewers. He had, also, found publicans who were sincerely good persons, and who as fa; as he knew, were really trying to carry on their trade legitimately, and he had always felt that if a publican did conduct his trade properly he was a benefactor, rather than otherwise to society. He however, wanted to express equally strongly his feeling of the need that the church and the clergy, and every- one in earnest, should take up the great cause of temper- ance, and do their utmost to prevent drunkenners. They must try and realise what misery flowed from drink— look into the drunkards' home and see what misery and poverty there was there. There was such &low stand- ard where there was drunkenness. Mr. Willis then refer- ed to the Society, which he said was formed on the dual basis of moderation and total abstinence. He advocated total abstinence for those to whom drink was really a temptation, and - moderation for those who did not altogether abstain. With regard to the young he would strongly advocate total abstinence, for if they never tasted beer or wine they would never feel the want of it. (Applause.) The Rev. T. A. Easterling said that he hoped that the society would be a great factor for good. He had not been much in the manufacturing towns of the north, but he did not think he had ever been in a town where drunkenness was so rife as it was in Warrington. He had certainly never seen so much drunkenness amongst i women. It could not be denied that there was a pressing need for some measures to taken to prevent a spread of this foul disease, and to prevent people becoming victims to it. He did not say that drunkenness alone wa..3 the national sin. There were also the sins of im- purity and of gambling, which, with drunkenness, made a terriblejtrio. Unless conquered they would soon bring England low. Although he had been a total abstainer from his earliest years, he did not like to hear intemperate language made use of regarding those who were not total abstainers, and he did not like to hear those who really were temperate derided as the weaker brethren. • (Applause.) The Rev. C. E. Jackson also gave an address.—To- wards the close of the meeting, the Rector remarked that it WS under medical advice that he was not a total abstainer, and he felt bound not to disregard that advice.

RHYMES IN THE DIALECT. m UNCLE TUBS. A blunt streytforrud Lanky chap, As dud his nook at work; He paid his rooad, an' acted square An' honest, pp to th' mark. His monly face wur allus breet-- Aw never see'd him glum; This world cud do wi' mooar o'th' sooart, Like my Owd Uncle Turn. A merry twinkle in his een Towd he wur fond o' gain; Plain an' rough-lookin', in his heart Here gentle as a lamb. Aw ne er heard nayburs co him "near," He ne'er med fooaks een dim, For thoose desarvin' sympathy • Fun few RS kind as him. Wong his own rough an' ready sooart lie allus sed his say, An' if he promised owt, he'd do't, Wodever coom th' way. He hated humbug woss than owt, An' wodn'd own a friend— So whoa id wor—as sowd a mate To gain a selfish end. Fdr years he lived up Forgate yon, His loomheawse wur at th' back, He'd weyve an' sing his ditties theer, To th' hand loom's dull "click-clack An' if he wearied o'thad job— Ridin' th' owd timber tit— He'd rnek odd things, an' addle brass Wi' joinerin' a bit. Wod wheezes th' owd lad used to spin O'er th' hot-aril's-brewed pint an' pipe; He'd laff an' j.ioak wi' cheeks as red As appo's plump an' ripe. Hey, mony a " buzz" he's towd wi' glee, As med his hearers grin; An' oft he's 'sift hind, till tears Run tricklin' off his chin. 'Twur varra seldom as aw geet Up to his sunny nest; But when aw went aw bed to stop Awhile an' feeast on t' best. An' then he'd reych his fiddle deawn, Wi' th' bow, fro' t' nail i'th' wo, An' play a lilt • music sweet, An' sing to t' strain and o. - Sometimes one heeard him finger t' streng, An' hum a melody, • Then, stertin' off, he'd draw his stick 0 er t' fiddle lovin'ly ; He'd use id gently, like a child, An' bend his heyd to hear To th' mellow seawnds as floated up, So touchin', soft, an' clear. He loved thad fiddle frooar than owt I' th' world, beside his wife., Mi owd Aunt 'Becca, boo wur th' lass As shared his lot i' life. Like others, they'd ther' ups an' deawns, An' weather rough an' fair; But when aw knew 'em they wur owd— A comfortable pair! At monv a weddin' " do" an' stur, 'lliad fiddle's music rung : Good songs th' owd iella sung. beside While seawnd i' heart an' lung. At last, Death snapt ther' strengs teavr, Worn eawt wi' th' world's rough tune; An' Ixe.ntli wur ta'en to join t' sweet host 0' singers up aboon ! JACK 0' ANN'S.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATLRI)AI, NOVEMBER 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATLRI)AI, NOVEMBER 10, 1888.

HOW A LANCASHIRE MAN WAS VIC- TIMISED IN LONDON. By " DUCIALD GUN?." I saw it discussed lately in one of the quarterly magazines by an antiquary of authority whether Lon- don has a greater population than that of ancient Babylon, Nineveh, or Rome. The writer contends, with great show of proof and researcb, that although the ancient cities occupied smaller areas, they contained within their walls a larger population, as the tenements were loftier, bearing numerous Rats or storeys, some- what after the style of Old Edinburgh, a single tenement sometimes having under its roof upwards of a hundred souls. Well, London, with a population equal to that of Ireland, and considerably in excess of that of the kingdom of Scotland, is large enough in all conscience.

London! What memories and associations are awakened by the name? Hardly a volume or news- paper but teems with allusions to it. The rendezvous of the illustrious of all nations, the fountain of our legisla- tion, the heart of the commercial ssorld, the repository of the ashes of our greatest in war, science, art, and letters, it comprises within its bounds a greater variety of characters, wealth and poverty, learning and ig- norance,diseaseand crime,than any other city in the world. Into this" wilderness of brick and stone,' on the day following my arrival in the Thames, I sallied forth for the first time, alone, and made my way as best I could for St. Paul's Cathedral, which was the first item on my programme. There is perhaps no building so familiarly known as that of St. Paul's. No view of London is con- sidered complete without it, and deservedly so, not only on account of its architectural symmetry and massive- ness, but because it dominates the whde of the city proper. I spent a pleasant hour in the examination of the tombs and monuments of theinterior,butexperienced a disagreeable sensation of loneliness in not being ac- companied by a friend. It is an old adage that no company is better than bad company., but to be alone in London, without a friend to communicate a thought to, inclined me to question the veracity of the proverb, and to feel that any kind ot companion would have been a welcome relief to me, seven if it were only for the purpose of speaking at him, and giving expression to my feelings and having the luxury of a response." It was while leaving St. Paul's with this reflection on my lips,that a gentleman in light summer holiday attire, with straw hat to match, accosted me in the most cour- teous accents with : " Good morning, sir." I returned the salutation. "What is your opinion of St. Paul's, may I ask ?" I had just turned round to have a full survey of the stately pile, and replied— " Very high, sir."- "Yes, I believe the height of the finale is 369 feet." "Indeed, but Lmeant to say that! had a very high , opinion of the architecture of the building." I "Excuse me, you're from the North! Am I correct ?" "Yes, from Blackburn, in Lancashire." "What a strange coincidence! I beloog to the same county, and was born in Bolton. Do you know the firm of Shand and Sharpies, practising as solicitors in that town?" "I can't say I do." " Well, Shand is my brother, and Sharpies an old pall of mine." Supposing St. Paul had dropped from the Unknown, or in compassion furnished me with a being ready-made to my hand and purpose, I could not have experienced a greater flutterof delight and surprise. "Have you ever visited London before ?" he in- quired, as we sauntered along together in St. Paul's Churchyard "No, this is ,my first visit, and I'm a complete stranger in the city." Being free like myself for a few holidays lie at once volunteered to be my fidus Achates, and installed himself in a manner which gave me no choice of acceptance or rejection. He entered into absolute pos- session of me, and when in a coffee tavern, to which we bad adjourned for a small refection, he drew out a pro- gramme for the remainder of the day and the next, and the next. He evidently knew the city thoroughly, and took a deeper interest in, and showed a greater kind- ness towards me than either my father or grandfather. could have done. He was communicative to a fault. He related to me his whole personal history, how he had been in business in Leeds, and was at one time the secretary of the Liberal Four Hundred there, showed me a genuine auto- graph letter from Mr. Gladstone to himself, how he had I married and succeeded thereby to a property valued at live thousand pounds, which he had converted into cash ; how he speculated, lost and won; in fact, his de- cline and fall and risings again during the last decade. , While he was discoursing on these topics, a young lady and gentleman were shown into our little parlour. "How do, old boy," said the latter, addressing and shaking hands with my friend. They were introduced to me as Mr. and Miss Cottam, brother and sister, and living in the neighbourhood of Chelsea. They had a cup of coffee each, and appeared to be intimately acquainted with Shand, and in great haste to meet certain friends at the Albert Memorial Hall. Having finished their coffee we exchanged a hurried good-bye, and Shand saw them out. " Now my first watchword to you before we do the lions," he said to me on his return, "is mind your pockets. I always keep my coin here ;"—tapping his vest watch-pocket with the forefinger of his right hand —" shoals of sharpers are constantly prowling about the places of attraction just now, and one never knows what new game they are up to. Have you heard the latest 2"

" N. I can't say I have." " A boy down Clapham went into a fashionable con- fectioner's shop to purchase a penny sweetcake. 'Please ,sir,' he said to the shopman in a whining, pleading whimper. you be so kind as put it down my back, as some boys outside are watching to steal it from me.' He undid his collar, and the accommodating , shopman secreted it several inches down. The boy wasn't two minutes gone when another entered the shop an excited manner. ' Please, sir, was there a boy here buying a cake?' Yes, what do you want?' Well, he has stolen your watch and guard.' The shop- man discovered his loss in a moment. 'Which way— which way did the little scoundrel go?' he thundered, as he bounded over the counter wild with excitement. The boy pointing to a street the third down, showed him where he saw him disappearing. Without waiting for any further palaver, the shopman was off like a shot in full hue-and-dry. On his return a few minutes afterwards, panting and perspiring all over but without the culprit or watch, he found the shop minus boy the second, his till rifled, and not a eopper left. Now,l call that sharp." "Rather," I replied. ' Shortly before this I had begun to suspect that my friend himself was not the clean potato, but my suspicions were disarmed by such revelations and his precautionary advice. However. I had my misgivings and my whole being was on sentinel. What annoyed me most was that I had at that very moment in my vest watch-pocket all the money be- longing to me in the world, amounting to the modest sum of eleven pounds ten shillings sterling. How to get that money shifted into safe custody was a problem that sorely agitated me. I hit on the following efpedient. I explained to him that I had sailed up to London with my triend, Captain Rollo, and thgt I had left my money in my bag in the cabin of the steamer, and would be under the necessity of returning there for a supply. All right, he woula accompany me. Now, that was exactly what I didn't wish, as I was so anxious to get quit of this new friend, as I had been an hour ago to secure him. I thanked him for his kindness, gave him my card, and laid myself under promise and obligation to meet him again. No, that wouldn't do, he would esteem it a favour to be in- troduced to my friend Rollo, and be shown over the steamer. Be clung to me like a tlesh-fly. I did not appreciate this pertinacity, but how could I he ungrate. ful to one who had proffered me, a stranger, so much kindness and consideration? I had not the moral courage to cut him abruptly. How much I regret it now! To the steamer, therefore, we went. When we got there, we had great difficulty in getting en board on account of the tumult and confusion attending the dis- embarking the cargo. We found the vessel deserted by all the officers except the steward, who informed me that Captain Rollo had gone to the Company s office and had left a message for me to call for him at the manager's address any time during the evening. I asked the steward to be so good as show my friend over the steamer, and during their absence I safely deposited my treasurer in my bag, saw it locked and safely stowed away. I now breathed freely, I have at times felt very purse-proud when my pockets were lined with bank notes and gold, but I candidly confess I never felt more independent in my life than I now did, after being divested ofithat superfluous cash. I felt as light as Christian when the burden was taken from his back, and as proud as if I had out-generalled the greatest Artful Dodger ever trained by a Fagan. But I must inform my reader on the quiet, however, that I was not without a few shillings in my pocket, not in my vest pocket, though; oh, no ! I now felt in the best of form to do all the " lions " of the city, and my friend was also in the best of spirits as we left together. And why? Because he knew I had been for a sUpply, the poor, unsophisticated simpleton that he was! But pause, I do an injustice in thus casting aspersions on the hnnoue of one who.has as yet approved himself as my friend, and possessing all the manners and virtues of a gentleman. We visited, in turn, the Monument, Thames Embank- ment, Houses of Parliament, and Westminster Abbey, and during the round I had ample opportunity of gauging the properties and intelligence of my friend,and found them considerably above the average, but there was an unmentionable something about him which con- stantly aroused my suspicion. On leaving the Abbey, I proposed to keep my engage- ment with the Captain, and pressed him to accompany me in a hansom, which I at that moment hailed and engaged. Contrary to my expectations. however, he excused himself on the ground of a prior appointment, but agreed to ride with me as far as Charing Cross, by which route I directed the driver to travel. On

separating there, we arranged to meet again the fol- lowing day at the Coffee Tavern, where we had lunched together in the morning. I found Captain Rollo, Mr. Cowan, and supper waiting my arrival. We spent a very convivial evening, and before leaving I was laid under embargo,. to sing my favourite song of the " Efighlandman's Party," with the popular chorus— There was Donald More and Dngaid Gunn, And twa-thry mair, and we had some fun, But it turned oot a deevil o' a mornin', On our way home to our quarters on the Thames I entertained Captain Rollo with a detailed narrative of all my adventures during the day, and when we reached the steamer, shortly after twelve o'clock, we found the steward sitting up in bed deeply engrossed in his Weekly Beedget. " I thought you were to spend the n'ght with Mr. Cowan," he said, staring very hard at me. "Why so ?" "Because the gentleman who came with you in the forenoon called for your bag about three hours ago, stating that he had been charged by Mr. Cowan to bring it to his house, as he had insisted on your staving over night with

"Dash it alt! I never But did you give him the bag 2" I ejaculated hastily and angrily. "No : but when Mr. Cowan's servant called shortly afterwards with your card and message written on the back, I delivered it to her, thinking it was by your order. Here is the card."
"Whew !" whistled the Captain; "I have it all in a cockle-shell; the lady you met. and the card you gave that rascal in the coffee-room."

"So have I, Captain; but the bag, hew is it to be recovered 2" I shouted hysterically. "Keep cool, Gunn. • Well, the bag may be recovered, but its cargo, I fear, never! Even had it been entered in the articles of the vessel before sailing it would have fared no better. Besides, they're three hours ahead of us." Here he violently upbraided the steward, whom I as stoutlT defended. _ _ _ _
After holding a council, we decided to report the matter at once to the authorities at Scotland Yard.

A few minutes sufficed to carry us thither. Before setting out we enlisted the services of the constable who acted as night-watch over the warehouses of the Wap- ping Wharf. We were ushered into a small ante-room, and closeted with two sergeant detectives, named Sin- clair and Savage, and a little bald-headed man, who took elaborate notes of the interview. The questioning was interminable, although I descended into the minutest details of the events of the day leading up to this most painful episode. They seemed more concerned over the linen in my bag than the money. It contained three shirts, one sleeping-gown. two handkerchiefs, two time- tables, and four collars. They 're particularly curioui over the shape size, and makers of the latter, and although they had been in my possession for months, 1 was unable to satisfy them on many points, to their evident chagrin. My fetqings that night can be better imagined than described.

The following morning Detective Sinclair called again for me to obtain some supplementary information about the dress and appearance of my friends. I waited two days, but to no purpose, as neither money nor information was forthcoming. On the third I was obliged to ret,nrn home. I called at Scotland Yard to say so, and leave my address, as it would neither suit my family nor firm to remain longer in London. By n kind accommodation from the Captain, I was enabled to return to Lancashire by rail. No one, unless he has been • similarly situated, can possibly Gonceive my misery and mortification on leaving the scene of my misfortune. I could not help wondering how this world of ours keeps growing older, and one would naturally suppose wiser and better. Yet each generation but repeats itself, producing fresh crops of fools and vampires to feed upon them, in spite of the accumulated experience of centuries, and so it shall continue to the end, whenever that may be. God knows. At the end of my journey I saw before me bright faces lit up with the sunshine of a joyous welcome home, and little plump hands eager to pounce on my bag and dig out the promised treasures of London buns, dolls, and. pictures. What havoc that wretch had accomplished. I drew the curtain, as I shall now, on the deepest wound that has ever been inflicted on my memory. It is exactly three months ago, and time, while he wrinkles many a brow, smoothes many a ruffled temper. I was just contemplating, yesterday morning, withmuch fkstisfaction, how gently his hand had moulded this little incident as a relic of the past, when I was surprised by the following letter, bearing the London post-mark :

Scotland Yard. London, W. 0., August 27th, 1888. Dear Sir,—l have to inform you that while Constable B 989 was rescuing a ohild in a perambulator from the Serpentine, yesterday, he stumbled on a travelling bag loaded with stones. On comparing it with the description you furnished us of yours, we have concluded it to be your property, and shall forward it to you if desired on hearing from you by return. We have as yet felled to Alscover any trace of your friends, Shand and Co.—Yours truly, C. A. SINCLAIR. Mr. D. Gann.

Now, the bag was an old one, and of very little value, having done good service over twenty years, and its condition now must be very sorry indeed, so I wrote by return informing them that they might keep the bag until they found the thief. I considered it quite in keeping with cockney impertinence to ask me to be at the expense of the carriage from Lonetsn to Blackburn of an old bag which had suffered from three months' immersion in the Serpentine. Relics, no doubt, are very interesting, but a man like myself with a numerous family has arrived at that point when he is disposed to look upon sovereigns with greater favour than relics. Shand undoubtedly did 50, and is in all likelihood at this very moment wearing one of my best shirts in memory of his sharp practice and my simplicity. Moral.—Never make too familiar with any person you do not 'know. Quod erat demonstrandam.

div.head: REV. W. MULES.-ACTION FOR DIVORCE.
div.p: THE REV. W. MULES.-ACTION FOR DIVORCE.

In the Divorce Division, on Saturday, Mr. Justice Butt had before him the ease of Mules v. Mules. The petition was that of the wife for a divorce by reason of the cruelty and adultery of her husband, the Rev. William Mules, formerly a Warrington clergyman. Mr. Pritchard appeared for the peti- tioner, and there was no defence. Mrs. Mary Margaret Alice Mules, the petitioner, said that she was married to the respondent at the Wesleyan: Chapel, Rushholme, on the the 25th November, 1882. He was then .a clergyman. She lived with him at Warrington and Eccles, and there were two cliff; dren of tie marriage. At Eccles her husband was the vicar of a Reformed Church, where he met Miss Jessie Brackenridge. to whom be subsequently paidi great attention, neglecting witness. One night in July, 1887, be returned home.—Mr. Pritchard : What condition was be in? Witness: He was not sober.—Examination continued: She was fright- I ened. Ile came after her and threw her violently in a chair. No one else was present on that occa- sion. In August, 1837, she and her husband went to the Isle of Man, and were met there by the Brackenridges, they all going about to different places together. Witness had occasion to complain of his conduct with Miss Brackenridge, owing to ivhich witness "became• hysterical." When they returned from a visit to the Exhibition, be pulled her off the bed, threw her down, and attempted to I strike her. lie afterwards threw her violently into a chair. In January, 1887, there was a concert in the Eccles Town Hall. She went there with her husband. Miss. Brackenridge was to sing there.— Mr. Pritchard: Did anything occur on that occa- sion? Witness: We. were there to have eupuer at the Brackenridges, and when he came home he was in a violent rage. He held his clenched fist at me and dared me to speak. 'Examination continued: On another occasion he pulled her off the chair and swore at her, throwing her into the middle of the room. He gave her a very violent shaking. On one occasion she was in bed with one of the chil- dren, who was asleep.—Mr. Pritchard: What did he do? Witness: He sharpened the razor and Came towards the child.—Mr. Justice Butt: That is a distinct act of cruelty, very barbarous cruelty indeed. Examination continued: At Eccles be showed her a revolver and also some cartridges, and he then informed her that he would shoot anyone whom' he found watching him with Nris Bracken- ridge. On Feb. 20 last he left her. He said he was going to speak at a public meeting at Accrington, and afterwards intended meeting a "ministerial friend." A few days after she received some letters from him. Some of these were read, from which it appeared that he was now at New York, hepleading for forgiveness. stating that he would do all in his power to atone for the past. In another letter he wrote, "J ustiee is not what I ask for but mercy " .Corroborative evidence was given of the cruelty, after which the landlady of the Royal Hotel, Burscough. near Oimskirk, deposed that oil the 20th February last a lady and a gentleman came and stayed the night at the hotel. The evidence of identification, however, mainly relied upon photographs, in regard to which his lordship said that the court never acted.—tiitimately the peti- tioner was granted a judicial separation, with costs, by reason of her husband's cruelty, with cus- tody of the children. .

WARRINGTON BOAIth OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday evening. the Rev. G. F. Roberts presided, and there were also present Messrs. Balharrv, ,Blackhurst, Greening, Jolley, J. Houghton, W. Houghton, Clarke, Eckers- ley Humphries, Owen, Isherwood, Ratcliffe; J. C. Sutton (clerk); S. Sutton (assistant clerk); C. H. Ward (workhouse waster); and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Piulgate schools.)

SCHOOL COMMITTEE The minutes of the Padgate School Committee stated that letters had been received from Grimsby about the boys sent there. Two of the boys wrote themselves expressing satisfattion with their present position, and a form of indenture for their apprenticeship was submitted. The doctor reported the general health of the children to be good. Mr. Henry Stephens, H.M. Inspector, visited the schools and reported that great improvement was being made in the yard. The houses were very clean.—The eIIAIR- MAN moved the adoption of the minutes, and remarked that in a conversation with Mr. Stephens after his visit the latter gentleman said that he was decidedly pleased with the results of the visit.—Mr. GREENING seconded the adoption of the minutes, which was agreed to. SCHOOL FEES

The School Fees Cominittee reported that they had allowed fees in 71 cases, el of which were old, and 10 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. BLACKHURST, seconded by Mr. GREENING, the minutes were adopted.

div.head: PROPOSAL FROM RARLESTOWN.
div.p: A PROPOSAL FROM RARLESTOWN.

The Clerk read a letter which he had received from the Earlestown guardians, Messrs. Ratcliffe. Clarke, and Eckersley, giving notice that at that meeting of the Board they would move that there be a relief pay station at Earlestown, so that the poor people there would not be compelled to walk to Newton through the winter months for their sinall pittance—a distance of a mile and a quarter, many of the old people being from sixty to eighty year of age. The Guardians, the letter continued, had provided a vaccination station at Earles- town which was not of so much importance. The Clerk thought the best course would be for the Newton Relief Committee to get their officer to report alto the number of relief cases there was at Earlestown4Wand the Com- mittee could then recommend what ,they proposed to have done to the Board.--Mr. ItArcuttp said he should move that they have a pay station at Earlestown. To take poor people from Earlestown to Newton to receive relief was something like taking them from Warrington to Sankey Bridges. He had met these peoples sometimes on the Mesnes drenched with rain going to. Newton where they would have to wait sometimes a considerable time. —The CHAIRMAN suggested that Mr. Caldwell, the reliev- ing officer for Newton, should be called in to give infor- mation on the subject, but to this 'Mr. RATCLIFFE and Mr, Qwirs objected. They thought the Board ought to decide a matte? of that kind itself without asking the opinion of an officer.—Mr. GREENING moved that Mr. Caldwell be called into the room, Mr. OWEN moving a negative to this as an amendment. Five voted for both the amendment and tire motion, the Chairman giving his vote in favour of the latter.—The CHAIRMAN then explained the circumstances of the case' and in the course of his remarks Mr Ratcliffe interrupted.—Mr. GREENING, thereupon, said he thought such interruption was very much ,out of place.—Mr. RATCLIFFE said if he was wrong the Chairman would call him to order; he was not going to be called to order .by Mr. Green- ing.—The CHAIRMAN said Mr. Greening was quite right in speaking as he did to a pointof order. He (the Chairman) only wished to observe that they ought to deal with that matter in the same spirit and kindly feel- ing as they dealt with other questions that came before them. (Hear, hear.)—lt was then decided to refer the tnatter to the Newton Relief Committee to make a recommendation to the Board at is next meeting.
SCHOOLHISTRR&S FOR PADGATE SCHOOLS.

Two candidates—Miss Keay, of Manchester, and Miss S. M. French, of Ross, Herefordshire—for the post of schoolmistress at the Padgate School, had been invited to appear before the Board, but it was explained that Miss French had been unable o attend. h was there- fore decided to leave the appointment to the Schools Committee. • THE coursvv COUNCILS.—SUGGESTED CANDIbATE.

Mr. OWEN intimated that he intended to move the following resolution :--" That the Board recom- 'mend the name of Mr. J. C. Sutton, of Warrington and Frodsham, to the ratepayers of the Winwick division as a most fitting and suitable gentleman to represent them on the County Council."—The CLERK, however, pointed out that the Board of Guardians represented the whole Union and not merely that part comprised in the Win- wick electoral division. Speaking individually, he believed he should be qualified to sit in the County Council either for one of the distritts of Warrington or for the rural district, but lie did not know what his answer would be if the question was seriously put to him. But that Board sitting there for the whole Union could scarcely deal with the matter, but if the Rural Sanitary- Authority chose to consider the question for their own district (which comprises the Winwick elec- toral division) they would be quite competent to do so. It was for Mr. Owen to decide whether or not he would bring his proposal before that Authority, but he wotld he doing a personal fav,iur to him (the Clerk) by not bringing it forward at the Board of Guardians.—Mr. 0 waN said Mr. Sutton had been named to him by many- of the ratepayers in his own township (Croft) as a suitable gentleman to represent them in the County Conned. He would bring his motion forward •at meeting of the Rural Sanitary Authority.—The matter then dropped and the relief cases were next taken.

After some inquiries amongst other friends and many entreaties from Ursula that her brother should have his name entered at the college of which Fielding himself had a pleasant experience, Raymond, who had failed-in his first metric, Was de- spatched in the following January with rather too well-filled a purse, and plenary power to improve himself, to the College of D---, at Oxford. The interval had been an anxious one to all his friends; but the doctor by careful management had kept him well employed. "" In the College of D—, , as in most colleges, there were several sets of young men, varying in nature and pursuits. First there was a reading and intellectual set. This set was mainly composed of scholars. They were worthy young men. Besides their reading they found time for much enthn. siasm in the direction of literature and politics. They met weekly in one another's rooms and discussed obscure poets and -prose authors over tea and toast. Some of them had been beard to denounce • the Church of England in no measured terms, others even^ denied the light of their countenances to the College Chapel, thereby much vexing the soul of their dean. One of them had once tried to convert a muscular and orthodox member of the college to agnostie opinions, but had been picked up bruised and sorrow- ful by a free-thinking sympathiser at the bottom of the muscular one's staircase.

Some of them were rather lackina in worldly experience, apt to consider that the world was inhabited wholly by poets and poetaaters. Acting on this view of life, one of their number had onee invited a large part of the college to his .rooms and read M alt Whitman to them. Whereupon the college asserted its preference for good honest prose by ducking the young fellow under the college pump and Confiscating his library. They offered to "lend him some sense," and aent him a large collection of "yellow-backs" to begin with. After these experiences this set of young men had cooled intheirenthuaiasin for the regeneration of the rest of the college; sinking back into a resigned privacy. They would be the "illuminati"; and others who were perverse might grovel in the dark. They contented themselves therefore with meeting in, private, and eenstituted a sort of secret' tribunal for settling all politics, letters, morals, and theology for the benefit of their fellow undergraduates.' It was not their fault that the saisr undergraduates made no use of the results oftetheir deliberations —they had been generous and had been repulsed. Generally speaking they were regarded with a sort of Mild tolerance by the rest of the college. alley were not considered " form " of coursesand were excluded from " the set." But this exclusion was regarded as sufficient punishment for eccentricity and hete- rodoxy. In the eyes of "the set" it was a very severe punishment. • Personally, the latter could neVer imagine how anyone could exist outside their pale. They managed the ,college affairs, and were both socially and gymnastically leaders. They set the college "tone," and it was by no means a bad tone, for D— was far above the average as a college—a fact which Fielding had remembered when he , recommended it ,for Ray. They managed the boating, and made it a point of honour that the college should ,hold a good i place on the river. Next in mport:thee came the cricket; in this they also took care that the college should be well to the foie. They did not much care about the football. It was comparatively a new game. After the games, and in a proper place of subordination, came the "schools." They thought books inferior things; they would read them when they got older and could not play cricket, owing to the ,out. Like Wordsworth they thought reading a "dull and endless strife." However much a man read, there was always more coming. But it was prudent and wise not to get "ploughed " in the "schools." So "the set being, steady young fellows always took their passes regularly like doses of medicine. You would tee one of them looking a little iad and thoughtful for about a fottaight once a year, and you knew he was" getting through." After the fortnight he would look merrier than usual. He would -not have a school " on now,, for ages, you know." For the rest, these men played cards' a good deal, and drank a fair amount, but all in a steady regular sort of way. Ideal John Bulls, they were intensely patriotic,and would do anything for that vague aggregate" the college." They considered that to adopt any habits or opinions which had not been customary among their predeceSsers down to the third 'and fourth generation was a mai* ,of intensely bad form. Their own political opinions wore mainly hereditary. -They-ere Tories for the most part, since their fathers were Tories also. But if a man happened to be unfortunate enough to conic ot a Liberal stock, it was; considered excusable in him to hold Liberal opinions. Otherwise Liberalism or Radit &ism was looked upon merely as a form of conceit, 'originating in a desire to be different from anyone else, and waa treated adcordingly. As for religion, they went to chapel regulaile, and "intended to take orders" if they had family livings, or if they failed in everything e else.' They. accepted Christianity, as they would 'z' have. accepted Hindooiam or Mohametanistn, because it had been handed down to them, and would have been offended if reminded tat the " nobility " of earlier Christians "who searched to see that these things were so." It was not considered good form to talk about such things. They took their religion for granted, like their literature and their politics. All that was "shop." No decent man talked about- anythins but the weather, boating, and horses. If it got dull you could vary it with the seasons. What shOuld we do as a nation without our climate? Half of us *wild be dumb. • There was another set Which "Me set " looked upon with a disapproval no less severe than that with which it regarded "the reading set." That was the "fast set." " The set" occupied the mean position, the reading and fast sets were the two extremes. "The et" struck the via media for the re* of the college. Their's was the one way in which fathers were to walk. But unfortunately young elm re- semble their elders in liking to "gang their ain gait." Primarily and fundamentally the fast set differed from the rest of the college in having more money. The duty of spending it on themselves followed as a necessary economical consequence. Spending on others is condemned by all the best political econo- mists. When "the set" stood aghast at their extra- vagances, the fast set merely laughed. "They would do the same if they had as much money," was their comment on the selfrighteousness of their neighbours. They were not a bed lot as young men. go. They had no vugarity, and were necessarily free from priggishness as they had nothing to be priggish about. "'they lost their weeks ; they vexed the seeded deans; They rode; they betted; made a hundred friends; And caught the blossom of the flying toms." What did it matter.if they occasionally took more champagne than was good for timm ? It is mono- tonous, as one of their number always maintained with philosophical earnestness, to be always perpen- dicular. When Providence has given you two ways of progressing—this piing; sophist argued—one horizontal and the other perpendicular—why use one exclusively?, One of them occasionally disappeared like a Amaing star into space. Perhaps he was a scholar (not all scholara read) and the President of the College suggested that his scholarship was not gives him to spend on cigars and champagne. Which sug- gestion was sometimes, followed by a vacuum at the scholars' table—a nine days' gossip in college--and then things went as usual. The floods closed over his head, to change the metaphor, and to abandon it altogether, he went down. The fast set were great enemies to the peace of the reading set. When "honour mods" or "greats " were coming on, it Was their peculiar delight to hire all manner of instriunc. 's—" trumpets also and shawms "—from Gopoffsh she Polish music-seller's, in the klig, and to make night hideous in the Quad, and on the staircases of those who read. Copoilaki's instruments Were warranted to make a din which no number of oaken doors or wet towels would be proof against. But the manner of life spent by the fast , set, in order to be kept up in any consistent way at all, required a- constant supply of money. 01 course you could have credit to a considerable extent. But there was a limit to the extent, and the Vice-Chancellor's court loomed in an ugly way in the back-ground. Besides' when you went into lodgings "it was d unpleasant to' have duns occupying all the spare room at your breakfast table." Thus it frequently happened that a man would suddenly leave the fast set and settle down into sober reading ways. "Played out!" was the comment of his friends. Perhaps he had been,unlucky at cards, for you can lose a good deal at unlimited 100, ins dear reader, or at Ban John, though, of course you or I can only conjecture how much.. (I have thinly heard of a man

losing 2200 in one -night). Or perhaps agricultural or trade depression had ,played havoc with his estate, and he had to "draw in." Or perhar4 again, he had underc,alenlated the amount or money required , merely , to keep bitneelf and his friends supplied with ehameagee and cigars, and he was forced to change his frietelships in the direction of those who,metaphoricaily spenknie;, prefer locusts and wild honey to nectar and ambrosia. Such being the perils (4 the " fast set"' at D— .College, Oxford, these young fellows who devoted the flower of their youth to these ennobling pur- imits, eagerly welcomed anyone who came to the college flush of tin," combined with a similar view of lfe to their own. " 'Raymond was a recruit not to be despised. He would help the college to return to the golden days talked of by the "elder scouts" when • a score of gentlemen used to Inerlfast, in pink mornings,ind 200 would wine. together, evenings." And besides helpieg the call( „ in this vegne general was, ..he would help their net in particular in their lauda- ble desire to keep the ce!lege tom: above the sordid level at which. "Me t;eemell to aim. They would make him give hceps of wines—tell him it was the "proper He should be incited to procure the vcry- best cigars and the ' best Champagne. In fact, they would take him in hand early, as Johnson says yon must take a Scotchinan, and educate him up to thieltine that their way of life was the way of life for any undergraduate who de7 sired to be considered correct. "it is wonderful what you can do with a freshmen if you are only persever- ing." . Now Raymond was just such a lad as would make the most promising ciaccrt. As chance would have it, the fast set leteptned to Le very low in the world at the. time v. hen flay Janie up in all the gullibility of fresh manhood. One of their richest had lately " broheu," as we should say in another sphere of life. That is, his fatlorr and the college had suddenly discovered a ce,tain incompatibility between the state of the ;;;;:-k'llturol '...'rket and his personal expenditere. Lying a prudent man, and having a desire to take • ,his--elegree ",after all that trouble, you know. I had over past mods " (which he bad surmounted n.ter thtee . etveral attempts), and having also FiJel!'7lt 1412il:AC of honour to refrain from his friends leispitAlity when circumstances pre- yented him five' retnrning it in kind, he had retired, toti to areal:, on .half-pay, and was now living in a quiet way in St. Gilee'r. His Immo was Grant, and he lived in the saute louse with Fielding,who indulged somewhat sparsely in his company, but found him- . useful. Fielding was in his fourth year, and was now reading for.. honours--classical ;Teats. He was 6 scholar, but not a very gregarious man, and had always managed to keep out of any particular set at college, liking none of them e,ulliciently to reserve himself entirely to the company of any one, but, at the saute time, from an outside point of view, seeing the merits of each.. He had a great influence in the college for good in e, strong, quiet sort of way. Ile was loolied up to se the strongest int-dlectualforce. He led the Liberal party in the college del tiles, but never sacrificed hi, influence by the enunciation of extreme . views. Ail sets equally Jeoked 'upon him as a very decent 'chapteyho never boated or was .priggish, or gave him- self airs. Nobody ignored him. He was not a quantit6 to use a political phrase. He was a good -athte—had rowed in the College Torpid; and was one' df the hest cricketers in the college-e-notbing adds to the esteem with which an undergraduate is regarded by his fellows so much as gymnastic ability. Everybody can understand it.
( To- be continued.)

i THE PA lINKLL COMMISSION. WARNING TO THE PRESS. The Parnell Commission resumed its sitting on Tues- day morning, in the Probate Court, London. The in- terest taken in the proceedines appeared unaltered, and the Court commenced to fill immediately the doors were opened; a large proportion of the visitors who took seats in the gallery being ladies. Mr. Parnell and Mr. Devitt were among the first te arrive, and were soon followed by officials, cwansel, Pressmen, and persons Whose names are closely associated with the Commis- • eion ; so that by the time the judges put in an appear- ' ince the Court was full. The Attorney-General, who held a newspaper in h:s band, and pointed to a paragraph which he did not read, wed he had no wish to refer to such matters, or take any Steps regarding them unless it was absolutely necessary ! but having regard to the nature of these paragrapbs, he thought that their lordships should express some ?pinion, for it might become necessary for him to bring oefore the court evidence of the intimidation that was being practised to prevent witnesses giving evidence be- fore the Commission. He would remind their lordships that one of the persens named in the paragraph was a Person charged in the charges that had been made by. 2he Times. • The President was handed the newspaper, and he Perused it for some moments. The AttorneylGeneral again speaking, said he did not iutroduce the matter because he wished to interfere 'with any publication, but because it might be necessary to stop any proceedings which might have the effect of carrying on still further that which he should at some time bring before their lordships—clearly the intimida- tion of witnesses. Sir Charles Russell said he also had some matters to refer to, and alluded to the advertisement in The Times, regarding the pamphlet on " Parnellism and Crime," and the letter attributed to Mr. Parnell. The President: I should think it desirable, not only ila the interests of the undisturbed course of justice, but in the interests of the persons themselves, that I should say this much—that if it can be established that the language reported here has been used, it amounts to in- tinildation of the clearest possible kind, and would sub- ject the persons guilty of using such to the action of the court. I am willing to let it pass, as the Attorney- General only invites opinion. Let me then express the hope that those who seek to guide public opinion will abstain during the inquiry, which imposes upon me a burden which 1 feel very doubtful whether I can sus- tain. I do entreat both parties to abstain from comment and to leave us undisturbed in the performance of the' Painful duty we have undertaken. The President afterwards alluded to Sir Charles Rumen's observations about The Times, and said he hoped that in whatever The Times published during the Commission, in reference to the letter, the word " alleged" would be introduced. Sir Charles Russell disclaimed all knowledge, on the part of his clients, of any acts of intimidation. Mr. Alfred Chester Ives, formerly London correspon- dent of the New York Herald, was then sworn. He pro- duced a copy of the paper containing a report of at. interview between himself and Mr. Parnell in 1880, when various Irish matters were discussed, but the cross- examination of the witness was deferred until to- morrow, when the witness will produce a transcript of his notes. John Reflerte, of Moseand, Galway, was next put into ' the box, and said he took land in 1879, the previous tenant of which had settled with the landlord. In June of the following year his house was entered by moon- lighters. Sir Charles Russell, interrupting, asked what connec- tion this outrage had with the parties charged by The Times. He objected to any evidence, unless a direct , connection was shown. t 'rhe President remarked that it would be necessary to lay down some definite lines as to the, evidence to be celled respecting these outrages, and suggested that the , question should be settled at once. The learned Counsel then argued the matter at length. The President afterwards said the difficulties were _ such that they must merely rely upon the discretion of learned counsel not to call more evidence than was t , necessary. Rafferty then continued his evidence, and said that ~ the moonlighters illtreated both him and his wife, and ' said lie ought to give up his land, but he still held it. Cross-examined, witness said he could not ,say that the Land League had anything to do with this outrage. He did not think it had. They were not injuxed by the Outrage. Re-examined, Rafferty said he WAX ill for a month after the outrage, hut went about his work. The moon- lighters scraped nails down his back. Sub-Inspector Barry, of the lri3h constabulary, spoke of the shooting of Peter Demeeey in 1881 after having taken an evicted farm ne-r Loughrea. Wit- ness. in cross-examination, denied that there was any general feeling among the people against land-grabbers. Before 1879 there might have been individual cases. He had no distinct recollection of Mr. Michael Devitt warning the people at Loughrea against outrage in 1879. --Re-examined, witness said he had frequently heard land-grabbers denounced at/ Land League meetings, I)ernpsey's widnw kept on tier husband's farm, but had tr, be protected by the police. Mrs. Dempsey, a very respectable-looking woman, was next called. She confirmed the evidence of Barry, and Spoke generally of the had treatment she received from neighbours, who practically boycotted her. Confirmatory evidence having been given by one ' Patrick Hughes, , ' Mrs. Julia Connors, widow of James Connors, said her L husband took some bog land, after a tenant had received ' notice to quit, near Loughrea. The neighbours after- wards boycotted them, and they had to get their food through the police and shortly afterwards . her husband 'was mtwdered while they were driving together to the funeral of witness's father. The neigh. hours did not attend the funeral of her husband, and continued to boycott her. She knew three of her hus- band's murderers. They were tried, but acquitted. , The Court at this point adjourned for luncheon. - After the luncheon interval, the witness Hughes was recalled, and said he hod often seen the men Ryan. Keogh, and Fahy, namco by Mrs. Connors as the mur- derers of her husband, taking part in Land League meetings. John Lewis, a magistrate, living near Woodford, said the relations between landlord and tenant were good in that district before the establishment of the Land League. Re spoke, as his mother's agent, ot the difficulty he afterwards had in obtaining the rent; and of an attack on his house, after there had been a National League meet- ing in the neighbourhood. Witness's wife was threatened by Father Fahy, who said he would be murdered; and witness was boycotted. This was during 1886:and 1887. John Lambert, a Galway landlord, said he had lived in the county since 1849, and never knew the tenants to , be threatened for paying their rents before 1879. Witness was boycotted. and fired at in 1881, because of di-putes With his tenants. Flis.men were obliged by the Land League not to work for him, and his houses had been A burned down. Thomas White, the next witness called, caused con- siderable amusement by his bearing in court. His ell. deuce was nearly ell unintelligible, but he was under- stood to say that his sister, himself, his father, and his father's public-house were boycotted, because his sistet married a man employed by Mr. Lewis. The witness e.aused frequent bursts of laughter, and the Presider." himself could not in view of the ludicrous incident, fine it in him to check the merriment. Witness at length produced a piece of paper on which he said a Mr. Lewis had written down his (witness's) evidence. Mr. Lockwood took possession of the paper, but did not read it out, and a series of further questions failed to draw anything from the witness that could be under- stood hes-end the fact that. his family was boycotted. Bartholomew Coursey, a 'police sergeant, gave evidence as to the Land League meetings at Woodford, the mur- der of the man Finlay, and the boycotting of Finlaye widow. The court then adjourned. WEDNDSDAY. The Commission was occupied on Wednesday in hear- ing the evidence of police officers as to outrages which had occurred in county Galway since 1880. • One of the Principal witnesses was District Inspector Allan Bell, who stated that in the district of Athenry trouble gener- ally followed the holding of Land League meetings. Sir' Cliarles Russell cross-examined the witness to show that I the crimes occurred only on estates where landlord and tenants were at variance, and the witness gave the names of several estates upon which there had been few ' evictions and practically no crime. Mr. Ives, correspon- -' dent of the "New York Herald," was cross-examined . as to the interviews between himself, Mr. Parnell. and Mr. Dillon, and he said that Mr. Parnell had never during conversation suggested his reliance upon outrages. THURSDAY. Matthias Kerrigan, whose testimony had to be given through an interpreter, spoke of the murder of the bailiff Fluddy and his nephew in 1882. Mrs. Kerrigan also gave evn'ence, and was followed by members of the Irish police force, who were called with a view to con- necting the Land League with the outrages. Evidence 'was also given by several other witnesses, one of whom, , Thomas Connaire, farmer, . said his house was burnt down in November, 1880, and that he received £BO com- pensation, but the reason of his house being burnt was unknown to him.

A lANnON MOB AND YR. DAVITT. • After the rim ng of the Commission, Mr. Michas., Davin was the suoject of a hostile demonstration. A amall crowd followed him along the Strand, crying out. " Convict." Mr. Davitt stopped once or twice and faced the mob, but otherwise took no notice of the demon. Siration, to which he did not seem to attach serious importance. He finally reached his lodgings, in cous- PanY with a friend, without further molestation. GOVERNMENT OFFER TO THE DYNAMITERS. The Freeman's Journal states that the Government re• "ently made overtures. on behalf of The Times, to tilt lYnamiters in Chatham prison, with a view to inducing :hem to give evidence, if they were able, connecting any trish members, or prominent Nationalists, with th. dynamite conspiracies. They were promised release iss the event of giving the sort of testimony required, or they craild give information which would lead to the discovery of such evidence. The prisoners, however, ail refused to give any information.

div.p: COLLIERY ExPLOSION IN FRANCE. - SEVENTY-THREE LIVES LOST.

PARIS, SUNDAY NIGHT.—One Of the greatest colliery explosions ever known in France took place on Friday night in the colliery of Cransac, in the Aveyron. The accident took place at a depth of 5001 t. in the St. Bar bara's pit. Soon after a rescue party was sent down it brought up 23 bodies and three wounded men. Half an hour later nine more bodies, reduced almost to pulp, were raised from below, and later in the night, or rather morning, 41 more. Only three of these could be Went'. ded. A gallery of 340 yards in length fell in during the explosion. THE SLAVE TRADE IN AFRICA.

BERLIN, MONDAY I,BGHT.—Yestorday, the conatitutios of the African Union of German Catholics took place under the presidency of the Archbishop of Cologne.. Cardinal Lavigere presented the union with a donation of 50,000 marks from the Pope. The General Missionare Review and some of the daily papers publish articles deprecating the intended anti-slavery expeditions. The sending of some hundreds of volunteers to suppress the. slave trade in Central Africa is, they maintain, only playing at war, and in Africa such play is doubly dan- gerous. The advance of Europeans into the interior will, they say, only make matters worse, and fan the sparks which have appeared here and there into flame. An evil a thousand years old cannot be suppressed with one blow of the sword. The slavery question can only be solved slowly, and with the greatest precaution and patience. These two essential qualitier are unfor- tunately, they add, wanting in the modern colonial policy of Germany.

THE ACCIDENT TO THE CZAR'S TRAIN. Sr. PETFRSBO 1/ O, SATOFDAY.—The Officio/ ../tfesseng., this morning states that in the accident to the Imperial train the Czar was injured on the foot, and the Czarina on the hand. Of the attendants, 21 were killed out- right, one died subsequently, and 37 wee seriously 6- jured. The Czar picked up a piece of a rotten sleeper at the spot, and handed it to an officer of Gendarmerie. to be produced at the official investigation. ODESSA, SATIN/DAL—According to intelligence whith. has reached here, M. Alenikoff, the manager of the Can- cassian Railway, Upon which the Czars' train was recently wrecked, has blown his brains out with a re- volver. The catastrOplic at Reda had completely un- hinged his mind. BERLIN, SUNDAY Nun-tr.—The Ta ghlatt learns from -vell-informed source, in St. Petersburg that the Czar attributes the principal blame for the recent disaster to himself. The train had been delayed an hour and a h•Jf, and the Emperor gave orders for it to be made up by increasing the speed. The engine drivers warned -Admiral Possiet, the Minister of Ways, of the danger of doing this. When the order was repeated, they increased the speed somewhat. By special order they at last ran versts an houroafter, having declared that trains could only run ffil versts an Mut as the line was not well laid. The Czar ordered them to be doubly cautious. As his Majesty gave the order himself, Admiral Possiet is reproached for not having sufficiently supported the engine driver's warning. ST. PETF.RSETO3II, TSIONOAT. —After his return here the Czar issued a manifesto deela ring that his Mr jesty share,' with his people the feelings of thankfulness to God for his miraculous esosne.
PRESIDENTIAL ELECTION-RETURN OF GENERAL
HARRISON:

NEW YORB.—WEDNESDAY.—The Republican party in the United States has been successful in the Presidential election. The "New York Herald," the organ of the Democratic party, announced on Tuesday morning that General Harrison has been elected, the figures received up to that time showing the following condi- tions of matters in the Electoral College :—Electors for Harrison, 207 ; for Cleveland, 168 ; doubtful 26. Later telegrams affirm the fact of General Harrison's success, and give his electoral vote as 218, while Mr. Cleveland has only 183 votes. NEW Yorat, TEURSDAY.—The election of General Harrison as President of the United States is now placed beyond all question. He received 233 electoral votes, against Mr. Cleveland's 168. The Republican papers claim that their party have secured a decided majority i n the Huse of Representatives. - GENERAL HARRISON'S CAREER.

General Benjamin Harrison, of Indiana, is a grandson of President W. H. Harrison, of Indiana, a great-grand- son of one of the signers of the Declaration of independence, and a descendent of Harrison who signed the-death-warrant of Charles 1., and was afterwards executed at Charing Cross. He was born in Ohio ig 1833, and was educated for the career of a lawyer. In 1853, when he was only twenty years of age, he married Miss C. L, Scott, the daughter of an Ohio clergyman. He removed to Indianapolis in 1854, and afterwards became a reporter of the Indiana Supreme Court. By that time he had already commenced to take part in politics. He entered he Union Army as second-lieuten- ant at the opening of the rebellion and served throughout the war, being mustered out i n 1865 with the rank of briga- dier-general, which had been conferred upon him for his gallant conduct at the battle of Peachtree Creek. In 1880 he was elected Governor of Indiana, and in the following year he became United States SeLator for Indiana, in 1880, and served six years, being beaten in the next election by Mr. David Tarpie, Democrat. Like Mr. Cleveland, he is an Advocate of civil service . reform.

div.head: I DISASTROUS COLLISION IN THE
div.p: I DISASTROUS COLLISION IN THE
CHANNEL

On Sunday, the survivors of the crew of the steamer Saxmundharn, of Newcastle (Captain Milne, ma(ter), and of the Norwegian barque Nor. of Tonsberg, were landed at Weymouth, their vessels having been in collision at two a.m. thirty miles eastanorth.east of St. Catherine's Point. It appears that the steamer, which is of 1,832 toms, left Newcastle on Friday fnr Ancona with coal and coke, and everything proceeded well until Sunday morning, when she was run into amidships by the Nor, 798 tons. bourfidfrom Stettin with petroleum. The effects of the collision Were so serious that within ten minutes the steamer foundered. Almost immediately after the cellision' the Saxmundham's jolly-boat was successfully launched, after which the starboatd lifeboat was launched. At this time, the stern of the steamer being under water, tan men got into the jolly-boat, and five into the lifeboat The remainder were engaged in endeavouring to launch the port lifeboat, but, owing to the heavy sea, they were unsuccessful, and before another boat could he got out the ship went down. Captain Milne, the second engineer; and one of the firemen were afterwards picked up by one of the boats, and efforts were made to save other men, but without success. The boats afterf wards cruised about, and hailed the captainnf the ,Nor, but did pot get any reply. The chief mate, who was in charge of the jollyboat, warned those in the lifeboat not to go near the barque, as she appeared to he foundering. and they accordingly left her. The two boats cruised about tor some time befnre it was decided to pull for t. Catherine's. It is said that the jollyboat sienelled R barque showing a light, so that jt is probable that some of the missing men got on hoard, hit no tidings have come to haind. At daybreak, the men in the lifeboat were picked up by the schooner waterbini, and landed at Weymouth, and during the afternoon the whole of the crew of the Norwegian barque were landed et, Portland. The names of the eight men belonging to the Sa.Nlnundlatrn now at Wey- mouth are Captain Milne, Mr. Nicholson, second en. gineer ; Mr. Jackaon, third engineer; Thomas Patterson. fireman; W. Mc.Kenzie, J. Mc.Farren, W. Mc.Alieter, and E. Saunders, seamen. The steamer had a crew of 30 nll told, so that 22 remain to be accounted for. A barque flying signs of distress was observed off Vontnor on Suit. day morning. This was probably the Nor, as that yews was subsequently found abandoned, and when last seen was drifting towards the shore. . Captain Hassen flintiness, master of the Nor, has mace a statement at Weymouth, in which he says his ship war, on a voyage from New York to Stettin. Ile left America on October 2nd, and all went well until Sunday morning. when, at about 2 30, in clear weather, his ship was run into by the Saxmundharn, injOring her to such an extent that he was obliged to attar:a:A, 1.e.. The steamer sank, hut. he and his crew took to their boat, and stood by the Nor. At daybreak,, as she still fated. some of the cress boarded her again, and tried to get her before the wind. The steamer Jupiter afterwards catne by, and atterant.eii to take the barque in tow; but the line parted. ;Two other steamers were afterwards spoken. and asked to take the barque in tow, but thay declined. Al lasi, when the vessel threatened to founder. she was *halt :toned, at eleven o'clock in the foronocn, and me crew were afterwards picked up by the steamer tiliagbrook-. and lauded at Portland.

A YORKSHIRE TRAGEDY.—The wife of James Pennock, platelayer, whose home was in a gatehouse near Picker- ing, North Yorkshire, was found in bed murdered On Wednesday. There was a fearful wound on her temple; and on the kitchen floor an axe, blood-s ained, was lying. The woman's husband is missing; and the supposition is that he murdered her in ungovernable rage fostered by jealousy.
