div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 1888.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER 10, 1888.

varied, and who has been honoured by the con- fidence of the Liberals of the country as I have been honoured in being chosen to be their leader during what is now a lengthened period. I do not deny that some special facilities must necessarily accrue to him in rendering services to this great and very special and peculiar case of Imperial interests and obligations. (Hear, hear.) On that account I have thought it my duty never to whisper to myself such a word as that of retirement from public life—(cheers)— so long as the Irish question is at issue, and so long as health and strength are continued to me in a measure sufficient to enable me to hope that I may be of use in promoting a solution. But having said that, gentlemen, let me add another word. I must emphatically dissent from all those who may regard my continuance in public life as an essential element in this great controversy. The deputation shortly afterwards withdrew.

In the course of the afternoon Mr. Gladstone drove to Hag,ley Park, the seat of Lord Lyttleton, where he re- mained to lunch. On the way there he left Mrs. Glad- stone at Watley Hall, where a reception was held by i Mrs. H. G. Reid n connection with the meeting of the Women's Liberal Federation, which had been held earlier in the day. On his return in the evening a presentation was made to Mr. Gladstone on behalf of the working men of Bir- mingham, the present taking the form of a number of .necimens of Birmingham manufacture. Mr. Eli Bloor, Chairman of the Working Men's Committee, presided. Mr. B. Cannon read an address to Mr. Gladstone, ask. tog his acceptance of the gifts, and reading a list of trades represented by the deputation. Mr. CiLADSTONE, who was received with cheers, said: Allow me to say, in the very first place, that it is with particular satisfaction that I find myself associated with my wife, the partner of nearly 50 years—cheers)—and any further years that please God He may grant to us, and I may venture to assure you all, and with most per- fect and absolute truth, that in the statements which I .hall endeavour to lay before you she participates as fully and as warmly as if she had the most formal and largest share in their utterance. You were good enough to mention my career associated with the motto of yowr town, which is the significant word "Forward." My career has been a very long one. I have done much in the public service, and not all of it wise, but at the same time I have, during the 56 years of my public life, at all times acted for the best, according to such light as I possessed. (Cheers.) Your chairman has spoken of two obstacles in the way of the industry of this town, one of them which is commonly known to the public under the name of railway rates, and the second, that of technical education. With regard to railway rates, you have seen that there is a disposition on the part of Par- liament to afford all such aid as can be practicably made available. I cannot say that any wonderful results are to be expected from the intervention of Parliament, hut I do hope that a gradual diminution and mitigation of di ffl- nultieo will be found. As to technical education. there is a strong disposition to supply what is lacking in that respect. For my own part, I hope that as far as can be found convenient, that will be done upon the responsibility, and with the close and vigilant supervision, of local effort.

be made use of, for the attainment of the object they had in view. The right hon. gentleman afterwards proceeded by train to West Bromwich, and was met by the Hon. Philip Stanhope, whose guest be will be till Saturday. He was greeted on his arrival by a large crowd. Replying to a number of addresses, he urged that the balance against the Liberal party at the last election did 'not reflect .the true sense of the population, but was brought about by the operation of plural votes held by property owners. The result of this was that Ireland still groaned under coercion, and had to lament a system of administration which in England would not be tolerated for a week. He had no misgiving whatever as to the result of a general election, and when the time came he trusted that the Liberals of that district would share in the general victory. Mr. Gladstone's drive through the Black Country—which was so arranged as to bring him 'in touch with most of the large towns between West Bromwich and Wolverhampton—occupied two hours and a half, the distance covered being fourteen miles. At Wednesbury, Bilston, Darlaston, Deepfields, and Sedgley large crowds had assembled, and the right hon. gentle- I man met wi h an enthusiastic reception. There was, however, no speech-making, nor were any addresses presented. The weather was dull, and at the close of the journey foggy. NATIONAL LIBERAL CONFERENCE. On Tuesday, the eleventh annual meeting of the Council of the National Liberal Federation commenced at Birmingham, Sir James Kitson presiding. The Chair- man, in moving the adoption of the report, pointed to the welcome given to Mr. Gladstone as a justification of the decision of the Council to hold its meeting in Birmingham. Resolutions were adopted rejoicing in the progress of the Home Rule movement, condemning the harsh and capricious administration of the Crimes Act, and objecting to a further grant of money by Parliament for piecemeal extension of the Irish Land Purchase Act of 1885. WEDNESDAY.

At Wednesday's meeting of the National Liberal Federation a resolution was passed declaring it to be of the first importance that the franchise should be based solely on the principle of "one man one vote," and that the laws of registration should be so amended as to ensure to every citizen his electoral rights. The Council further recorded its opinion that the duration of Parlia- ments should be shortened, that returning officers' expenses at Parliamentary elections should be placed upon the rates, and that all elections should be held upon one and the same day. The Council condemned the proposals of the majority of the Education Com- mission, urged the necessity of immediate legislation for the provision of technical education, continuation schools, and intermediate education, and reaffirmed its opinion that all elementary education should be free. Resolutions were also passed on various other subjects, the Council expressing a hope that an early settlement of the Irish question would enable Parliament to devote its attention to those reforms upon which the Federation has repeatedly declared itself, among them being the land question, Welsh disestablishment, local option, and the House of Lords. Sir George Trevelyan, speaking to one of the resolutions, said the Liberal party had lost some men whom they regretted; others, again, were better away; but in any case the process was a healthy one, inasmuch as those who remained were taught self-reliance. Sir William Harcourt also spoke. The present, he said, was a critical moment in the history of the Liberal party. No doubt schisms had taken place. but these, however much to be deplored, had not touched the heart of the 'Liberal party, nor would they affect seriously the political history of he party or of the country. The secession of the Dissentients would, how- ever, not be without its effect on the future. He regarded it as the final departure of the Whigs from the Liberal camp; and inasmuch as the Whig connection had derived its force from popular support the inevitable consequence, if the seceders joined the Tory party, would be to give an immense impulse to democratic reforms.

div.head: !A.R. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO BIRMING-
div.p: !A.R. GLADSTONE'S VISIT TO BIRMING-
HAM.

Mr. Gladstone, who was accompanied by Mrs. Glad- stone, the Bev. Harry and Mrs. Drew, drove, on Monday, to Saltnev station, near Chester, whence they proceeded, at 11 10 a.m., by special Great Western train, conducted by Superintendent Morris and Inspector Brooks, to Birmingham. The assembled crowd cheered Mr. Gladstone on his arrival and departure. Mr. Gladstone appeared to be in the best of health and spirits. Wellington, at which the only stoppage in the journey was made, was reached at 12 27. At many of the stations en route small crowds had assembled in the hope of catching a glimpse of the right hon. gentleman as the train passed. The platforms at RuabonWhd Shrews- bury were lined with people, the train going through at a slow rate of speed. At Ruabon the spectators took off their bats or waved handkerchiefs, and at Shrews- bury there was much cheering. The weather was bright. A large crowd assembled at Wellington, where a table, furnished with luncheon, had been laid out in the six foot way. There was great cheering as the train drew •ip at the platform. Captain Patceett and Mr. Moore presented an address on behalf of the Wellington and Shrewsbury Liberals respectively, and there were loud cries for a speech. Mr. GLADSTONE contenteil himself with replying in a conversational tone. He said he received the addresses with great pleasure. He was delighted to observe, on perusing them, that they fully recognised that the Irish question was really the English, Scotch, and Welsh ques- tion, and that, without a'settlement ot it, there could be , neither solid peace nor effectual progress in this country.

--;1:ie-ClOors of the Town Hall were opened shortly after 12 o'clock, and from that time forward ticket-holders arrived in a continuous stream until the spacious build- ing was packed in every corner. During the long inter- val of waiting the selection of popular and patriotic airs was given on the organ. The object of the meeting was to enable the Birmingham Liberal Association to present an address to Mr. Gladstone. Mr. Osier, presi- dent of the Association, presided; and in addition to the gentlemen mentioned above there were on the plat- form Mr. Shaw-Lefevre, M.P., Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., Mr. Winterbotham, M.P„ Mr. A. Tangye, Mr. Allard, Lady Foster, and Mrs. Osier. Mr. Gladstone arrived at the Town Hall at 1 50, and immense crowds of people lined the streets to see the right hon. gentleman pass, and his progress from the railway station was marked by one continued roar of cheers, intermingled with groans and hisses at some points. Thanks to the barricades, and the admirable police arrangements, the people were kept in check. At, the Town Hall Mr. Gladstone's appearance on the plat- form was the signal for an immense display of enthusiasm. Deafening cheers lasted for several minutes. and when this outburst had subsided the organ struck up "Auld Lang Syne," the whole audience rising and joining in the refrain.
The CHAIRMAN, in his introductory remark; referred to Mr. Gladstone as our revered leader, when there was renewed cheering. Be afterwards made the presentation of the address.

Mr. Gtansroxii, in response, said there was one phrase in the address which touched him to the heart. It was where the address expressed the pleasure of the Birmingham Liberal Association at welcoming him "once more" to Birmingham. That threw Lis mind back to eleven years ago. He came to Birmingham now, as he did then, and received expressions of good - will from assembled thousands which were not to be mistaken. Birmingham to-day, however, was not in all respects the Birmingham of other times. When he was last in the town the Liberal party were represented as being the enemies of England, they were now reproached with a desire to separate the different portions of the Empire. &kb of those accusations were big and bold accusations, hut for his part he thought that one of them was worth just as much as the other. (Cheers.) Upon one of those questions the country some time after had the opportunity of pronouncing an opinion, and they knew what. that sentence was. Upon the other they would also have an opportunity, and they in Birmingham would have no small share of responsibility in the determination of what the verdict should be. (Cheers.) The majority against them Was 96; it had been 116. (Cheers.) It required 48 ,rotes to be transferred, end of that number Bir- mingham possessed nne-seventh. Whatever efforts Bir- mingham might make to alter and amend tier representation he hoped nothing would ever induce her to forget the splendid and long-Continued services of John Bright. (Cheers.) He was sure everybody in Birmingham would join him in the hearty wish and ' prayer, that it might please the Almighty God to raise him from the bed of sickness; and restore him to health and vigour. (Renewed cheers.) Passing on to the work of the House of Commons, Mr. Gladstone maintained that the 'autumn session was entirely the fault, of the Government, which left only seven nights to private memhers. The Government had been enabled to pass the National Debt Bill. They were told that the National Debt, Bill was the work of the Liberal Unionists. But he and Mr. Childers had assisted at its passage, so they had no claim upon it. The Liberal Unionists had no need to claim this measure in order to show that they had been busy. The Liberal Unionists could claim that great and glorious trophy, the Coercion Act—(cheers and laughter)—pa aged for the pur- pose of altering the law of the land so as to make rents more easy of collection, and in order to keep 16 Irish members of Parliament in prison. They were told that the Local Government MI also was passed with the assistance of the Liberal Unionists, but Mr. Ritchie said that the GovernMent were indebted to the Opposition for the assistance they gave in passing the bill. (Cheers.) He said the ultimate result. of the Irish question was sure, but' what was better than sure WAS that it was just and right, Their aim was to bind toge- ther England and Ireland by those bonds which alone were permanent, and to establish in our dealings all round the world, beyond our shores and within them. the supreme rule of those principles by which alone it was impossible to make an empire strong. (Loud cheers.) The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to Mr. eladstone, who briefly replied. Notwithstanding Mr. Gladstone's great exertions on Monday he appeared in good health on Tuesday, although it was noticed during his speech, in reply to the pre- sentation of an address from the Walsall Liberal Associa- tion, that his voice WAS somewhat hoarse. Yesterday morning Sir Walter and Lady' Foster, with whom Mr. and Mrs, Gladstone are staying at Ashfield, Hagley-road. entertained a large party at breakfast- Among those invited to meet the right hon. gentleman were the Earl of Aberdeee. F.arl Compton, Sir J. Carmichael, Mr. Cobb, M.P., Mr. Schwann. M.P., Mr. Ca.uston, M.P., Mr. Waddv, M.P., Mr. Colman, M.P., Mr. R. Tangye, Mr. Jos..Arch. and others. Shortlwafter breakfast Mr. Richd. Tangye presented to Mr. Gladstone. as a personal gift. a beauti- ful Malacca silver-mounted cane which he had brought home from Australia. The head of the cane was formed by a magnificent chrysolite. bearing an engraved por trait. of the right lion. gentleman. Mr. Gladstone accepted the gift with great pleasure, observing that it was the finest stick he had ever seen. The cane was also admired by Mrs: Gladstone.

Advantage was taken of the fact that Mr. Gladstone was the guest of Sir Walter Foster. the president of the Walsall Liberal Association, to present him with an illu- minated address from the members of the association. A deputation, consisting of Alderman Holden and Mr. W. Bayliss, waited upon the right hon. gentleman, at Sir Walter Foster's residence, during the morning, and were received by Mr. Gladstone in the library. Mr. Gladstone was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, Miss Gladstone, Sir Walter and Lady Foster. the'Earl of Aberdeen, Earl Compton, Sir Chas. Forster, M.P., Sir Jas. Carmichael, Mr. C. E. Schwann, M.P., Mr. R. Carston, M.P., Mr. S. D. Waddy. Q.C., M.P., Mr. 3. J. Colman, M.P., Mr. H. P. Cobb, M.P., Mr. T. B. Potter. M.P., Alderman Cook. Alderman Manton, Messrs. R. Tangye, A. Albright, H. G. Reid, and Joseph Arch. Sir CITAI4I.I2S FOSTIM. MT.. in introducing the deputa- tion, said there Was no constituency in the country more devoted to Mr. Gladstone than Walsall. (Hear, hear.) Personally, he had, during HS long Parliamentary career, been unswerving in his fidelity to Mr. Gladstone, and he looked forward to the time when he would be called upon to settle the Irish question. The question could never be settled except by Mr. Gladstone, and it, would be the crowning act of a great career, which had always been devoted to the interests of the country. (Cheers.) Alderman Borns"; then read the address, which was beautifully illuminated on vellum, and hound in self- coloured pigskin, lined with blue silk. Mr. W. BAYLISS said the deputation approached Mr. Gladstone with the deepest and sincerest feelings of loyaity. He could say that Mr. tiladstone's name was very dear to the Liberal population of Walsall. They look to him with feelings of confidence, and their sincere prayers were that his valuable life might be spared, to accomplish the object he had set before him, and they hoped his life might be spared to the country for many years. (A ppla se. 1

Mr. GLADSTONE was received with cheers on rising to acknowledge the presentation. He said Sir Charles Foster and Gentlemen,-1 need not tell you that I have been accustomed for a great many years to look upon Walsall as a model constituency. You have been good enough to speak of my position in reference to the present political attitude of the country. T am here in the midst of political commotion and contention, at a period of life when nature dictates repose, and it has been upon grounds altogether exceptional. While have felt that the self-governing energies of this coun- try as a general rule are wholly independent of the action of this or that particular individual, ypt the case of Ireland is altogether a special case. Any one who has so long sat in Parliament as I have done, and has had so much to do with the case of Ireland in one shape and another, owes a debt of gratitude to her—a debt of a very special kind. It is also a debt to the empire, and I do not disguise the fact that one whose experience in Irish matters has been so long and

div.head: GREAT MEETING IN BINGLEY HALL.
div.p: GREAT MEETING IN BINGLEY HALL.

The long-expected and elaborately-arranged meeting in Bingley Hall, under the auspices of the National Liberal Federation, took place on Wednesday evening. The doors were opened soon after six o'clock, when a continuous stream of people—estimated at 18,000— poured inte the vast hall, soon filling it in every part. The multitude watched with the keenest interest the arrival of the principal persons on the platform, and those whose faces were recognised were enthusiastically greeted as they came forward to take their seats. Mean- while several political and other songs were sung with huge gusto, the singing being led by a brass band stationed in the centre of the hall. Cheers were also lustily given for the illustrious visitor whose utterances were being 'eagerly awaited. In this way the time was pleasantly passed until the arrival of Mr. Gladstone. The patience of the vast crowd was at length rewarded when Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, accompanied by the other distinguished visitors, were seen to emerge from the reception room at the rear of the platform. The throng at once burst forth into a perfect tumult of cheering as Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone and their friends took their .seats. This demonstration Was accompanied by a striking spectacle, only to be appreciated by those on the platform, of a waving forest of hats and handkerchiefs. Round fol- Towed round of enthusiastic cheering. and Mr. Gladstone (who was wearing a heavily fur-trimmed overcoat) stood forward and several times smilingly bowed his acknowledgmnits. " He's a jolly good fellow" was then struck up and rendered with great heartiness by the multitude, who had not yet exhausted their pent- up feelings in welcoming the ex-Premier. Mr. A. C. Oster (Chairman of the Birmingham Liberal Federation) presided. and there were on the platform, in addition to Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, Earl Spencer, the Earl of Rosebery, the Marquess of Ripon, the Earl of Aberdeen, Earl Compton, Lord Wodehouse, the Hon. P. Stanhope, M.P., Sir G. Trevelyan, M.P., Sir W. Har- court, M.P:, Sir U. Ka.y-Shuttleworth, M.P., Sir A. and Lady Hayter, Sir H. Roscoe, M.P., Sir W. Lawson, M.P., Sir J. Kitson, Sir W. Plowden, M.P., Sir J. Carmichael, Sir Walter Foster, MY.; the Right HODS. H. C. E, Childers, M.P. ; John Morley, M.P., G. 0. Morgan, M.P., A. J. Mundella, M.P. H. Campbell-Bannerman, M.P., and H. H. Fowler; Messrs. H. Gladstone, M.P., Arnold Morley, M.P., W. B. McLaren, M.P., A. J. Williams, M P., Halley Stewart, M.P., R. K. Causton, M.P. ; W. Woodall, M.P., C. Crompton, Q.C., T. D. Sullivan, M.P., *S. T. Brunner, M.P., ,T. P. Price, M.P., Professor J. Stewart, M.P., C. E. Schwann, M.P., Handel Cossham, M.P. ; the Revs. Harry Drew. Dr. Crosskey, C. Leach, E. F. M. MacCarthy, and W. Tuckwell • Alderman Barratt, Colonel Tomkinson, Messrs. F. SC.hnadhorst, I R. Tangye, H. G. Reid, C. B. M'Laren, R. Leake, J. Edge (Burslem), F. Wright, and Councillors Eli Bloor, Wallis, and Martineau. Mr. Gladstone, replying to a resolution of confidence, denied that Home Rule was dead. The Irish must, and did, he said, resent an administration which, while professing devotion to the execution of the law, never failed to manifest its contempt for the law when it-was inconvenient to its purposes and aims. Having con- trasted the law of combination, the law of public meet- ing, and the treatment of prisoners in England and Ireland, the right hon. gentleman pointed out that whereasin Scotland the crofters were enabled to obtain relief from their arrears of rent, in Ireland the power to deal with arrears was withheld, and the tenant was left at the mercy of the landlords. He held the Government to be responsible for any fatal consequences which might result from evictions, and charged them with having shown more unblushing and un- scrupulous contempt for law whenever it was inconvenient for their purpose than any other Government during the last half century. After de- scribing Mitchelstcwn as an instance of the manner in which the Government - omitted to make proper inquiries, he accused them:. of shamelessly upholding lawless conduct. While professing to be the cham- pion of order, Government, indeed, was endeavour- ing to make the sacred principles of law and order odious in the sight of every rational man who had the smallest spark of that love of constitutional freedom by which this country had become great. He accused Liberal Unionists of abandoning the traditions of the Liberal party in respect to Ire- land, of not maintaining thd pledges they gave at the last election, and of resorting to the very worst practices of the old Irish ascendancy in endeavour- ing to set different factions of Irish people against one another. They had broken their engagements with respect to coercion, and also with respect to local government for Ireland. The practice of setting differ- ent classes in Ireland by the ears was an old device with English wire-pullers, and had been all along an essential element of the system of Irish misgovern- ment. Alluding to the address of the Irish Non- conformist ministers to Lord ' Hartington and Lord Salisbury, Mr. Gladstone said that if local knowledge was to be the test of capacity to judge the Home Rule question, subscribers to the address ,were out of court. It was useless to suppose that the Irish people would change their minds and give up the battle they had been fighting for 700 years, espe- cially now When they had constitutional privileges. Dissentieht Liberals desired this country to go on fight- ing a hopeless battle, but he could not see why the people should persist in a policy the fruits of which had been unmitigated bitterness, mischief, disparage- ment, and dishonour. Ireland ,was now fighting with the weapons of confidence in a' powerful party and the affections of the people of England. He besought them by resolute persistence in the policy they had adopted to foster, to cherish, and to consolidate that sentiment, , and so to act that in space it should spread from the north of Ireland to the south, and from the west of Ireland to the east, and in time it should extend and endure front the present date until the last of centuries that might still be reserved in the councils of Providence to work out the destinies of mankind. Mr. Gladstone spoke for an hour and fifty minutes, and resumed his seat amid an unparalled demonstration of enthusiasm. Brief speeches were afterwards given by Sir William Harcourt, Mr. John Morley, mg Earl Spencer, the pro- ceedings closing with a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was moved by Mr. Gladstone.

div.head: DRIVE THROUGH THE BLACK COUNTRY.
div.p: DRIVE THROUGH THE BLACK COUNTRY.

On Thursday, at the residence of Sir Walter Fester, Mr. Gladstone received a deputation from the Irish residents of Birmingham, wha presented an address. In his reply, the right hon. gentleman pointed out three positive evils from which, he said, Ireland Is suffering, and which only admitted of remedy by the agency of Irish representatives sitting in Dublin. These were— first, coercion; secondly, an administrative system , thoroughly anti-national in its methods ; and lastly, the absence of power on the part of the people in Ireland to manage their affairs according to their own ideas. He recalled some of the horrors of past Irish administration, and these he contrasted with the present state of feeling, holding up the change that has taken place as an encouragement to the Irish people to continue, in a constitutional way, to pre.sstheir demands. In conclud- ing his address Mr. Gladstone said that the little residue of his life was the property 'cd Ireland, as far as it could
RECOVERY or CARDTWAL NEvrimt.—Cardinal Newman is reported to be out of danger, and thanksgiving was offered at the Oratory Church, on Sunday, tor the great hnprovement which had taken place.

Mr. Leader Williams, engaged on the Manchester Ship Canal, and a party of English engineers and surveyors visited Ballinasloe on Saturday, and inspected the new bridge and sluices, with the view of constructing similar works on the Manchester Ship Canal. The "last scene of all that ends the strange, eventful history" of the Great Eastern steamship takes place on board on Tuesday, the 20th of this month, when auc- tioneers will submit to the hammer the whole of the Iron and other metals, boilers, engines, machinery, timber, sails, rope, boats, furniture, &c. The King of Bonny is on his way to England. Far from being a savage, one who knows him intimately describes him as a well-behaved gentlemen, particularly as to the cut of his clothes, and speaking and writing English like an Englishman. Be was educated in England, and has been here several times. Rumour says his Majesty is very hard up. Hence his visit. FCILI.RSSNESS WITTE FIRRARMS.—& peculiar revolver accident has occurred at Sheffield. A gentleman had taken a revolver to a shop with a view to its repair, and while a boy connected with the establishment was handling it, it was discharged, and the bullet from the barrel, alter injuring the youth's hand, passed through the window, and struck an adjoining shop, a cabman having a narrow escape in its transit. Sergeant Norwood, of the West Riding police, was drowned at Shipley, on Monday. He and others were searching for a bag of silver-plate which had been thrown into the river by a man named Dinsdale, who is accused ni robbery. They had found the property when the boat in which Norwood was seated was swept down the river Ire the strong fresh caused by the recent heavy rain, carried over a dam, and capsized. The body was recovered three heurs later.

GALLANT C,AProax OF A Stsva DTTOW.—Lieutenant Fitz Herbert, of the Algerine, has made a gallant capture of a large slave dhow, which had carried 200 slaves, off the north coast of Madagasca.r. Both his boats were capsized; hut he righted them, and continued the chase with one rifle and four revolvers. The Arabs main. tamed a heavy fire till all the boats had grounded on the surf. The Sikalavas then carried off all the slaves, save 27, who were rescued by Mr. Fitz Herbert.

TER NEW WIMBLEDON: ANOTHER PROPOSAL.—A new site has been proposed to the National Rile Association for the annual mite meeting the ground being situate at firoOkWOO(1. in Surrey, about 28 miles from London. : and near to Woking and Pirbright. The land, a large , portion of which belongs to the Government, has not , vet been completely inspected, but the distance from London, nine miles further than Staines, is regarded in some quarters as a difficulty, unless the railway accom- modation can be improved. San DEATH OP A YOUNG WOMAN.—The dead body or Elizabeth Reville, aged 19, belonging to Rotherham, has been found in the river Mersey, at Urmston, near Man- chester., She went to Urmston as a domestic servant. and WM courted by a man who proved to be married. Her employers cautioned her, but, being infatuated, she continued to have clandestine interviews with her lover. A fortnight ago the girl disappeared, and it is supposed that, grief-stricken and frantic owing to her condition. she committed suicide. UNFORTUNATE Tows' COLINCILLORS.—A municipal difficulty has arisen at Crewe over the names of two membera of the Council whose names have been acci- dently left off the burgess lists, but whose service as members of the Cerporation does not expire until November next year. It is the opinion of counsel that the gentleman thus treated may be summoned to corn• inittee and Council meetings, but that any votes they give would be accompanied by liability` to a penalty. It is not improbable that something more wilU be heard of the affair. , Novut LICENSING Chnorriow.—At Rotherham,: Police- court, on Monday, Geo. Smith, of Firvale, who described himself as "a gentleman rabbit catcher," was fined £2O, indluding costs, for sell!, ig, by retail, beer without a license on Oct. 28. Evidence was given to the effect that on the day named, between 12 and 16 men were in the defendant's house. They all had beer, for which they paid. Notice of appeal was given, it being argued in defence that there was no sale. The men lodged at the house, and four pinta of beer were allowed each per- son every day, which were included in 28., the amount charged for board and lodgings. AERIAL NAVICIATION.-011 Saturday, at the weekly meeting of the Council of the Balloon Society, held at St. James's Hall, the Chairman, Captain Parry, R.N., stated that the subscriptions to the Aeronautical Fund amounted to upwards of £3,000. Mr. Putman, the secretary, announced that over 300 letters had been received in response to Mr. Sangster's offer of a prize of £l,OOO for improvements in balloon appliances, and clergymen, scientists, chemists, engineers, and others were anxious to compete. On the motion of Mr. Swan, seconded by Captain Warren. a resolution was carried affirming the desirableness, in the interests of science, of holding an Aeronautical Exhibition in London next year. INTEMPERANCE CURED.—A wealthy American Lady whose , only son was for years a slave to intemperance, after seeking in vain for a cure, and trying all known remedies, at last found a simple means that cured and save him from a drun- kard's grave. Anyone suffering or desiring to help others in this worthy cause, by sending a self-addressed stamped en- velope to Mr. James Holland, 25, Hart-st., High Holborn, London, will receive this information free of charge. Men- tion this paper.—Advt.

SHIPPING DISASTERS.—The British steamer Westphalia, from Rotterdam for Cardiff, in ballast, was towed into Queenstown, on Thursday, disabled. Her funnel was swept overboard by heavy seas on Sunday last during an easterly gale.-4 large barque is supposed to have founded off the Nore on Thursday morning. The war- ship Locust was sent to her assistance, but returned without news of the ship or crew. The barque is supposed to have been in collision. STORMWARNINd.—A severe storm may be expected every day of the week in all domestic circles where Hudson's Dry Soay is not in regular daily use. A Penny Packet will prevent it. It leaves no taint nor smell. Is quick, safe and sweet. Splendid for Washing Flannels and Winter Underclothing. Sold very- where. For Family use in Dozens and Half-Dozens, also in 141 b. and 281 b. Boxes..—Advt.

div.p: MPER lAL PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—Tursosr.
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4 15 p.m., for the first time since the adjournment of the House on the 13th August.

div.head: ZANZIBAR SLAVE TRADE.
div.p: THE ZANZIBAR SLAVE TRADE.

The Earl of HAEROWBY drew attention to the slave trade in Zanribar, and asked the Psirne Minister for in- formation on the subject, as to which he had given pri- vate notice. He drew attention to the position taken up by the Germans, and asked what course her Majesty's Government would take with regard to the course pur- sued by Germany. At present the German name was in bad odour with the natives, and he thought that the English Government ought to be careful before allowing themselves to be identified with the German flag. The Bishop of CARLISLE, on behalf of the Universities' Missions, presented a resolution passed by the Council that day, and expressed the hope that the Government would be careful not to allow the English to be identified with the German in the minds of the natives. •

The Marquis of SALISBURY said, in consequence of the events which had taken place on that part of the coast ef Zanzibar under German influence, the German Go- vernment thought it right to take more active measufes. the object of the German Government was to put down the slave trade, and they were doing their best to strike at the root of the cursed traffic by colonising along the coast. Her Majesty's Government had joined the Ger. man Government in carrying out the work of mercy, and, by the naval blockade proposed, they would, for the first time, get the right of searching all vessels under whatever flag, and he believed that the French Govern- ment—which had hitherto resisted the right of search— were going to send a ship to join in the object of putting down the slave trade. He thought that the suggestion that England should not join with Germany in thir blessed work, for fear of some prejudice in the minds & the natives, not worthy to be entertained.

THE COURSE OF BUSINESS. The Marquis of SALISIMRY, replying to Earl Granville, said there was very little work for their Lordships to do, and he proposed that they should sit for the present on Tuesdays only. LORD SACKVILLE AND THE UNITED STATES

div.head: GOVERNMENT.
div.p: GOVERNMENT.

Earl GRANVILLE: I wish to ask the Prime Minister if he has any statement to make to the House with regard to the painful incident which has occurred in the United States? Ido not press for any answer if the noble mar- quis thinks it would be to the public interest to reserve it. - The Marquis of SALISBURY: r will take advantage of the choice which the noble earl has given me, and I will avoid making any observations now on the painful in- cident I Trill only say that papers are in the hands of the printers, and will be delivered to-night or to. morrow. _ _

div.head: TheVouge adjourned at 4 55 p.m. until Tuesday.
div.p: TheVouge adjourned at 4 55 p.m. until Tuesday.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TUESDAY. The House of Commons re-assembled after its long vacation, and at 3 5 Mr. Speaker took the chair, thern being probably 70 members in attendance at prayers. At 3 15 Mr. W. El. Cross took his seat for the West Derby Division ot Liverpool (being introduced by Mr. Whiteley and Mn. Forwood), in the place of Lord Clam I Hamilton, resigned. .
The SPRAKER Sllb9eqUently read communications ac- quainting the Rouse with the convictions ot Irish mem- bers of Parliament during the recess, amid cheers from the Irish benches. PUBLIC BUSINESS. _ _

Replying to Sir Win. Flarcourt, the FIRST LORD of the TRRASDRY said it was proposed to treat the Civil Service Estimates in Committee of Supply of the present week without interruption, the English votes to have prece- dence, in order that the Scotch and Irish members should have notice of the estimates with which they are mere intimately concerned. The Education Estimates would be taken on Friday next.

Sir GEOR 1 CAMPBELL Will Wednesday afternoon still be at the disposal of private members? Mr. SMITH : Surely the hon. member has forgotten' that an order of the House has already placed Wednes- day afternoon at the disposal of the Government_ PERPEMPAL PENSIONS.—MT. BRADLAtIGH called atten- tion to the fast that the Treasury minute on perpetual pensions, laid on the table of the House on Jply 20th, was not distributed to members until August 11th. He asked for an early opportunity to discuss it, and gave notice to move that the House dissents from so much of the minute as proposed that the holders of pensions and allowances,- or payments, which the law officers con- sidered of a permanent chSracter. and to which no obli- zations of an onerous kind attached, should be invited to commute on the same terms as commutations had already taken place, and that the House approved of the report of .the Select Committee, which set forth that the present state of commutation—about 27 years' purchase —was too high. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Slurs said it never had hem the intention of the Government to act upon the minute referred to without the House having full opportunity of expreQsing an opinion upon it, and he would take steps to afford the hon, member an oppor- tunity of proposing his resolution.

Twr. SLAVE TRADE.—Mr. 0. V. MORGAN, in the absence of Mr, S. Buxton, gave notice to move on the earliest possihlellay„ and in view of the increasing and extended desolation of Africa caused by the slave trade, and also of the large responsibility which Ruropean nations had assumed by their declarations against the slave trade. that a humble address he presented to her Majesty pray. ing that she be graciously pleased to call together, in I.,ondon if possible. a conference of the powers in order to devise such measures for the repression' of the slave trade as may be at tim same time effective and in accord- ance with itistiee. and under the regulations of interna- tional law. (Cheer,: ) THE MRTROROI,ITAX Ponies—Mr. PICIERSGILL asked ander what, circumstances Mr Munro, the Assistant Commiesionr of the Metropolitan Police, resigned hi, post, and if he were still in the public service.—The HOUR SRORR.TARY said that to his great. regret Mr Munro thought it necessary to resign his office on ac• ount of differences of opinion between himself and the Chief Commissioner on a question of police administra., don, fle (the home Secretary) bad made arrange- cents to enah!e hint to have the benefit, of Mr. Munro's advice on matters relating to crime when it might seem desirable.—Mr. P/CKFRS,III.I.: Is a new office to be created for Mr. Munro? —Mr MATTnEws : I have ;elating to add to the answer I have already given.-- Mr.; BRADLAI7GR • I shall call further attention to this matter in moving trhe reduction of the police vote. (Opposition cheers.) SUPPLY.—THE LAND COMMISSION.

The Flouse then went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Service eat imat4s. The vote for the Ent=hell Land Comtnission was first taken. Mr. Moturt moved its reduction, on the ground that there were too many Land Commissioners.

The debate was continued by Mr. BANBURY, who said !ie should be disposed to vote for the reduction unless the Government. could furnish a fuller explanation than 'id yet been given. Appointments on the Commission were merely reserved As patronage posts, and were given to Treasury clerks and private secretaries. Mr. CONYBPAILY called attention 'to the enclosure of commons and theii. absorption by private owners; and Mr. Lanoncssas complained that the heavily-salaried officials were never at. their posts, while the junior ser- vants had to work specified hours. Mr. CONVBgARN: moved the reduction of the vote by £.BOO of the salary of the resident. le,val assistant Com- missioner, hut this was rejected without a division, aud the vote was then agreed to. The amendment was also supported by Mr. Brad- laugh, Mr. John Ellis, Mr. Molloy, and others, but was negatived on a division by 15t votes to 69. . - -

On the grant in aid of teachers of poor-law sthools, Mr. -CARDWELL called favourable attention to the Scotch system. under which pauper children were educated with other children at ordinary schools.—Mr. Samuel Smith, Sir Walter Barttellot, and Mr. Pickersgill spoke in favour of the boarding-out system.—Mr. WALTER' Lmila assured the House that everything possible was being done to secure the extension of the system—The vote was debated for fullS•an hour after the adjourn- ment for dinner, and was then agreed to without a Several other votes were agreed to. and progress was reported at midnight. The House adjourned at 12 10 a.m.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.-WEDNESDAY.

The SPEAKER took the chair at twenty minutes past twelve, there having been same difficulty in getting a House together. THE SLAVE TRADE.—Mr. Hanbury sought informa- tion ag to the Anglo-German demonstration on the East African Coast for the suppression of the slave trade. The Under Segetary for foreign affairs was absent, but Mr. W. H. Smith replied to Mr. Hanbury, stating that the Government had no intention of undertaking any opera- tions on land in East Africa. Nor did he give Dr. Clark, who had asked a question on the same subject, much encouragement that the Government would sup- port by military force the consuls and missionaries on Lake Nyassa who were being attracted by Arab slave traders. SUPPLY &c.—The House went into Committee of Sup- ply, and a number of votes were /treed to. On the vote of £7,634 for the Record Office, Mr. T. E. Ellis asked whether the Government could not cheapen the publica- tion of the papers, and make provision for the produc- tion of a calendar of the manuscripts and records of Wales. Other hon. members pleaded that provision should be made for the transcription of Irish MSS.. and Dr. Hunter asserted that if the records of the Union between Great Britain and Ireland were allowed to be examined he believed that such a story of rascality Would be unfolded as would smash the arguments of the Unionist party. The vote was agreed to. Some talk followed relative to the great cost of blue-books, and reference was also made to the new arrangement for the publication of the debates. At half-past five o'clock the Houseiadjourned, after a somewhat dull sitting. HOUSE OF COMMONS, THURSDAY. _ - . -

The Speaker took the chair at th'ree,o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Questions were asked with respect to the African slave trade, the imprisonment a a mem- ber of the Salvation Army in Switzerland, the salt ring, and the sugar bounties. Mr. S. BUXTON pleaded that the Education Estimates be postponed until next week,

as an important debate might arise on the report of the Royal Commission; but Mr. bid ITN said the debate had been fixed for Friday, and be could not break through the arrangement. He also added that the Govern- ment could not enter upon the discussion of the report of the Royal Commission. The Chan-e r calor of the Exchequer, in reply to a question, said Us- wheel-tax proposals of the Government were to be pro ceeded with, but he was not in a position to fix the date. Mr. S. Darling took his seat as member for the Edin- burgh and St. Andrews Universities. Information was sought as to certain native trade righ s on the Niger, anal as to what help the Governrratit proposed to send to the British subjects on whom a pirate chief had made a raid at Sherbro, in Sierra Leone. The House then went into Committee of Supply, and a number of votes were agreed to. The vote for £5,000 for the Office of the Mercantile Marine was under discussion at I welve o'clock, when the proceedings in Committee were adjourned. The House adjourned at 128.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

Benjamin Bart, formerly Liberal member for West Meath, died in Dublin. on Saturday, aged 79. Twelve young men of Woodford returned to their homes on Saturday night, after serving a month's itn- prisonment in Galway Gaol for resisting the sheriff at the recent Clanricarde evictions. All the houses in the town were brilliantly illuminated, and the men were entertained in the National League rooms.

A boy named Geary, who was bitten near Armagh by a rabid dog last August, died on Saturday of hydrophobia. Ile had been treatei by Mr. M'Gavern, known as the "Irish Pasteur," who had discharged him as cured. D. Perrfus having certified that the boy had died of hydro- phobia, the coroner did not deem it necessary to hold an inquest. SUPPRESSING A NATIONAL LEAGUE MEETING.

An attempt was made on Sunday to hold a proclaimed Nationalist meeting at Drumßah, but the police success- lully charged the crowd, and in the struggle the chair- man of the local Poor-law Board was batoned. Capt. Stokes, with 60 Hussars and 200 police, proceeded to Drumlish, following the National League con- tingent from Longford, headed by Mr. Cox and Mr. Luke Hayden, members of Parliament. Mr. Cox walked towards a platform erected in the centre of the village, and Capt. Stokes and the Hussars followed. Captain. Stokes was accosted by Mr. Cox, and in reply to Mr. Cox said he should not allow that gentleman or Father Connefrey, parish priest, to tell the people nn go home quietly. rattler Connefrey thereupon said he would address the people from the altar, and Captain Stokes said he would follow him anywhere he went. Father Connefrey entered the chapel, and advised the people to go home. Several policemen entered the chapel, but there was no further incident, and the people dispersed quietly.

ARCHBISHOP WALSH AND MR. BALFOUR. The Roman Catholic Archbishop of Dublin (Dr. Walsh), in a letter, replies to Mr. Balfour's statement that there is more illusion on the subject of arrears even among the Irish bishops than about any question con- nected with Ireland, and that the Irish tenant has been fenced round with law after law until he stands in an incomparably more favourable position than any other debtor in any part of the civilised world. The Arch- bishop quotes a resolution unanimously adopted by the Episcopal body last June, referring to the accumulation of arrears of exorbitant rent, in which it is stated that the Cotirt is powerless to lessen the arrears, and thus to ward off the danger of eviction, leaving the tenant at the mercy of the landlord, while there is in operation in Scotland an Act specially devised to afford protection in this very matter to Scotch tenants. The reductions granted by the Scotch Commissioners amounted to 30 per cent, on rent and 60 per cent, on arrears. The Arch- bishop assumes that Mr. Balfour does not exclude Scot- land from the "civilised world.'

div.head: CURRENT POLITICS.
div.p: CURRENT POLITICS.
MR. JOHN MORLEY ON THE HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Speaking on Momlay at Newcastle, ate luncheon in honour of the Princess Louise, Mr. John Morle,y, M.P., said that though it was the fashion occasionally to dis- parage the House of Commons, that House, since the, great admission of the popular voice into elections, was, in his opinion, in no respect inferior to the House theel preceded it. For standird of character, in range oe ability, and in public spirit the House of Commons kept' up its old historic level. Alluding to the meeting of Parliament, he said he did not greatly rejoice at the fact that the next night the House of Commons would re- assemble. He believed all members of Parliament felt that an autumn session was an institution and a luxury which could very well be dispensed with. Roth parties within the past eight, years had indulged in this ques- tionable luxury, and if they were to have nine months of session in the year, and had besides what was called' extra-Parliamentary oratory, he would ask when the thinking was to be done.

div.head: EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.
div.p: THE EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY BILL.

The Borne Secretary. accompanied by Mr. W. H. Smith and Sir Michael nicks-Beach, on Monday received a deputation representing the trades unions of the United Kingdom, who presented a memorial urging that the Employers' Liability Bill, now before Parliament, should be amended so as to prevent employers from contracting themselves out of the Act, and to make 1,500 the sum recoverable for compensation. One hundred and twenty delegates attended, headed by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., -who explained that unless the' bill was amended in neat-A-dance with the Trades Congress memorial, they would prefer the Act of 188/Y to the Government Bill.—Mr. Mary-alms, in reply, said. he could give no definite pledre. The statement that, they would prefer the Act of 1880 was extremely grave. The Government in their bill had ,endeavoured to give effect to the recommendations of a Special Committee of the Flouse of Commons. He reminded them that, some degree of compromise .was always necessary; otherwise they might have to go on many years with the Act of 1880. He, however, promised careful con- sideration of their views.—Sir Mien Ant. Flrcxs-BEAcic Raid he was far from saving the provi,ions regarding seamen were incapable of amendment. Be would con- sider the deputation's views. LORD GRANVILT.E AND SIR U. KAY-SEILITTLE-

div.head: ivorrni AT OPENSIIAW.
div.p: ivorrni AT OPENSIIAW.

On Saturday, at Openshaw, the Liberals of Openshaw accorded a very hearts, reception to Lord Granville, who laid the memorial tablet of a new Liberal Club which is being built in the township. At the close of this cere- mony a meeting was held in a marquee close to the site of the club; and in the evening.a soirée and public meeting was held in another part of the township. Lord Gamey!Lte, in returning thanks for au address which was presented to him in the marquee, delivered a speech in which he briefly cli,cussecl the Irish question and the question of Protection, with special reference to the sugar bounties. On the latter subject he counselled the electors to impress upon their representatives the importance of keep- ing a watchful eye on the proposal to ask the sanction of Parliament to a convention which he be-, lieved would be fraught with present mischief and which would form a dangerous encroachment on Free Trade principle.. With reference to the Parnell Corn- ' mission, he remarked that the Judges themselves seemed to he doing what Parl'ament ought certainly to have done for them-'-restricting the absolutely indefinite limits of the inquiry. As to Horne Rule itself, he owned that he was a convert.. He had not always been in favour of Home Rule, but he was converted by the arguments used by Lord Spencer and other valued friends of his.. and he now fe;:.., convinced that Home Rule was not Only an absolute necessity, but one of the greatest questions the Liberal party had ever taken in hand. Sir UGHTRED J. KAY-F,UrrTI LEWORTH moved, "That this meeting tenders its warine4 thanks for the distin- guished services rendered to the Liberal party by the Right Hon. the Earl Granville, KG., and expresses the hope that. at the next election the party of true union may find itself in a triumphant majority." Speaking in support of the motion, he alluded, in etilogistic terms, to Lord Granville's services to his party and to the State. He expressed regret that Mr. Peacock, the member for the division, was not present, and said it would be a comfort to him in his illness to know that he bad stood side be side with Mr. Gladstone in support of principles which- had had such happy results for many rising nationalities in all parts of the world, and that he had taken his part in a movement which must ultimately result in the contentment and happiness of Ireland. fie (SirsUghtred) believed that, the policy of Mr. Glad- stone was, as the resolution said, the p,.icy of true union. Liberals wculd recognise more and more, the more they examined it, that it was the only means by which we could establish that brotherhood between the peoples of England and Ireland which it must be the desire of every statesman to bring about. The plain duty of the Liberal party was to support Mr. Gladstone and his colleagues in their great constructive policy, which had for its ob- ject the making of the union between England and Ire- land a uxion not only in name:but in reality. Mr. War. AGNICW seconded the resolution, and it wee unanimously carried. THE NEWEST THING IN TORYISM.

Mr. Baumann, M.P.. has started a Conservative organisation, with, writes the London correspondent of a contemporary, the awe-inspiring title of "Conserva- tive Working Men's National Defence, Liberty. and Justice League." I doubt myself if the numbers and influence of the new organisation will ever justify the magnificence of its designation. Itsobject is aprarently to supersede the existing Trades Unions, which have become mere gatheriogs of Radicals, and which do nothing—so says Mr. Baumann—lint create claw discontents and jealousies. The new League is to be a nenefit society on one side, and a Tory political organisation on the other. What particular advantage it is to confer on working men Mr. Baumann did not say, but he suggested that one of its objects is to place "reasonable restrictions on monopoly and competition." The new League has an air of unreality—perhaps I should say of humbug—about it, and probably ita activity will never get beyond its initial stage. It has, however, had life enough to pass a vote of confidence in the Government.

The National Liberal Federation has been ha) a great time of it in Birmingham, which is posed to be the stronghold of dissenters , the true Liberal faith. The Unionists, as they. themselves, have for the present got possession the representation of the capital of the Midlallci!l., but it is scarcely likely that they will maintain at the next election. There has been every 1 deuce in the demonstrations which have tak place during the past week that Liberalism, 14 Mr. Gladstone as its leader, still retains its - upon the people of Birmingham. With such 4 chief as Mr. Gladstone, it is impossible not to 1)9 enthusiastic in the caw.. His presence is inspiration, while his activity is contagious. NlT'' the experience and foresight of a man close uk eidlity, he combines the energy and vivacity of youth of efghteen. One of the speakers, on 16( day, thinking of all this, was led to exclaim ' Adam in "As you like it "

" Master, go on, and I will follow thee To the last gasp, with truth and loyalty. In the address which Mr.. Gladstone delivered. the members of the Birmingham Liberal tion, on Monday, there were two points , of especial cohsideration ; the one was . a reful tion of Mr. Balfour'sstatement that Mr. Hi ton, M.P.,, whilst in prison under the in Coercion Act, was treated exactly as vi') he was put in prison under Mr. Gin administration. The other point had ence to the fact that, although the Government was returned to power in 1' by a majority of votes, it was not backed a majority of the voters. As the prison treatment, it seems that, in the instance, there was reason to complain of harsh way in which Mr. HAR RINGTON was dealt with. Mr. PARNELL brought his case ' 4 Parliament, and the result was that as soon es vi facts were brought under the notice Of SPENcea he gave instructions on the matter. knots Mr. GLADSTONE'S words : He ordered the English practice wllich is of great leniency, decency, and humanity.- English practice to be applied in Ireland. directed that Mr. Harrington should be retool from Mullingar to Galway. He was removed his own clothes. Ile was not put with crimini Re took exercise alone. He was not in the mary nor in ill-health, but his diet was altered,' he got everything that in reason he liked tc, for; and the doctor acquainted him with I cause. He irad a good bed, be had good food, was also allowed newspapers, stationery, and ing materials. (Cheers.) Now, it may be that Mr. BALFOUR, who has "unbounded stomach" for the sort of fare NO Irish officials have to offer him, knows nc about Lord SPENCER'S hnmane action; but cannot plead ignorance after Mr. GLiesrorts speech, and, if he is not lost to all shame, he apologise for his misrepresentation. Further, is called upon to consider whether he, too, abet not reverse a vicious course in the treatineo Irish M.P.'s who are sent to gaol. If he does ni his persistency in wrong-doing will give point the assertions of Mr. WILFRID BLUNT, that it is, confessedly, the object of the Irish $I tary to incapacitate Irish leaders by pl, them whilst in prison. As to the question of ing strength, Mr. GLADSTONE states that the i Tory and Liberal Dissentient vote was 1,429,' while the total Liberal vote was 1,353,009. shows a majority of 76,000 in favour of the ~ Dissentients; but this was composed of a large 01., ber of ownership votes—that is of votes give°.l. electors who; as property-owners, had several There are of course Liberals as well as Torlee this privileged position ; but votes of this dais in the main, to the Tory party. Mr. GtAnsrel estimate is that at least three-fourths of the oN ship vote went against the Liberal party. total of that vote was no less than 327,000; taking it off both sides in just proportion, he that, as regards the actual number of votergt Lilferals had a majority of 8,700. The moral of 1, is that the scale was turned by property, and persons, and that the time has come for insis_a'l'. , on what is called the "the one-man- one(' principle. . Mr. GLADSTONE delivered three minor s on Tuesday, and on Wednesday eveniug.‘ addressed, for close on two hours, an audiedl7oo' , 18,000 people in Bingley Hall. His speech listened to with profound attention, and mad% extraordinary impression. Mr. JOHN M" spoke of it as" one of the most powerful, _IA argumentative, and most eloquent speeches 'fi-ij made on behalf of one of the noblest of lit 1.01? causes." It was devoted entirely to the . Iri• i question, and, if it.be reprinted, as no doubt it be, it will form the text book of the case for 11:1131, ' Rule as it stands to-day. The great orator 110' what a mockery it was to talk about " equa 0 ' lin face of the oppressions committed under Crimes Act; and denounced the Governias; : which professed to be a Government of " law 944 order" as having shown the most unblushing , unscrupulous contempt for law. But he did_rnf b; , than denounce, for he cited cases in stipPnru_ca, statements; and thrilled his hearers with a re_cier itulation of the circumstances attending the 111 T by. at Mitchelstown, the effect being heightettr,.o the production of ph( tographs of the scene . f,otie calling out that the wing had ,no feathers on ,it, ho wittily turned the idea to account, remark- lug that it would be better if it was feathered, for en there would be a chance of its flying away. ..e Dissentients were made to feel that history, I tradition, and their own pledges were against 'them in the course they are taking, and that the stars in their courses are fighting against them. A brief but exalted peroration at the close of a noble speech po stimulated the vast audience that they cheered as if they would mover tire of cheer- ing, after which "Auld Lang Syne " was sung by Way of further vent to overpowering enthusiasm. It is needless to say that the Liberal party will gather new strength from the, demonstrations at Birmingham. Ireland will, ere long, have justice done to her; Home Rule will be granted; and, this accomplished, Englishmen can turn to the great reforms that require to be effected in their own country.

Lord GRANVILLE has for more than a generation rendered signal service to Liberalism, and it is fitting that he should have received so enthusias- tic a welcome on his visit to Laneashire. He is always genial and he is always sound. Ho opened a new Liberal Club at Openshaw, oh Saturday, and in the course of an interesting address he dealt with the sugar bounties question. There has been a great deal of nonsense talked about the injury these bounties were doing to English trade; and the present Ministry has made itself not a little ridiculous by pandering to sugar refiners who have all along been thinking more of their own pockets than of the pockets of the people. Referr- ing to the action taken by the Government, Lord GRANvILLE said—" I deprecate sending an envoy from capital to capital, cap in hand, to beg all the nations not to contribute subsidies in order to niche sugar cheaper for ourselves." And again : "I hope you will press upon your representatives the importance of very scrupulously watching, if a request is made to Parliament, to sanction a con- vention which I believe will be fraught with mischief, and not only fraught with mischief at present but giving an example of encroachment Upon Free Trade, which I believe to be of a very dangerous character." (Cheers.) This will be rather startling advice to people Who have been• hugging the delusion that the gugar Convention was an achievement of which the Government had every reason to be Proud. But, really, is it not patent on the face of it that we have lost something if the result of the Convention is to make sugar dearer? The pro- 'Posed agreement will not, of course, until it iS ratified, seriously affect the price of this article of general consumption, and as to this we have great doubts as to whether the sanction of Parlia- ment will be given. The people of this country have only to have their eyes opened to the trap into which they are being led to set themselves against being caught in its clutches. Why Should we cry out if our neighbours on the con- tinent give bounties to their manufacturers in order that sugar may reach us at a low price? What if they should let us have it for nothing— would that be a calamity? It will be said that by giving these bounties they have driven to the wall the sugar refining industry of this country. Granted that they have, still if we gain More than we lose by the operation we have 110 ground of complaint. It is estimated that the jam and confectionery business of this "Mtry has been so stimulated by the low price of 411 gar that additional employment has been found

for -a much larger number of workpeople than the number displaced at-the sugar refineries. It has thushappened that so far as trade alone is concern- ed we have actually benefited by the folly of our neighbours. But when, added to this, we take into 4ee,ount the fact that sugar has been supplied to every ,househojd at a remarkably low rate, it is obvious that the balance of gain to this countiy
has been enormous. A Germ-an deputy, speaking in his own country, calculates that Germany, in One year has contributed as much as £2,000,000 in

sugar bounties; and he adds:— " I cannot discern the smallest gain to our.country. The profits of the system have only been reaped by England. It is German sugar that has enabled Eng- land to give sugar to her cattle ;.it is German capital That has so developed the English manufacture of sweets, that it successfully competes with the .oerman manufacturer in the markets of the world and in Germany itself. We pay one and a half to two millions sterling' to enable England to consume 'what would probably be worked up by our German industry. Gentlemen, I fear that this system has roade us the laughingstock of our English cousins !" The laugh has undoubtedly been on our side; but it will no longer be on our side if we reject

What is given us by sanctioning the Convention. When the housewife is called upon to pay one Penny, or perhaps twopence, per pound more for "sweetening," she, at any rate, will realize that someone has blundered. But it will be too late

then to rectify the mistake.. If we would be wise, We must be wise in time. The agreement which the Government have been so anxious to effect has not yet bccome law; it will have to come before Parliament to be approved. There is yet time to strangle it, and it ought to be strangled. Alto- ether there are, ordinarily, about 6,000 people omployed in this country in the sugar refineries. It,would pay England to give every man £2 per Week and let him remain idle rather than sign the Convention. The loss in that way would be £600,000 per year; but if we persuade foreigners to cease to supply us with bounty-fed sugar the , loss will be many times £OOO,OOO. We ought to be content to let well alone; and take the good the gods provide us. He was reckoned a foolish fellow who killed the goose to see where the golden eggs Came from; and it seems to us that we are in danger of following his example and becoming the laughing-stock of the world.

TEE NEW Loan Mkyon.—Alderman 'Whitehead, the !-,ord Mayor-elect, was on Thursday afternoon inducted into office with the usual ancient ceremony. The exceed- ingly scanty proportions to which he has curtailed the Lord Mayor's Show has caused great dis Satisfaction.

The Catholic Bishop of Salford and the Protes- tant Bishop of Carlisle have been reviving the old controversy as to which is the true Church. They will be no nearer a settlement of the question when they have done. They are milking a barren cow.

Mrs. McCabe, of St. Helens was fined 40s. and costs for stealing a clock from the house of a neighbour. Her way of taking Time by the forelock was too irregular. Like procrastination, Mrs. McCabe is condemned becauseishe is "the thief of time."

Speaking at Liverpool, on Wednesday, Lori Derby, who is anything but a sanguine man said he thought we were on the eve of better times. The Board of Trade returns for October confirm his view • they show an increase of imports over October last year of £4,471,828, and an increase of exports to the value of £2,157,305. It is a remark- ably good sign when both imports and exports reveal an increase.

A good,thing may be used or it way be abused. The phonograph has been abused, at New York, by an attempt being made, by its aid, to steal, the music of Gilbert and Sullivan's new opera of " The Yeomen of the Guard." But the thief was caught and stopped, though there does not appear to be any law to .punish him for the attempt, as the phonograph IS newer than the law. What next, and next?

Lord Salisbury is taking the right course in com- bining with Germany, France,and Poitugal to sup- press the slave trade on the coast of East Africa; and we have no sympathy with those who are try- ing to stir up a feeling of jealously between" Ge- rmany and England. United action is the only effectual way of striking at a traffic which is a dis- grace to our common humanity. International relationships are a mockery if they are not to be relied upon in matters of this kind.

The National Union of Conservative Associa- tions has been meeting at Wolverhampton, -int in view of the doings at Birmingham— How it goes and how it fares Nobody knows and nobcdy cares. One odd thing about it is that it would have nothing to say as to Fair Trade. Mr. Howard Vincent did his level- best to get a vote, but he was snuffed out with "the previous question." Fair Trade is now as 'dead as a coffin nail.

Churchmen are beginning to see that it will never do to demand money from the rates in aid of Church schools; it is coming it too strong; and so at a National Conference, with the Arch- bishop of Canterbury in the chair, it was resolved that such a course would be inexpedient ; that is, if they could get their way in other things. The next move will be to obtain more money from the National Exchequer; but as the State even now pays two-thirds, why not go the whole way and let us have Free Education?

It is stated that Lord Salisbury is desperately anxious to get the Tithes Bills through during the present session. He knows that the longer the issue is delayed the worse it will be to get a settle- ment on the present lines. The Bills, if passed, will effect no real settlement ; they are merely intended to relieve the clergy of the odium of making a collection for their churches in the name of the law. We shall require something more drastic than these Tithes Bills to settle the tithes question.

Judging from the returns as to the municipal elections, the Tories are losing by their alliance with the Dissentient Liberals. Including such seats as the Dissentients have been able to secure, they have gained 61 seats throughout the country; but the Liberal gain is 96, or, deducting the 61 gained by the Tories, a net gain of 35 seats. If this is typical, as it probably is, of what we may expect at the general election, the Tory party are likely to have occasion to exclaim—" Save, oh save us from our friends l"

They manage some things bettor in Liverpool. On Tuesday, at the monthly mooting of Liverpool University College Council, the chairman announ- ced the receipt 4 a communication from Lord Derby to the effect that Mr. Henry Tate had oftered £16,000 for the completion of the new cone g buildings. It was resolved that the addi- tion be called "The Tate Library." When will somebody do something for Warrington Library? There is a rare opportunity for a man with money and generosity.

It is fitting that Mr. Chamberlain should go to America to be married; it is the land of United States. The lady who is to make him happy is Miss Endicott—after all that has been said to the contrary. Mr. Chamberlain is 52 year of age, but he leeks very much younger. In the shop Win- dows of Birmingham, he fs shown as photographed along with his son; and, as the two are thus seen together, the first thought is—Which is the father, and which is the son? We trust that Mr. Chamber- lain's matrimonial venture will have happier results than his political one.

The many good thingssaid at.the National Libe- ral Conference which has been held this week at Birmingham have been highly appreciated by the' wide-awake delegates.' Mr. Chamberlain has been let severely alone by Mr. Gladstone; but the Rev. C. Berry had a shy at him on Tuesday. He rejoiced, he said, that their chairman recognised that the seat he sat on was only a ehair—(laugh- ter)—and that he was not placed in it to dictate or com- mand, or to utter expressions of high or Highbury authority. (Laughter and cheers.) No, they had leaders who had learned the simple lesson that one of the essentials of leadership was the presence of followers— (laughter and cheers)—that, in fact, the followers made the leader and not the leader the followers; and that the man who broke away from all restraint and companion ship was not a leader but a "bolter." (Renewed laugh- ter and cheers.) It was an extra turn of the " s:.xew," was it not? to speak of the member for West Birmingham as a "bolter."

Mr. James Kitson was quite as happy in his references. They saw, he said, in that magnificent meeting delegates that they at all events approved of the attempt to storm the citadel of Birming- ham. (Cheers.) Personally he felt in the posi- tion of a junior partner, who had felt it his duty to leave his old and obstructive seniors, and who on revisiting the scenes of his youth found the old firm in a very bad way—(laughter)—with every sign of a disastrous liquidation—(renewed laughter)—and, he fancied, with no good=will to dispose of. (Laughter and cheers.)

Ought a Town Councillor to take part in Town Council proceedings when he is no longer on the burgess list? . That is a nice question which is just now receiving some attention. At Crewe the "names of two members of the Council have been accidentally left off the burgess lists. It is the opinion of counsel as to the difficulty that the gentlemen thus treated may be summoned to committee and Council meetings, but that any votes they give would be accompanied by liability to a penalty. Councillor J. V. Taylor, of Warring- ton, is another councillor who is running a risk. He is not on the burgess list, and he is not entitled to be on. He would therefore do well to retire from the Council, and make way for a bona fide burgess„

Tory sneakers have credited the Government with more than they Were entitled to for their amendment of the Employers' Liability Act. The changes that are proposed are so much on the principle of taking back with one hand what is given with the other that miners and other work- men are altogether dissatisfied with them. A depu- tation of Tildes representatives, headed by Mr. Broadhurst, M.P., waited on. Monday upon the Home Secretary to point out the defects of the amended bill; and, as Mr. Matthews showed no sign of making the required concessions, he was plainly told that the Trades Unionists of the country would rather have the Act as it stands than the new bill. It is obvious from this that the Government have "amended" the Act with- out "improving" it.

WIDNES c.g.T.s.—On Thursday evening there was a good attendance at the weekly meeting of this Society arida .capital, musical programme was gone through. The Vicar presided. BETHISDA IMF acayEmEwr Soctury,Rusxmons.--The mem- bers of this society commenced the season on Tuesday evening with a social meeting. The proceedings com- menced with a• capital tea, and then followed a brief concert, the rest of the evening being spent in a fashion congenial to all. A WOMEN'S DRUNKEN SPREE AT WlDNES.—Yesterday, at Widnes Police Court, a woman named Ellen Roach, of 13 Peel-st was charged with having caused grievous bodily harm to Catherine Lancaster, who lived in the same house, by striking her on the head with a can.— The prisoner was committed to the Assizes for trial. THEFT BY A SERVANT GIRL AT WIDNES.--011 Thursday, at Widnes Police Court, Elizabeth Nott, of Stow-street, Runcorn, was remanded on a charge msf having stolen as bailee, a purse containing 225., the property of Elizabeth Kelsall, of Albert-road, Widnes. She was also remanded on a further charge of stealing a skirt and two chemises, I the property of Elizabeth Scott, Oakland-street, Widnes. CARDIFF PRIZE Cumn.—This celebrated choir of Welsh Prize Singers is announced to make a first appear- ance in Runcorn next week, and give three concerts in the Public Hall. Each member of the choir is a prize winner, and one has taken no less than 84 prizes. Parti- cular's will be found in our advertising columns, and no doubt our readers will be pleased to have the opportu- tunity of 'hearing the choir. ALLEGED THEFT AT WIDNES.—At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Wm. Byers, of Warrington was charged with stealing three pairs of boots, the property of Paul Gold Straw, of Liverpool. The prosecutor occu- pies a stall inthe Widnes Market, and the boots had been missed on differentoccasions during the last month. On the 20th tilt! P.C. Massey apprehended the prisoner, and in a cupboard in his house found a par of the stolen boots: There were also found pawn-tickets relating to other boots.—The prisoner was remanded until Monday. RUNCORN (719) STARR BOWKETT BUILDING SOCIETY— The annual meeting of the members was held on Thurs- day evening in •Bethesda Lecture Hall. Mr. Thomas Handley was voted to the chair. The directors in their fourth annual report stated that the society was making steady progress. The income from subscriptions had been £BlB 145., an increase over last year of £l2O 7s. 3d: The amount received from repayments of mortgages had been £144, an increase over last year of £B2. The sum of LH had been received as commission on transfer of appropri- ations. The sum of £6odl'had been advanced during the year on mortgage of property, making a total of £2,200, since the commencement of the society ; and it was satisfactory to note that not one of the repayments on these mortgages was in arrears.—The report and balance sheet was adopted on the motion of the chairman who pointed out that the amount in favour of the society had been doubled during the year. The retiring directors were re-elected as follows : Messrs. W. Armstrong T. Handley, Cr. Moss, and S. Pope, Messrs. Hugh Rowe and C. Pownall were appointed auditors. UNITED CHESHIRE AND LANCASHIRE PERMANENT BENE- FIT BUILDING SOCIETY, BUNCORN.—TIBI 25th annual meeting of the shareholders of this society was held in Trinity School on Thursday evening. Mr. T. Simister presided. The Committee m their report state that the nett profits of the past year's working amounted to £1,588 7s. Bd. From this was tube deducted one tenth to be added to the Reserve Fund, also £57 for outstanding accounts, leaving a, balance which would enable the Committee to recommend a dividend of 5 per cent. In realisino• some of the worst propert of the society, a loss I of £399 had been sustained, but this had been made up 1 out of the year's profits and the reserve fund would now stand at £.1.0,095 10s. 11d, which is £2O higher that last vetti.• The report and balance sheet were considered highly satisfactory and were unanimously adopted. The dividend was declared and recommended, and it was remarked that this was the first interest fund for six years. Before the close of the proceedings Mr. John Johnson, on behalf of time Committee and officers of the Society presented Mr. T. Simister with a handsome silver salver in recognition of his services as president during a period of 13 years. ,Mr. Simister suitably acknowledged the gift. RUNCORN MUSICAL SOCIETY.—A public meeting called by advertisement was held in the National School on Tuesday evening for the purpose of considering the desirability of forming a musical society in the town. The Rev. W. Bryant occupied the chair, and there were upwards of 30 persons present. After some discussion it was resolved to establish the " Runcorn Musical Society,"and that the subscription should be gentle- men, 55., ladies, 3s, ; music to be found by the members themselves. Mr. Wynne Huinplireys urged that it should not be thought that the society was confined to the church, because that meeting was held in a church school room. The society was entirely unsectarian and all interested in music would be welcomed whatever their religious belief. It was .resolVed that the Committee should endeavour to secure the use of Bethesda Lecture Hall for the purpose of rehearsals. It was further decided to ask Mr. John Brundrit to accept the position of president, and the 'following officials were appointed : —Conductor, Mr. Wynne Humphreys; librarian, Mr. R. Moore, secretary. Mr. F. A. Smith: treasurer, Mr. R. Pierpoint ; Committee, Miss Isherwood, Miss Pierpoint, Miss Jones, Miss Simister and Miss Simkin ; Messrs. Birkett, Johnson, Kay, Morris. and Williams. Mr. W. B: Kay has undertaken to fulfil the duties of pianist, and the first rehearsal will be held on the 15th inst.
