CONCRRT AT RUNCORN BOARD Sciroot.-:-A concert, promoted by the teachers of the Runcorn Board Schools, was given in Greenway-road school on Monday evening.. The teachers being desirous of maintaining and, if pos- sible, improving the present admirable average attend- ance.of the children at school, and of giving the scholars a deeper interest in their work, have conceived the idea of providing, at stated periods, entertainments to those scholars who are credited with the virtues of regularity and good 'conduct. The love of the young mind for spectacular display is well-known, and as the Chairman of the colleen (Mr. Pritchard) observed it is the ambition of the teachers to procure a suitable magic lantern by means of which to amuse and instruct the little people under their care. The object of Monday evening's concert was to secure the sum necessary to attain this end, and it is pleasing to record that a numerous audience lent their ' support. A capital programme had been arranged, but in consequence of the absence' of Mr. Lamb, of Liverpool, considerable alterations had to be made.. Miss Simkin and Miss C. Taylor contributed the first item, in the duet "What are the wild waves saying," and then Miss Williams, of Liverpool, rendered a song not mentioned on the programme. Later, the same lady sang "What would you do, love" Miss Taylor, in whom Runcorn possesses a rising vocalist of much ability gave a charming interpretation of "Ora pro nobis " to which her full, sweet, and expressive voice was well suited. ' "Tit for Tat" was given by Miss Cord, of Widnes who might have achieved greater success had she exhibited more confidence in her own powers. Miss Shnkin is always listened to with pleasure, and on the present Occasion she delighted the company with her capital vocalisation of " Angus Macdonald," the Skilfully played accompaniment adding highly to the effect. Mr. Williams is an acquisition to local musical circles, and his bright clear tenor voice was heard to great advantage in the songs.' Anita," and" Yes, Let me Like a, Soldier Fall." For his rendering of the la•ter song,' Mr. Williams was awarded the only encore of the even- ing, a fact which must be ascribed rather to the lack of appreciation, hen to the discriminating critidsm of the aOience. • The I,e-appearance of Miss Nellie Handley at our loeal concerts must be noted with pleasure. She sang " fill the Dawning of the Day," with her customary artistic method and power of expression. 'Me trio "Memory" was rendered by Miss Shnkin, Miss Taylor, , a mid Mr. Williams in good style. Two enjoyable items were the trio (piano, violin, and 'cello) "Gipsy Rends " . by Mrs. Kay and Messrs. Kay and Simkin and the piano- forntedt,uet by Mrs. Kay ad Mr. Wynne Humphreys. The rt conce concluded with the National Anthem. Mr. Wynne Humphreys was •an able and efficient accom- peis • ,

The subject was a • highly interesting one, and was illustrated with anatomical charts. At the close of his lecture, the doctor was cor- dially thanked. . . DEFRIES SAFETY LAMPS, sele agent J. S. Plimmer, of Liverpool. The views illustrated various scenes and subjects and were much enjoyed by the children, who crowded the room. ,The chair was occu- pied by the Rev. J. Bryant: THE NEW MARKET STALLS AT RUNCORN.—In conse- quence of the improvement of the market ground,, and re-arrangement of the stalls, the Board of Comtnissioners determined to ascertain the value of the various "stand- ings" by auction. Mr. Yarwood was the auctioneer and the bidding Was very spirited :Several of the stalls fetched 6s. 9d. per week, and those used for the sale of fish were let at ss. 3d. per week. THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER, AT WIDNES.—John Browne, who is now in confinement awaiting his trial on a charge of manslaughter, will be brought before the Widnes Bench on Tuesday next. Although the Coroner has only committed him on the minor ch.rg,e, the police intend to accuse him of murder. It is said this course is adopted in consequence of fresh facts which the prisoner's feflow-workmen; have divulged. STOVES In great variety at Garland's 51. Eridge-st.,Warring- ton.—Advt. • . _ . . .

- WIDNES LIBERAL CM:IL—A billiard match was played at this club on Thursday evening between a team from ,he Irish National Club (Islington), Liverpool, and a team of the Widnes Club. At the conclusion Widnes were the victors by 101 points. Previous to the com- mencement of the play, a substantial knife and fork tea was partaken of by the players, Mrs. Doyle, of Victoria-road, catering in satisfactory style. On sepera- ting, the company gave loud cheers for Mr. Glad- stone. .

THE CATHOLIC BAZAAR AT RUNCORN.—The bazaar pro- moted by the Catholics of Runcorn was brought to a successful conclusion on Saturday evening, when Dr. Gastaldi publicly thanked • his numerous Protestant friends for their sympathy and kindness, Which was shown in many instances in a very practical form. The prize drawing excited considerable interest and was very satisfactorily carried out. The first prize, a pony and chaise given by Dr. Gastaldi, was won by Mr. D. Speak- man. The total receipts of the bazaar, realised nearly £4OO. RUNCORN Semoor. BOARD—The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. Present: Messrs. James Pritchard, chairman; Dr. McDougall, S. ! C. Beckett, F. A. Lake, E. Imison and G. Moss (clerk). ! It was repbrted that during the 'month of October ;08 parents appeared before the Attendance Committee for not sending their children regularly' to school, • and they were suitably dealt with. The resignations of S. In,gles- ! field, caretaker of Greetiway-roadßeard School, and of Miss Williams, head teacher, of Mill Brow Board School ! were accepted. , ALRO-CARBON-LIGHTS, agent Garland, Ironmonger, Warring ton; branch, Eariestown.—Advt. A NEW Cmmicm MISSION Room FOR MD NES.—For some time the necessity for a mission Room on West Bank has been keenly felt, and during the first few• weeks a census of the inhabitants in. that locality has been taken with the object of ascertaining the number of adults and children, and their religious persuasion. The Church Council consider that this e.ensus would justify them in erecting a mission room, and a site, has been secured in Davies-st. It is intended to have a building capable of accomodating about 300 persons, and the cost is not to exceed £4OO. A Committee has been appointed to carry out the scheme. div.head: LIGHT WEIGHT AT RGNUORN.
div.p: LIGHT WEIGHT AT RGNUORN.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Mr. James Handley and Dr. Steele, Samuel Crosby, coal dealer, Waterloo-road, pleaded guilty to hav- ing in his possession two weights which were unjust. -- Superintendent Hollingworth said he visited defendant's coal yard on the 27th October, and found two 561 b. weights which were an ounce and a half light against the purchaser. These weights were apt to get light through being exposed ' to the atmosphere. Mr. A. Crosby said the weights belonged to an old pair of 'scales that were seldom used.—A fine of Is. and costs 8.4. 6d. was imnosed.—A similar penalty was imposed upon Wm. Stanway, coal dealer, of Shaw-street. In this case there Were two 561 b. weights each two ounces light, and a 281 b. weight one ounce light.—Thomas Reynolds, coal dealer, Vine-st., was charged with having a pair of • scales which were unjust.— Superintendent Hollingworth said the scales were 111). out of balance, not against the Iturchaser but against the defendant.—Tbe defen4ant : Robbing myself. (Laughter.)—A -fine of Is. and Bs. 6d; costs was imposed..—Henry Fletcher, coal dealer, Railway Arches, Runcorn Bridge, was ()barged with being in possession of a 56tb. weight, three ounces light,. a 561b.1 weight two ounces light, and a 28Ib. weight one ounce light. He was further charged with nosing a pair of scales which were 18 ounces out of balance against the seller.—A tine of is. and costs 88. 6d. was inflicted.—Joseph Nicholls, coal dealer, Queen-st., was also fined is. and costs Bs. 6d. for being in possession of light weights. There was a 561 b. weight 3 ounces light, a 5611). 11 ounces light, a 281 h. weight 2i ounces light, and a 281 b. weight half-an-ounce light.—The superintendent remarked that weights used in a coal yard should be adjusted at least every three months.

div.head: ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A WIDNES
div.p: ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY A WIDNES
BLACKSMITH: INQUEST AND VERDICT.

Mr. S. Brighouse, the County Coroner, on Satur- day held an inquest upon the body of Thomas Maley, who' died on the previons Wednesday even- ing. it was alleged in consequence of the violence of John Broome, a blacksmith's striker. Mr. G. Rideal appeared for Broome, who was brought up in custody, and Mr, Superintendent Johnstone watched the proceedings on behalf of the police. Mr. 11. N. Wharton was the foreman of the jury, which consisted of fifteen jurors. Hannah Maley said the deceased was her husband, and had lodged at 76; Church-street. His home was at 2, Station-road, Sutton, St. Helens. Ha was a fitter and turner by occupation, and was employed at the works of Messrs. Mort Liddell and Co., chemical manufactur- ers in Widnes. He was 63 years of age. He left home on Monday morning in good health. She saw him at his lodgings on Monday night. He was unconscious, and continued so until his death on Wed nesday evenintr. Hethad previously enjoyed the best of health.—By Rideal : They had been married 34 years. He was not of an excitable temperament, and it was not his habit to swear or speak roughly. He was a stout , man ; but had never complained, that when he hurried for the train he had a pain at the kft side. Mr. Thomas Glover deposed that he was the chemist at Messrs. Mort Liddell's works,and resided at Bro.,ghton Drive, Cressington. The deceased was foreman at the works and had been employed ,there since April. The. prisoner *nom° was a blacksmith's striker, and had been at the works since 1882. On Monday afternoon he (witness) was in the General Office about 20 past four, and Maley came in and made a statement to him. In consequence of that statement, he went in search of Broome, whom he found in No. 2 Revolver Shed. He asked Broome if it were true that he had struck Maley. He replied "Yes, he had thethammer in his hand, and , was going to hit me, and if Iliad not struck him in self- defence he would have hit me with the hammer." Witness told him ashe had admitted striking someone in authority, j he must, leave the works at once. Broome refused to do so, and witness persuaded him to come and see the j deceased. , He asked Maley if he wanted Broome to work ' any longer for him, and he replied—" No, I don't." He (witness, again asked Broome "Did you strike Maley." ! He replied—" Yes I did, and I haven't finished yet," Maley remarked—" If you hadn't taken me unawares You would never have done this," and Broome retorted— "A re you ready now ?" Witness said," We have had enough fighting here; it is cowardly to hit an old manlike that. If you want to fight, go out into the street and I • fight a younger man." A few minutes later witness met I ! Broome in the yard and the latter said—" I am going Le ' j wait outside ;" and he advised Maley not to go home his j usual way. When he first saw Maley in the afternoon, he was bleeding from the nose, and had a scar on his hand. He visited Maley four times at his lodgings, and on each occasion he was unconscious. The fitters' shop, where the assault took place, is paved with bricks. By Mr. Rideal : During the time Broome had been at the. works.he had been a good average man. The disposition of Maley was irritable, but he had never seen him have any disagreement or conflict with the men.liy Fore- man : There were no signs of drink upon the ditcease,d, and he could not say tnat Broome was the worse for drink, but' he was excited.—By Mr. Parkes': Men had a tempted to make complaints about the deceased, but, as he allowed of no appeal from the foremen, he would not listen to them. Broome had not Made any .complanit against the deceased to him. • Wm!. Crillan, 58, Bridge-st., said he was foreinan labourer at the Blaek Ash Department of the works. He saw Broome in the time office, and told him net to be foolish but take his money; a ..td added "You should not have strqek an old man." Broome replied that he 'could use his fists with different men than Maley, and stated—" The old— —has I not done with me yet." There were no marks of violence on Broome.—By Mr. Rideal : 'Broome had not told him that Maley had aggravated him.--Mr. Glover wished to add to his evidence that Broome had complained that the deceased "was always on to him like he was on to Geo. Wright." Chas. Green, blacksmith, of 14 Charles-st., deposed to the condition of the deceased at 5 p in. on Monday. Austin Young, labourer, of Farnworth, .deposed that on Monday night Broome told him that he was sacked for " Snouting Old Torn." Witness asked Pf. Tom defen- ded himself in any!shape or form, and! Broome replied • " He took up the hand hammer and threw it at me." John Prescott, of 110 Albert-rd., gave confirmatory testimony. Alexander McDonald,2l,Gerrard-St., West Bank, stated that about nine o'clock on Monday morning, beheard the deceased charge Broome with not having cleaned the fly wheel properly on the previous day. Broome, said he had m ade, a good ',job of it, and the deceased I replied that there was half an inch of dirt on the wheel. I He added " I will be finding you another, job some of I these mornings." There was no temper shown on either side. Frederick Henry Roberts, fitter and terrier, 76, Church-st., deposed to finding the deceased in the works at 6 o'clock. He was unconscious, and was conveyed to his lodgings in a cab. P.S. Robinson stated he apprehended the prisoner at Warrington on Wednesday morning last. In reply to a charge of wounding Maley, the prisoner replied, " If he is hurt, he must have *fallen."' Next morning he charged the prisoner with causing the death of Maley. He replied, " Is he dead ? It's not me that has caused his death." He afterwards denied having struck the deceased. Dr. Hutchinson deposed that, assisted by Dr. O'Keeffe, he had made a post mortem examittation of the body. Dr. MeCambridge and Dr. McDonnell were also present during a portion of the examination. There was an abrasion on the right side of the upper lip on the inside. The canine tooth was loose. There was also an abrasion of the knuckle joint of the middle finger ; and an abrasion near the little finger. There was also a little blackness over the right eye. On opening the brain he found in the left cerebral hemisphere four ounces of clotted blood. It was situated on the surface of the brain. There as also some evidence of disease of the arteries of the brain. The substance of the brain seemed healthy. The heart and lungs were healthy. The cause of death \vat rupture of abided vessel of the head, and consequent effusion of blood and compression on the brain. The deceased was predisposed to rupture of blood vessels of !, the head. Slight violence would ! cause them to be ruptured. A blow on the head, with- out a fall, would very likely cause a rupture of the
blood vessels.—By Mr. Rideal : If the deceased had a struggle and fell, that would cause a rupture. The whole of the abrasions might have been caused by Dr. O'Keeffe concurred in this evidence.

The evidence of Broome was then tendered by Mr. Rideal. Before permitting the accused to take the; oath, the Coroner cautioned him very seriously. Broome stated that he lived at 25, Appleton Village. On Mon- day the deceased found fault with the way in which he had cleaned a vacuum, and witness went outside. When he returned, the deceased commenced to blackguard him again. The deceased was at the anvil, and, as witness went towards him, he lifted up a hammer to strike him. He just got hold of the deceased's arm, and put the other round his waist. They both tumbled down, deceased being at the bottom, and he fell with the side of his head upon the pitchpine anvil block. He never struck the deceased at all. The deceased would have struck him had he not stopped him. The deceased afterwards threw a spar at him, as he was leaving the shop.—By the Coroner: Instead of getting hold of the deceased, could not you have turned round and gone out of the shop I again? No. He was obliged to get hold of him; he did not want to be struck with the hammer. 'The witness denied having made the statement attributed to him by the other witnesses. When he said he would wait out- side, he meant he would wait outside for his wages. The Coroner then reviewed the evidence at length, and remarked that there was only one person who could tell what really took place in the fitter's shop and that was the prisoner Broome; who) had made statements before he could possibly know that Maley was dying, quite different to what he had just given on oath. That was important to recollect, because was it not more likely that the statement made before Maley's death would be true. ,-..After being directed on the law on the matter, The jury retired, and after an absence of over three- quarters of an hour, the foreman stated that the jury unanimously found that the deceased's death was accelerated by the injuries received at the hands of the prisoner.—The Coroner: That is a verdict of man- slaughter. The prisoner was then formally committed to take his trial at the next Liverpool Assizes. The Coroner instructed that should the magistrates decide to liberate the prisoner on bail, he would also accept bail, the prisoner in £lOO and two sureties of £5O each. RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

THE ADULTERATION OF AMERICAN CHEESE. .The Deputy-clerk read a circular letter received from the.Warrington Farmers' Club, stating that that club had passed a resolution to the effect that the attention of the authority be called to the consular reports issued by. the agricultural department of the Privy Council, show- ing the extensive sale in this country,as pure cheese,of a mixture of tallow, grease, cottorr seed oil, &c., with the product of milk in the manufacture of American cheese, with the object of prosecutions being instituted for the purpose of suppressing this fraud. The Deputy-clerk added . that he thought this sale of adultered American ch3ese was unfair to the ratepayers, as well as pre- judicial to the interests of the farmers. He thought that prosecutions should be instituted in cases where the Inspector found this stuff offered for sale.—Mr. Hall remarked that it was a great injustice.that such rubbish should' be palmed off upon the public.—Mr. Aaron pro- posed that the Inspector of Nuisancbs (Mr. Farrington), be empowered to purchase samples of cheese for the purpose of analysis, with a view of prosecutions being taken if found advisable.—Mr. Hall seconded this proposal which was carried without further discussion.

WIDNES AND THE COUNTY COUNCIL. At the annual General Session of the Peace for the county of Lancaster, held at Preston on Thurs- day, under the presidency of Lord Derby, Mr. T. Ilibbert ischairrnan of the Electoral Division Com- mittee) moved the adoption of the report and appended scheme for the formation of electoral districts. By this scheme Widnes are only appor- tioned one member. Mr. Hibbert said the work would have been easier had the Local Government Board been as Liberal to Lancashire in the number of its representatives as to the West Riding and other parts, Westmoreland, for example, a small county, having 28 councillors for a population of only 64,000. Had Lan- cashire received the same proportion as the West Riding, this county would have had 108 councillors instead of 85, and then there might have been greater efficiency, and an absence of complaints from Widnes, Barton, and other places. He proceeded to analyse the claims of Widnes, and to contend that to do greater justice to Widnes would yrodnce equal injustice in the district around Whines or to other places. Mr. C. R. Jacson seconded the motion, which was opposed by Mr. II Meekly, who argued that the Com- mittee were really creating a fresh property qualification. Widnes ought to have .as much consideration as the rights of those gentlemen .who jived in the arcadian regions of North Lancashire. The property qualification did not find favour in the act.—Sir. A. J. ICaV Shuttle- worth supported the Committee.—Mr. Holbro7A csskell , inquired whether Council could be heird on behalf of the Widnes Local Board —The Chairnym : According to the practice of the court, it can only be addressed by its members —Mr. Gaskell said then the duty devolved on him to put some portion of the case for Widnes before the court, and he presented memorials from W;dnes and

Ditton. The Widnes memorial was signed by, he believed, all the manufacturers, and the 408 signatures represented a rateable value of £69,703, and held that Widnes was entitled to tworeprosea Ltives. The Ditton memorial was likewise influentially signed, and suggested the division of Widnes into north and South, including Ditton, and each to have one councillor. There could be no difficulty in finding small townships in North Lancashire which could be united under one representative, so as to give Widnes and other important places the representation deserved.—Mr. It. Townsend hoped the north would be better represented, as it paid the most in rates.— Mr. Fell pointed out that the urban districts of this country by this scheme had had had not less than three fourths of the representative tilembers allotted to them. hear.) The Committee had allotted to the Local Board of Dalton-in-Furness one representative. What were the facts regarding the Local Board of Dalton-in-Furness? In the first instance it had an area of little more than double the area of Widnes. It had a population not more than half the population of Widnes, but its rateable value was £160,000 a year, against £120,000 a year, from Widnes. (Applause.)--: m Mr. W. W. B. Hutton suggested that the inequality at Widnes could easily be rectified. Let Widnes elect Mr. Haskell as its councillor, let him be made an alderman, and then Widnes could send a second representative. He proceeded to argue that Barton-on-li-well had a stronger call than Widnes. Barton had 122,houses more than Widnes, though Widnes had a population of 14,000 more than Barton, but this population was migratory. Barton did not press its claim, and he asked the court not to pay too much attention to the pressure from Widnes.—After some; further discussion the report and scheme.of the committee were adopted without a division.
SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT
RUNCORN. PALL FROM AN EXPRESS TRAIN.

Anextraordinary accident occurred on the railway at Runcorn Bridge, yesterday afternoon. About a quarter past four the London express, passed over Runcorn Bridge in the direction of Liverpool at a speed of about fifty miles an hour. As " the traia emerged from the last span. several platelayers saw a carriage door fly open, and a lady was precipitated on to the up line. As another express was due, the men made all haste to the spot, and found a well dressed lady lying across the metals in an unconscious state. By the direc- tion of Inspector Taylor she was at once conveyed to the Widnes Accident Hospital. Later in the evening several relatives of the unfortunate lady arrived at the hospital from Liverpool, and it appears that the lady was travelling with her step daughter, a nurse, and an infant from Ruston to Liverpool, in a second class compartment. After leaving Crewe they had some refreshment, and at Runcorn the lady was standing against the door of the compartment in the act of emptying a tea pot of its Contents when the door shot open, to the consternation of the other occupants of the carriage. The parties observe great reticence with regard to their name and position. The lady is very seriously injured about the body, and has sustained severe concussion of the brain. She had not regained consciousness late last night.

Gould, Hurstfield, Eaton, Diamond, MOSS, and G. Clarke. Recitations and read- ing were also given. Tne SUSPECTED BOOT THIEF.—John Brown, who was charged at the Lvnup Police court, with having stolen a pair of boots, ana who refused to give any satisfactory account of himself has been found to hail from Stock- port and to have stolen the boots from that borough. He was therefore handed over to the Stockport Police on Tuesday. THE REV. THOMAS RIPPON AT lorstm.—On Sunday the anniversary services of the Lymm Wesleyan Chapel were held. The sermons were preached morning and evening by the Rev. Thomas Rippon, of Rhyl, and formerly of the Warrington Wesleyan Circuit. Large congregations assembled at each service, and collections were taken on behalf of ,he trust fund. MARRIAGE OF Miss H. BRAZENDALE.—The marriage of Miss H. Brazendale, youngest daughter of Mr William Brazendale, builder, Lymm, to Mr. H. H. -Forrest was solemnized at St. Mary's Parish Church, Lymm, by the Rev. G. W. Guest. The happy pair were the recipients of many valuable presents from friends in the neigbour- hood, including a silver sugar bowl and cream jug, presented by the teachers of the Lymm Church Sunday School. • LYMII MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY.—The usual weekly meeting of this society was held in the Drill Hall, on Monday evening, when there was a moderate attend- ance. "Readings from MS. Magazine" was the subject appointed, and papers on the following subjects were read :—"Books,' "Guy Fawkes," and "Stray Leaves from a Philosopher's Note ook." Criticisms were afterwards given on the various papers by Messrs. Gil- landers, Mort, and the Secretary (Mr J. Brecrley). Cumicu TOWER.—The work of taking down the tower is progressing rapidly. The stones are lowered by means of a in. steel rope made of very fine guage wire which make it as supple as a common rope. By this a stone a minute, can be lowered. The stone is found to be almost as sound as when first quarried. The work necessitates that the walls should be firmly bound together by internal braces for the safety of the work- men. It is expected that the work of taking down the tower will not be completed before Christmas. FELONY AT LYMM.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Thursday morning, before Mr. W. Long, Annie Boycott (18), domestic servant, was charged with having stolen a quantity of wearing apparel, value 18s. and some jewellery, the property of her master, Mr. S. Heyward, of The Nook, Oughtrington. It appeared that prisoner was under notice to leave, and on Friday morning, a silver spoon having been missed, her box was searched and a number of the stolen articles found.—Prisoner pleaded "guilty."—As numerous other articles had since been missed, prisoner was remanded for eight days in order to give the police time to trace the missing property.

div.head: SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON MAN IN
div.p: SUCCESS OF A WARRINGTON MAN IN
AMERICA.

The following is from the "Clermont Courier," an Ohio (U.S.) paper, which has been received by Mr. G. Mullineaux, who is a nephew of the subject of the sketch. The gentleman referred to serv-d his time with Mr. Gaskell, formerly a tanner at Latchford, and he is brother of Mr. Peter Clare, ropemaker, of Warrington. Mr. Zoseph Clare, the subject of this sketch, was born in Warrington, England, October 20, 1825. He was married to Ann Moore, of Warrington, at. an early age, from which union were born eight chil- dren, five of whom are living, all occupying good and responsible places in life. ' Mr. Clare was a tanner by trade, and worked at it during his early manhood in his native town, but seeing the possi- bility of better things for him in America; resolved to break away from the low wages of England and in 1850 came to this country, spending part of his first year in New York, but soon came West and. settled at Bethel in 1851, where he has since resi- ded. He engaged in his old trade, combined with saddletree making, with good success until the breaking out of the rebellion in 1861. Realizing , the need of supplies for the great arnry then being equipped;he enlarged his business and crowded it • with all possible energy, until nearly the whole population of Bethel was employed in his factor, and saddletrees poured out of Bethel until where.- ever you found soldiers in the field, you would find many of them equipped with saddles of his manu- facture. The writer of this visited the battlefield of Avesborough on the Cape Fear river, N.C., eight years after the war, and among the other interest- ing things he saw there was an old weather-beaten saddletree, bearing a brass stamp upon which was the familiar legend, "Made by Mr. Joseph Clare, Bethel, Ohio." It was during these years and in a few years of wonderful activity that followed the war that his very handsome fortune was accumu- lated. Mr. Clare has always been a public-spirited man, has been foremost in all the public enterprises in Tate Township. He was one of the projectors of the C.. G. and P. R. R., and it was mainly through his efforts that the road was built from Amelia to Bethel and Hamersville. He was appointed Receiver of the road when it became involved, after it had reached Amelia. After the purchase of the road by Henry Brachman be continued as Superin- tendent until the road was finished as far as Earners- ville, after which he resigned. He has served this township as Treasurer at least six terms, being elected by the Republicans, for politically he is an earnest and uncompromising Republican lie has been a successful merchant for many years in Bethel. He is energetic, quick, diligent, is benevo- lent. and may be seen upon the streets of Bethel any day with a pleasant smile and a kind word for all, and many mit' testify to his deeds of kindness. He owns the large building in which the shoe factory of Aaron A. Brown is carried en, which he I gave rent free for ten years to induce this import- ant industry to move to Bethel. This is in keeping with many other things that might be mentioned, that would show his broad and loyal liberality to the place. At sixty-three he is active and full of energy, and looks forward to many years of useful work.

Secretaries of Football Clubs are requested to note that reports of matches played oa Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later then ten o'clock en Wednesday morning.
RUGBY.

WIDNES V. TOTTINGTON ("A" TEAMS) —These teams met on Saturday at Widnes, on the Lowerhou.sedane ground, and the game resulted fh a victory for the home team by 2 goals, 3 tries, and 4 minors to nil. The goals were kicked by Jobnson and Holt. Charles obtained two of the tries, and Holt and Ball got one each. WARRINGTON STAR V. ST. HELENS WANDERERS IST TEAM.—This match was played on the ground of the latter at .t.e. Helens in miserable weather. The Wander- ers had a strong team the Stars being also strongly represented. In the first half tne Wanderers scored 1 minor, to Stars nil; in the second half, Stars had the best of the game but could not score owing to the ground being in wet condition. A pleasant game ended in a draw, the score being 1 minor each. RUNCORN TRUE BLUES v. Wuteres JUNIORS.—This match was played on Saturday on the ground of the former, who won by 1 goal (dropped) and 7 minors to 1 try and 2 minors. Pope dropped the goal and Bell got the try for the Juniors ih ttte last two minutes. Run- corn True Blues team: Full back, S. bough; three- quarters, Jones, Thompson, and urereton ; half backs, Cousins and Worrall ; forwards, Pope, Ditchfield, Humphreys, Dimelow, Jones, Hassell, Taylor, Goodier, and Dtitton. WIDNES V. Tcrrmorms.—This game was played on Saturday, and Widnes journeyed to Totting,ton with only 14 men, and a very poor team at that, to play with. Kiddie was playing in the county trial match, and Plumpton, Parkinson Morgan, and Gordon were also missing from the Widnes ranks. On the other hand Tottington had a very good team. The ground was in a wretched sloppy condition, and this, together with the fact that the new rules (with which players are not familiar) came into force on Saturday, rendered the game far from interesting. Indeed, it was one long . succession Of free kicks. In the first half Johnson, of Widnes, scored a try in a rather difficult position, after a grand dribble, in which he was assisted by Barber and Woods. The place kick by Farrell just failed. Up to half-time, when Widnes led by a try and two minors to nothing, the visitors had by far the best of the game, notwithstanding that they played a man short, and they also showed to great advantage in the early part of the second half, but towards the close th e home men worked well together, and succeeded in altering the aspect of the game, a goal being placed by Greenhalgh from a try by Fetcher. Thus the game ended in a victory for the home team by a goal to a' try and three minors. All the visitors worked hard, Bingham, Farrell, Hartley, Gandy, Johnson, and Woods playing a fine game. RUNCORN "A " TEAM V. ROCHDALE ALBlON.—Played at Runcorn, before a moderate attendance of spectators. Haslam kicked off, and Shaw returned. The Rochdale players dribbling well, matters looked considerably dangerous for Runcorn, but Woods cleverly kicked the ball dead. Baum returned the ball after the drop out, and Evans passed to Woods. and,the latter to Cawley, who punted well, causing Rochdale to touch down. A free kick, under the new rules, was awarded to Rochdale. Baum then got away nicely, Tipper arresting his pro- gress. The Albion forwards dri:bled to the centre. Bowyer, however, neutralized the advantage gained by a similar movement. Woods passed to Lunt, but Hickey got possession, and another free kick was taken by Met- calf. Woods was next prominent with a dribble, and Cawley put in a capital dodgy run. Baum and Haslam improved matters for the Albion team, and a free kick was given to Runcorn, which brought play into the visitors' half. Rigby, Gatley, and• Barker still kept the ball going, and in the midst of a combined rush Evans gained a try for Runcorn, but no goal resulted from the place kick. On resuming, after half time, Gatley dribbled to advantage, and IVhinyates punted to Green- wood, who caused play to be located in the Ruhcorn twenty-five. Woods then obtained possession, and , transferred the ball to Cawley, who contributed a grand run. Woodward, Hughes, and Kershaw executed a bit of good combined play, Booth returning with a powerful punt. The Rochdale forwards next brought play to ' neutral ground, when Lunt caught the ball nicely and I made tracks for his opponents' goal. Opposition soon awaited him, but he shot up the field and passed the three-quarters, who were lying in wait, and finally came • to the full back, which player he dodged grandly and scored a meritorious try, Woods kicking a goal. The remainder of the game was played in semi-darkness, and in the end Runcorn won by one goal, one try. and five minors, to one minor. Teams :—Runcorn: S. Booth, full back; W. H. Cawley, T. Woods, E. Lunt, three- quarters ; W. Evans and T. Whinyates, half backs • J. Gatley (captain), J. Bowyer, W. Shaw, Dutton, Lee, Barker, Rigby, Tipper, and Hailwood, forwards. Roch- dale Albion: G. Greenwood, back; Baum (captain), Hickey, and H. Metcalf, three-quarters; Calverley and Kershaw, half backs ; Woodward, Bcoth, Clarke, Whit- ham, J. Kershaw, Mharples, Hughes, Atherton, and Haslam, forwards. Referee, Mr. J. E. Warren, Warrington. WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS (A TeAms.)— This fixture was brought to a successful issue on Satur- day on Broughton ground, and was looked forward to with an unusual amonnt of interest owing to neither team having suffered defeat this season. The game was con- tested under the new rules, which certainly made the contest quicker, and several free kicks were allowed for infringements. Adamson having won the toss dgcided to play with the wind and hill in his favour' and Cooper kicked off, Isherwood returning into touch. The War- rington forwards broke away, and Horrocks, having his kick charged down by Ashurst caused play to be located near the home line. Fitton, Pickard, and Campion removed the pressure by a good dribble to half-flag, but Holmes, Lloyd, and Appleton carried the oval back again. Mclnnis was next prominent with a good run, and free kicks were awarded to both sides, play resting in the , centre. Isherwood and Donohue broke away with the ball at their toes, and Daniels caused the home team to \-• be again pressed on their lines, but they removed the 4. pressure by means of a free kick. Lawless passed nicely to Speakman, who kicked down the field, and Mclnnis getting possession made a grand run along touch. Daniels tackling him just in time. Holmes, Unsworth, and Molyneux relieved, but the Rangers' forwards came s away with a good dribble to the visitors' lines and missed a grand chance of scoring. Kicks between Appleton, Vorrocks, and Molyneaux transferred play to the other kad, where Mather passed to Daniels, who dropped at goal, but the kick was charged down, and Spencer and Marsh ran to the home 25. The Rangers were here allowed a free kick for a knock on, which Warburton returned into touch. Free kicks were the order of the day, Unsworth at length collaring Hood with the ball. Mather passed to Daniels who sprinted to the Rangers' line. Unsworth and Holmes came away from the scrimmage, kicking over the the line, and Horrocks fail- ing to kick dead, Unsworth fell, but could not ground the oval, and Holmes completed the try, which Isherwood failed to improve. Half-time was now

called, the score standing—Warrington 1 try to Rangers nil. Isherwood restarted, and Hood returned Appleton being tackled before he could get the oval away. Free kicks were here allowed to both sjdes for knocks on. Mather at length got in a pass to Lawless, who dribbled to the home 25, but E. Cooper, Richards, and Marsh put in a grand dribble to the visitors' quarters, Warburton relieving by kicking into touch. Unsworth, Ashurst, Adamson, and Beard ran the ball back again, and Cooper made strenuous efforts to get through. Unsworth bringing him down in the Warrington quarters. Free kicks were again given to each side, play eventually resting in the Rangers' 25, where Mather, gaining possession from a scrimmage; passed nicely to Daniels, who dropped a smart goal. After the kick-off, the home front rank dribhled to War- rington qnarters, but Lloyd, Beard, and Isherwood retaliated. and Mather passing smartly to Appleton, this player rounded his opponents in fine style and gained a brilliant try. The kick at goal was unsuccessful. Daniels being caught with the ball the referee allowed the Rangers a free kick at goal for the oval not being ' played at once, but nothing came of it. Good kicking by Appleton and Speakman carried play to the home line, where Adamson and Lawless tried to get in. Law- less, however, got in a good pass to Appleton, who again ran in at the corner flag, Isherwood failing at a difficult place. From the. drop out Ashurst made a splendid run to the home line, but the Rangers' forwards with a combined dribble carried the ball to the Warring- ton line, Warburton being forced to kick dead. Time was shortly afterwards called, the score standing—War- rington, 1 goal, 3 tries, 1 minor; Rangers, 1 minor. Teams :—Warrington Full back, W. Warburton ; three-quarter backs, Daniels. Appleton. and Speakman; half backs, Lawless and S. Mather; forwards, Adamsrm (captain), Beard, Isherwood, Molyneaux, Unsworth, Ashurst, Donohue, Lloyd, and Holmes. Broughton Bangers Full back, Horrocks ; three-quarter backs, Hood, Cooper, and Mclnnis; half backs, Marsh and Spencer ; forwards. Richards, Oman. Barnett, Campion, Hall, Fitton, Pickard, Kiffard, and E. Cooper. Rtmcom v. BIRKENHEAD.—The Runcorn team have commenced their season with a determination to carry almost everything before them, and maintain their position as champions of fair Cheshire. In eight matches played they have secured the extraordinary number of 13 goals, 12tries, and 46 minors as compared with 1 goal. 2 tries, and 13 minors obtained by the eight opposing teams, thus givino, a clear majority of 12 goals, 10 tries. and 33 minors in 'their favour. When the fact is taken into consideration that this result has been brought about whilst competing with such well-known clubs as Stockport, Salford, Bradford, Sale, Kendal Hornets, Burton-on-Trent, Broughton Rangers, and New Brighton, the scoring will appear to be the more important and satisfactory. On Saturday they paid a visit to Birken- head, where they played a mag,nificent game in the Upper Park in the presence of some 4,000 spectators, who had assembled notwithstanding the inclemency of the weather. The Runcomians, who had only suffered one defeat this season, and that at the hands of the powerful Bradford team, were accompanied by a. large body of football enthusiasts from Runcorn, a special train having been chartered for their conveyance at cheap railway rates On entering the arena of hostilities both teams were greeted with ringing cheers. Owing to the state of the weather, the ground was slippery, and grqatiy

interfered with the comfort of the players. At a quarter pastthree the match commenced, and the visitors having won :he toss, they elected to play from the lower end. Monteath kicked off for Birkenhead, and the play was centered in the visitors' ground. Riley, however, made a dashing run, after the ball was thrown into touch, to the home team's 25. Relief was obtained, and Brazendale, amidst immense applause, by his long and well directed kicks was the cause of a series of minors being put to the credit of Runcorn. He essayed an attempt at goal from half-way, and later on he attempted another. Black ran to midfield, but Riley, who was on the alert, collared and scrimmages ensued. An attempt was made by Blair to break through the Runcorn ranks, but his distress was quickly imminent, and Black almost immediately afterwards experienced a taste of Riley's strong embrace, and a little later on Crompton descended on Blair with success. On the half- way line scrimmages afterwards ensued, and L. Holden presented Blair with a chance, which, however, was mulled, and by a series of dribbles the ball was pushed on to the Birkenhead line. Relief was given by a free kick, and Wood and Jardine made an effort to effect a nassage. The Birkenhead forwards suc- ceeded in getting in a run, and the ball was dribbled to the line. Brazendale kicked dead, and put a stpp to what appeered to be a try. After the drop-out the visitors obtained a free kick, and scrimmages succeeded in front of the Birkenhead posts. Hughes made a splendid pass to Wainwright, who, however, was brought down before any serious mischief was accomplished. The Birkenhead captain obtained a free kick, which effected a clearance of the visitors. Hughes was accorded a sitnilar.indulgence, and Brazendale raised the hopes of his confreres. A notable movement on the part of the forwards then occurred, and Birkenhead secured an advantage within the territory of the visitors' team, and although relief was granted Jardine and Blair returned to the charge, anti the original opposition waS returned to. Riley, one of the Runcorn three-quarters, went to the front, and with the ball in the centre half-time was called with the score as follows :—Runcorn, five minors, Birkenhead, one minor. The ball was re-started, at the expiration of the interval, by W. Hughes, Blair returned. The play was then confined to the Birkenhead quarters. Wood showed good dribbling form, and Jardine, Blair, and Black put in some very god runs, and the ball was transferred to the Runcorn quarters. Brazendale with commendable celerity, came to the rescue, and a free kick resulted, but nothing Came of it. Jardine put Runcorn to the inconvenience of touching down. , A punt by Hughes followed, and C. Holden put in a tre- mendous punt into touch close to half way. From the throw out Park attacked the Runcorn quarters; but later on the visitors were enabled to travel the ball to the Birkenhead 25. Runcorn were afterwards credited 1 with a free kick, and long kicks followed by C. Holden I and Brazendale. The ball was then pushed on to the Birkenhead goal line, and a tight scrimmage ensued, but , Holden securing it, play was carried to the half-flag. Riley made one of his notable runs, and later on Brazen- dale was granted another free kick at goal, and was near scoring. Black, from the kickoff, made a first-class run, and finished up with a kick at goal. Brazendale again showed good form, and returned. A little later on he came prominently to front, aud the game resulted as. follows :—Runcorn, seven minors; Birkenhead' two minors. The teams were as follows :—Birkenhead Park: C. Holden, back; J. A. Black, „A. C. Blair, and A. Jardine, three-quarter backs; L. M. Holden and L. R. Paterson, half backs; A. G. Wood, P. H. Lockwood, W. T. Wood, G. P. Paterson, K. Monteath, R. P. Moodie, R. T. Moodie,C. Craig, and J. U. Kerr, forwards. Run- corn Brazendale, beck; W. A. Riley, J. H. Cromptan, and T. H. Davies, three-quarter backs; H. Hughes (captain) and J. Hollingworth, half backs ; W. Hughes, Hampson, G. T. Wainwright, P. Riley, W. H. Broady,F. Hancock, J. Gayter, R. Dolan, and E. Andrews for- wards

div.head: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. BROUGHTON RANGERS.

In wretched weather the rival forces of the above clubs met at Wilderspool on Saturday, when despite the miserable state of the elements, a fair attendance was accorded. Since the passing of the new rules by the Rugby Union, Saturday was anxiously looked forward to, and various opinions were expressed as to how the " wire-pullers " would fare under the new system of. play. Both sides were short of their usual team, having representatives doing duty in the county trial match at Whalley Range. A strong wind blew from goal to goal, necessitating the game to be contested in quarters.

Royle winning the toss, took advantage of the wind, and Frank Turner started, Hodson replying with a neat punt to the half-way flag. From the 'first line out Broughton broke away, and looked like scoring in the first minute, until Evans checked their career with a timely kick. Hodson, however, was instrumental in placing his side on the aggressive, and although the visitors got over, a glaring case of off-side play ruled the oval back. Edge made his mark, but Barnes quickly neutralized by a brilliant punt to the half-way flag. From the line out Fair Turner unintentionally knocked on, and a grand bid at goal was made by Boyle, a minor only accruing. The drop out found Warrington harrassing the Broughton defence, but Robertson came to the rescue of his side by a smart kick to half-way- Povey was applauded for o well-executed run, but Boyle was equal to the emergency, and transfered the oval from his line to neutral ground. Jolley was here afford- ed an opportunity of displaying his skill, but the slippery state of the oval was against him, and allowed McGowan to easily rush up and prevent his becoming dangerous. Barnes executed 9. tricky run, but his pass to Massey was unfortunately forward, and thus the chance was lost. The first quarter was ended with only a minor to the visitors' credit. Fair Turner responded brilliantly to the kick-off, and a grand dribble, in which Frank Turner and Ashton played a prominent part, almost had the desired effect. From the succeeding scrimmage, if it may be termed as such, a wild pass to Jolley served as relief to the Broughton men, but immediately after• pressure was again brought to bear on the visiting goal, by the smart rushes of the home forwards. Fortune, however, favoured the home team soon after, for from a pack near the post Antrobus secured possesion, and feiging to pass to Barnes he quickly eluded Boyle and planted the oval safely between the posts. Loud cheers greeted his smart play, and were reaewed when Barnes safely piloted the leather over the bar. The ball was again started from centre, and exchange kicks by the opposing backs ended with ailvantage to the home contingent. Massey was instrumental in taking the oval to the Broughton quarter flag, and Boyle subsequently kicked dead twice in succession. Free kicks were numerous, and although Fair, Turner, Barnes, mid Antrobus indulged in some neat transfers, and Evans put in some telling kicks, they failed to augment their , score, half-time being called, Warrington having an advantage of one goal two minors to Broughton Rangers one minor. Frank Turner resumed hostilities, and Fair, Turner from the kick-off lost a grand opportunity. The ball was got away, and Evans was to the fore with a smart drop well into the visitor's quarters. Quick passing by the visitors was now witnessed, but a kick by Massey added another minor to the score. The visitors now went away with a dash, and after give-and-take play they gradually worked the oval to the Warrington line, Hosker ultimately dropping a clever goal. Warrington now went away, but their efforts were easily frustrated by the smart play Of Boyle and Hosker. The last- named essayed to force an opening, but Speakman ' blocked his way. Robertson cleared his lines, and gained ground by a judicious kick. Fair Turner made a strong effort here, but the whistle sounded, and ends were again changed. The last portion of the game was all in favour of tile home division, but their efforts to add to the score proved futile, and when the whistle sounded for" no side" the telegraph board indicated that the match was drawn, the scores reading :—War- rington, 1-0-3 ; Broughton Rangers, 1-0-1. An robus, Evans, Jolley, Fair, Turner, Nevins, and Povey were the pick of the Warringtonians, whilst Royle,fHosker, McGowen, and Atkinson are deserving, of praise in the Broughton division. The following were the teams :—Warrington: J. W. Evans, back ; Massey, Barnes, and Jolley, three-quarter backs; Antrobus and Speakman, half-backs ; Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Ashton, Littlewood, Povey, Creaghan, Randles, Nevins, and Hayes, forwards. Broughton Rangers: Royle, back; Robertson, McGowan and Hodson, three-quarter backs; Edge and Hosker, half backs ; Atkinson, Skidmore, T. Squires, A. Squires, E. Jackson, Powell, Robinson, Higginbottom, and Moxon, forwards.
ASSOCIATION. STOCKTON HEATH V. SPEKE (2ND TEAMS.)—Played at Speke on Saturday, and ended in a draw of one goal each.

STOCKTON HEAIII v. SPEKE (IST TF.AMS.)—This match was played at Warrington before 300 spectators and after a good game ended in a win for the home team by goals to 3. Onions,Burgess,and Rose played a splendid game for the Heath.

ALLEGED MURDER BY A BOY.—A boy, 14 years of age, named James Ward, son of a miner at Muirkirk, was on Thursday at Ayr committed for trial on a charge of kill- ing a child named Jane Muir, aged seven. A younger brother of the accused and Muir quarrelled, and the accused, it is alleged, struck her with his clenched fist on the head, causing concussion of the brain, from which the child died a few days after.

Last Saturday Dillon figured prominently the i match East v. West Lancashire, and it s quite certain that' he will be an acquisition to the forward department of the county team.
FOUR CHILDREN BURNED TO DEATH.

Four children named. Ransom were burned to death on Wednesday night at Helmsley, near Malton, in Yorkshire. It is supposed that during theabsence of their parents the children playedwith a lighted lamp, or that the flame was blown by the wind towards the bedroom drapery. Anyhow, the house was "soon on fire, and burnt -quickly, the habitation being chiefly of timber and thatch. Two children were rescued alive from the burning cottage. but they had ,sustained such terrible burns that they died almost immediately, and the charred bodies of the two other children were not recovered until later. The mother is lying seriously ill with grief at the fearful fate of her little ones.

div.head: RE-OPENING OF ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, BURTON WOOD.
div.p: RE-OPENING OF ST. MICHAEL'S CHURCH, BURTON WOOD.

This churcb, after being closed for extensive alterations for about six weeks, was re-opened on Sunday. St. Michael's is really a chapel-of-ease for the Parish Church of Warrington, and was erected for the convenience of persons residing on the extreme outskirts of the parish. It was built on a small scale, and until some few years ago its interior presented a most antiquated appearance. In 1837 it was enlarged by adding to it at the east end a small chancel, sufficiently large, however, to contain communion table and rails. A few years back some of the old-fashioned pews were removed and replaced by others of a mo4ern type. The roof, which was of the old-fashioned ceiling type, had become entirely worn out, and the church- wardens decided to renew it. The church was therefore closed, and the Contract for renewing the roof given to Mr. Joseph Pennington, builder, Earlestown, who has ver'y deditably executed his work. In place of the hideous looking ceiling, which at one place came almost in contact tivith the top of the organ, a splendid gothic pitchpine roof has beemerected, which gives the church a greatly improved appearance, and all it requires now to remove what we have termed its antiquated state is a new organ. Owing to the removal of the ceiling, it has become necessary to make seine alterations in the chancel, over which a new arch has been sprung, and the improvement rendered is apparent at a. glance. On Sunday special services were held to commemorate the re-opening. The Rev. G. Bartle, of Southport, occu- pied the pulpit at the morning and evening services. Under the leadership of Mr. W. Sephton, the choir ren- dered at the morning service the anthem, "Behold how good and,beautiful.' and in the evening "The earth is the Lord's." At the afternoon service the sermon was preached by the Rev. F. W. Willis, M.A., rector of Warrington, and without , referring specially to the occasion for which he pleaded, he delivered a most instructive and appropriate discourse. There were large congregations at each service, and the collections throughout the day amounted to £33,95. 9d.

div.head: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERA.-
div.p: WARRINGTON TEMPERANCE FEDERA.-
TION.
The annual meeting of the members 6f this Federation as held on Monday evening at the Horsemarket-st. Coffee Tavern. The Rev. J. Yonge presided.

div.head: FBDERATIOtj.AND ITS WORK..
div.p: THE FBDERATIOtj.AND ITS WORK..

The Rev. J. J. Lartansat'', hon. sec.) read the report, detailing the work of the Federation daring the past year, which was submitted to the meeting recently held in the Co-operative Hall, and at that time published in our columns. Mr. W. ROBERTS (hon. treasurer) also submitted the statement of accounts for the past year from which it appeared that he had a balance in hand of .C 2 ss. Ild. —The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoptien. of the reports, said they might fairly congratulate themselves on the measure of success that had attended that new temperance movement in Warrington. One criticism offereu in days past had been that the Temperance Society was hardly doing the work which might be expected of it, but he thought that criticism could hardly obtain ,any longer. The public advocacy of temperance principles had been considerable, and the exceedingly useful work at the Licensing Sessions would commend itself to all the friends of temperance throughout the borough. (Hear, hear.) —Mr. J. WALKER seconded the proposal, and endorsed all the chairman had said. He suggested that the proposal should inolude a vote of thanks to the officials, and especially to Mr. Langham. (Hear, hear.) They were deeply indebted to Mr. 'Alight= f-ir the really admirable manner in which he had performed his work, which they all saw and felt was to him EV labour of love. (Hear, hear) He (Mr. Walker) thought the work that had been done by the Federation would compare favourably with that of any k previous year in Warrington. They had stirred up a feeling in the minds of the public which was not usually interested in temperance work, and he took it that it would be their duty in the forthcoming year to take advantage of that feeling and make the most of it. It was evident that they had a strong force arrayed against them which was organised,and they must also be organised to deal with it.—The resolution, coupled with a vote of thanks to the secretary and treasurer, was then adopted.— The Rev. J. J. LANGHAM, in responding. said he thought their cause was growing. It was a hopeful sign that the new rector of War- rington was. starting a temperance society in his own parish. They bad never had one thn.e before. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

It was decided to invite the Rector of Warrington, to become president of the Federation in place of the Rev. S. Wilkinson, who, it was understood, did not desire re-election. The other officers were re-elected with the addition of Mr. H. J. Longton as a vice-president, and Mr. Stringer as a member of the Committee.

div.head: TRH Vi'...TCH COMMITTEE AND ITS MEMBERSHIP.
div.p: TRH Vi'...TCH COMMITTEE AND ITS MEMBERSHIP.

Mr. J. WALKER said he believed it Vats7;;;;;;;:ed to appoint Councillor W. Bolton, who was a brewer and an owner of licensed houses in the town, to be a member of the Watch Committee. There was no legal objec- tittle to a btewer or a publican sitting upon a Watch Committee, but it was a rule pretty well acted on throughout the Kingdom not to appoint men who were interested in licenses or grocers' :licenses to sit upon these Committe&s, seeing that .hey would then have some control over the police whose business it was to carry out the licensing laws. The feeling that he (Mr. Walker) had was that that meeting should', if it were in order, pass some resolution expressing its regret that the Town Council propose 4 to make that appointment. It was just possible that a resolution from that meeting might have some weight with the more houghtful members of the Town Council. (Hear, hear.)— The Rev. J. J. LANOHAJd asked how it waskaown that such a proposition had been made.—Mr. WALKER said there had been an informal preliminary mee,tingof the Council to arrange the Committees.—Councillor H. ROBERTS said the proposal to put Mr. Bolton on the Watch Com- mittee was done very quickly, and before he (Councillor Roberts) entered the room, He was astounded when he heard of the proposal, and he told the Mayor that it would not go unchallenged. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. J. WALKER then moved the following resolution :—" That the members of the Warrington Tempefance Federation assembled in annual meeting, regret to learn that it is proposed to appoint to a place upon the Watch Com- mittee of the Town Connell a gentleman who is a brewer and the owner of several licensed houses. They trust that the members of the Town Council, acting in the best interests of the community will not confirm the appointment; and further resolve that a copy of this , resolution be sent to all the members of the Town , Council."—Mr. J. GANDY seconded this proposal which was agreed to unanimously.
TUE EEOECEMENT OF THE LICHNSENG LAWS.

Mr. J. (Many said that he saw they had been doing in Manchester some work with reference to the enforce- ment of the licensing laws, which they in Warrington had not as yet been so successful in doing as they wished. He suggested thlt the work be again taken up and that pressure be brought to bear upon the Watch Committee and the magistrates to enforce the licensing laws. He himself had a strong opinion that it was illegal for so many people who were really only servants of the brewery companies to hold licenses. He should like to see that matter pushed home.—some discussion took place on he point, and in the end it was decided to appoint a sub-committee, consisting of the Chairman, Coupcillors H. Roberts, Mr. J. walker, Mr. J. Gandy, and the Secretary and Assistant Secretary (the Rev. J. J. Longhorn and Mr. D. Houghton), to report upon the question of enforcing the licensing laws in the borough. A vote of thanks to the Chairman brought the pro- ceedings to a close.

div.head: WARRINGTON PUBLICAN AND HIS DOG.
div.p: A WARRINGTON PUBLICAN AND HIS DOG.

Judge Hughes, Q.C., sitting at Stockport County Court, has had a case before him in which Joseph Alli- son, of the Gladstone Arms, Warrington,sued Richd. Hulse, manufacturer and engineer, Manchester, and Tom Morley, of the Cross Keys Inn, Adswood, for the recovery of .£l3 10s., balance of a stake. Plain- tiff was represented by Mr. H. J. Longton, solicitor, Warringfon ; Mr. J. W. Lowe. barrister, represented the defendant Hulse. and Mr. Gray, solicitor, Stock- port, appeared for Morley.—Mr. Longton said the claim was for .£l3 10s., balance of a plize that was offered by the defendants, and won by the plaintiffs dog Just, at, the_Adswood Coursing Meeting in March last. Shortly before that plaintiff had a dog which Won the Great Cheshire Stakes at Adswood. ' and that affair was settled up by the defendants all right. It was then that the defendant Hulse asked. ' him if he would enter for the Eclipse Stakes, valued at £3OO, the entries being fixectat 64, with an entrance fee of £6 each. Plaintiff entered, paying £6 to Hulse: but, as 64 dogs were not entered, the prizes were divided as follow :—First, £9O ; second, £34 10s. ; third, £l5 10s. Plaintiff's dog won the third prize, but he only received £2, and was now suing for the balance. The defendants were in the unfortunate position of not knowing who ought to pay. Each had written 'hat the other was liable, and Hulse had offered to pay half the amount. He (Mr. Longton) contended that plaintiff had a right to obtain from one of the two, whichever it was.—The plaintiff stated that he won the first prize in the Great Cheshire Stakes, and got £3O and a Cup (the first prize), these being given to him by Hulse. He entered for the ' Eclipse Stakes, and paid the £6 in two instalments of £3, the second of which he personally gave to Hulse, who handed it over to Morley. He saw Hulse in Man- chester after the Eclipse Stakes had been run, and re- ceived from him an offer to pay half the amount claimed and his e ' xpenses if he would not take County Court proceedings, but he refused the offer.--Cross-examined: Hulse did the smooth work, and Morley he rough.—Mr. 'Gray here admitted that Morley was the promoter of the first sweep (Great Cheshire), but Hulse gave the cup.—Cross-examined: Understood Hulse had or- ganised the sweep for pleasure. As it was successful, he (Hulse) "cracked a bottle of • cham ' or two."—(Laugh- ter.)—James Bancroft,Warringcon, testified to Hulse par ing the first prize (£9O), and ordering Morley to get the rabbits ready.—Other witnesses deposed to Mr. Hulse being the responsible party, the pistol firer stating that he was paid by Mr. Hulse.—A man named John T. Newton said he was checker for the Eclipse Stakes, and the gate money went to Mr. Hulse.—Defendant denied being the responsible party. It was Morley who proposed the Eclipse Stakes, and Mr. Morley being put down as secretary was because it was thought that it would give the thing more respectability. He denied paying Morley for being secretary or for any other service rendered by him. He always handed the gate money over to Mr. Morley. Morley kept and trained his dogs, and in that respect was his servant.—His Honour gave judgment for the plaintiff, but reserved all all questions as to liability between the two defendants to each other, to be tried in another action.

div.head: LATE WARRINGTON CLERGYMAN'S
div.p: A LATE WARRINGTON CLERGYMAN'S
WIFE IN TROUBLE.

At the Hammersmith (London) Police Court, yesterday week, Elizabeth Montgomery, a lady about 40 years of age, residing in Church-street. Kensington, was placed in the dock charged with being drunk and disorderly.—P.C. Goodwin said on Thursday night he was called to the prisoner in High-street, Kensington, by a cabman who had driven her about all the afternoon. She refused to pay the fare or give her name and Address. She was very drunk.—Prisoner: I was not drunk.— Joseph Cole. the cabman, was called, and said he had only been paid a portion of the fare. Ile claimed 3s. more.—Mr. Paget offered to allow her to settle the fare with the cabman before disposing of the charge, but she refused to accept this, and said she had already paid the legal fare. However, the prisoner was taken into the gaoler's room with the cabman,and after a brief consultation the magistrate was informed that she said she would not pay any more if she stopped there all day. The magistrate then ordered a summons to issue fcr the fare, to be heard forthwith. The prisoner was then removed for the summons to be made out in the office and to be served upon her. After the charges had been disposed of the prisoner was brought into the court again, and allowed to stand in front of the solicitors' table, 'the place usually appropriated for defendants.—The cabman said the defendant hailed him in Church-st., and he drove her to Notting-hill, to Chiswick,and other places, returning to the place where he took her up. She refused to alight from the cab, and he called a constable. He received :is., but the fare was 88.— Mr. Paget ordered her to pay 38., with is. 64. costs, and asked if she had the money.—The defendant: No I have not any (pro- ducing an empty purse.) A; it was a civil debt Abe ,payment conl4l, not then be enforced. The magistrate asked her if she was married. The defendant said she was the wife of a clergyman. Seeing that the magistrate looked astonished, she added: "A clerk in holy orders. Do you under- stand ? "—Mr. Paget: Do you mean that ?—Defend- ant: Yes (laughing.) He, the cabman, says nothing about the two glasses of 'ale I gave him and six- pence besides.—Mr. Pagett referred to the Clergy List, and found that the Rev. It: W. Ph airs Mont- gomery was curate of St. Elphin, Warrington.— The defendant said he was now in Suffolk. Her husband was roving about. Her father-in-law had been a stipendiary magistrate in Ireland. She was living in a fiat, but she was leaving, as she was not somfortable.—The hearing of the charge was re- sumed, the Prisoner returning to the position in i which she had previously been placed n the dock. She said she was indignant and excited, but she denied utterly being drunk.—The constable said she had two bottles of beer, another bottle contain- ing port wine, and an empty bottle which had con- tained sherry.—The prisoner said the bottles were only pocket pistols.—Mr. Paget: You are fined 20s. —Prisoner: Oh I—Mr. Paget: Or seven days' imprisonment. —Prisoner (with surprise): No; what for P—Mr. Paget: For being drunk and disorderly. —Prisoner: I was not. Excuse me.—The assilitant- goaler then removed her, and she was locked up in the cells.

COMING-OF-AGE. FESTIVITIES AT WARRINGTON': ,

The festivities in celebration, of the coming-of age of Air. John Alfred Wilson-Pattern, grandson of Lord Winmarleigh. and heir to the Winmarleigh estates, were continued at Warrington and Rixtc n on Monday and Tuesday. __ _ _

- REJOICINGS AT RIXTON. On Monday afternoon the cottage tenantry on the Rizton estate, together with their wives ard children, were entertained to tea in a marquee that had been erected near Itizton Old Hall,the residence of Mr. R, T. Lose, one of the tenants. About 150 persons sat down to tea,which Was provided by Mr. Speakman,of the Saracen's Head Hotel, Wilderspool. Among those present were the Hon. Minor Wilson- Patten, the lion. Elizabeth Wilson-Patten, Miss Constance Wilson-Patten, the Rev. F. G. and Mrs. Roberts, Mr. John White' Mr. and Mrs. R. T. Lowe, Mr. and Mrs. Hindley, Mrs. G. Caldwell, Mr. and Mrs. Higham, Mr. and Mrs. Lawless, and Mrs. Down.

A GOOD OLD CUSTOM. II When tea was over Mr. John White, in the course of a short address, mentioned that neither Lord Winmarleigh nor his grandson were able to be present, the latter, who is an officer in the Ist Life Guards, being prevented from attending by military duties. It was a good old custom, and one which they did well to keep up, that on an occasion of that kind the landlord should call toge- ther his tenantry to rejoice with him. It was a day of great rejoicing for Lord Wißmarleigh, and to whom should he look for sympathy and affection if not to his tenants, with whom he had been so intimately asso- - ? It was a day of rejoicing, because whenever it should please Providence to remove him he could -feel that his duty had been fairly well done throughout his life. He could also feel that in the hands of his ...rand- son his inheritance would not be wasted, and that the good name he had always borne would be in no way tarnished. (Applause.) LORD WINMARLEIOR AS A LANDLORD. • After a few remarks had been made by the Hon. Ellinor Wilson-Patten, the Rev. G. F. Roberts said that during the eighteen years he had been in that neighbour- hood he had seldom heard anyone spoken of on all sides with greater respect and love than their landlord, the noble Lord Winmarleigh. Ile was an excellent landlord, and they all appreciated his many kindnesses. It was a very happy circumstance that the hoble lord was able to be so good a landlord; it was sometimes the case that landlords were unable, by reason of having paid too much money for the land at the time of purchase to be kind to their tenantry, although they were wishful' to do so. But, happily, their chief landlord had both the heart and the power to do it. (Applause.) He had no doubt they would join him in expressing a hope that Lord Winmarleigh might live longto show a bright example to 1 his grandson, and when the day arrived when Mr. Wilson-Patten became their landlord they trusted that he would deem it his greatest honour tsi walk in the foot- stepa of his honoured and noble . krandfather.—Loud cheers were then given for Lord Winmarleigh and Mr. Wilson Patten.—Professor Weber afterwards gave an entertainment.

TENANTS' TEA AT WARRINGTON. About 150 of the cottage tenants on the Warrington estates, with their wives and families, were on Monday evening entertained to tea in Holy Trinity schoolroom. Amongst those in attendance were Mr. John Alfred Wilson-Patten, the heir; the Hon. Misses Wilson-Patten, the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, Mr. and Mrs. John White, Mr. H. B. Melville, the Rev. H. E. Glenn, and Mr. William Johnson. After tea Professor i.e Mare, ventriloquist, assisted by Mr. Worsley, of Manchester, gave an entertainment.

LORD WINMARLEIGII AND CHURCH WORK. The Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, in proposing a vote of thanks to Lord Winmarleigh, said that they could not point to any department of Church work in which progress had been made in that parish without being bound to acknowledge that his lordship had contributed to that progress. He need not allude on that occasion to the good work done by other members of the family, and would only say there were special reasoas why the name of Lord Winmarleigh was dear in the affection of the people of Warrington, which made it especially gratifying to them to be permitted to share in these festivities. He expressed in their name, and in his own, their most sincere congratulations that Lord Winmar- leigh had been spared to see the coming of age of his grandson, and they might also sincerely and heartily offer their congratulations to Mr. Wilson-Patten upon having reached his majority under such auspicious and happy circumstances. (Applause.)—The motion was heartily carried. Short speeches were also made by Mr. JohtlWhite and Mr. Wilson-Patten.
DINNER TO THE' REIFFON-ARD WARRINGTON
TENANTRY.

On Tuesday evening the tenantry of the Rixton and Warrington estates, together With a number of invited guests, were entertained to dinner at the Lion Hotel, Warrington, when occasion was taken of the opportun- ity to present to Mr. .T. A. Wilson-Patten a handsome silver claret jug the gift of the tenants., The proceed- ings were presided over by Lord Winmarleigb, the vice- chairs being occupied by Mr. R. T. Lowe (Rixton), Councillor T. Hutchinson,. and Councillor T. Jolley. Amongst those also present dere the Mayor of Warring- ton (Alderman T. H. Sutton), the Rector of Warrington (the Rev. F. W. Willis), Mr. J. A Wilson-Patten, Mr. Gilbert Greenall, Mr. W. Beamont, Mr. R. Davies, Mr. John White, Mr. W. Sharp, Major Pickraere, Mr. C. Lyon, Mr. Mclver, Mr. H. B. White, the,Revs. S. Wilkinson, E. C. R. Carleton, G. F. Roberts, and E. W. Wilcocks, Councillors J. Shaw Green, J. Pierpoint, W. Bolton, R. Heaton, J. E. Wright ; Drs. T. Starkey-Smith, C. 'White,C. N. Spinks,and Messrs T J. Down,H. Milling, Robinson, H.B. Melville, R. W. Collin, Radnall, Tanstall, D. W. Finney, Bircha 11, H Ferguson, C. Wallington J. .Tiedgcock, W. Lawless, E. Richardson, Monk, Chad- wick, Ashurst; Rigby, Kiernan, F. Massey, John Higham, Hampson, .T. L. Tunstall, John Flesketh, W. Gill, S. Bar- low, Clay, Caldwell, S. Leas. James Marsh, Maginn, Toft, John Taylor, W. W. Westwell, W. Fletcher, &c. The usual loyal toasts were given from the chair and were duly honoured.

THE TOAST OF "THE CLERGY." Mr. Robert Davies briefly submitted the toast of "The Bishops and Clergy, and the Ministers of all denomina- tions," which was responded to by the Rector of War- ringon. Mr. Willis said that he could not, conceive of any occasion more gratifying to Lord Winmarleigh than such a one as the present, particularly in these days, when he supposed the relations had been a little bit strained betwecn landlord and tenant owing to the agri- cultural depression, and to know what a hearty and cordial feeling there was between landlord and tenants there. The clergy had not that relation of tenant and landlord, and yet some of them had a kind of relation with the ratepayers. He was utterly ignorant of all these things efew months ago. He was then a poor incumbent, paid by a cheque to the day—(laughter)— but now he supposed he was looked upon as a very rich one and he had relations with the land. He might men- tion the name of another noble lord between whom and his tenants he believed there was the same kind of feel- ing existing, and that was lils patron, Lord Lilford. (Applause.) The church wardens who represented three parishes which happened to be in his (the Rector's) gift came to him and told him of the difference there was in the incomes of the incumbents, and, aided by the gener- osity of his patron, they had been able to make their relations a little bit more on the same scale ;end footing than they were before—(applause)--a step which had given satisfaction bob to theincumbents and the rate- pa.yers. (Applause.) A NEW SHOOTING GROUND FOR THE VOLUNTEERS. Mr. W. Sharpe, who proposed the "Army, Navy, and Reserve Forces," referred to changes that had taken , place in the services. and incidentally mentioned that if ever the channel fleet arrived at Warringth n by way of ' the Ship Canal the officers and blue jackets 'Would- be heartily welcomed. With regard to the volunteers great difficulty was now experienced in finding rifle ranges. The local volunteers had been first of all driven from their shooting ground at Orford. They went to Lymm, but the range there was now closed, and he believed that, mainly through the kindness of Lord Winmarleigh, a new shooting ground had been obtained at Rixton, which would afford some of the finest shooting in England, not only for Warrington, but for several other corps. (Applause.)—ln responding to the toast Alder- man Pickreere observed that when the first volunteer corps was started in Warrington, in 1859, they cast about for a source from whence they could obtain a little money to help thefh out of their difficulties. At that time they were in a very plain, and he might say crude, condition, and they had to buy their own rifles and ammunition. .:The cartridges stuck in the rifles and they could not get them out again. (Laughter) But who was it that came forward and set them up? It was Lord Winmarleigh. He it was who gave them the first grand start in Warrington, and they had never looked back since that time. He had always been a friend to the corps, and the volunteers had always honoured the name of Winmarleigh. (Applause.) . . PRESENTATION OF A SILVER CLARET JTIO. _ . _

At this point of the proceedings Mr. John White explained that the Rixton tenantry were desirous of presenting Mr. Wilson Patten with a silver claret jug, which was then handed to the heir by Mr. Caldwell, the descendant of a family which has occupied the same farm on Lord Winmarleigh's estate for a hundred years. After a few remarks had been made by the noble Chairman, who expressed the hope that atoome future timo be should have the opportunity of taking his grandson round with him to see the tenantry, Mr. J. A. Wilson-Patten returned his thanks for the gift. In the course of his speech he expressed regret that ,his military duties had curtailed his stay in Warrington, and remarked that he had not been able up to the nresent to devote much time to the study of the commercial interests on which the welfare, not only of Warrington, but of Lancashire, in a great measure depended; but tie felt, as he thought every Lancashire man ought to feel, that nobody connected with the county should long remain ignorant of these things, and it was hisintention, so far as he was able, to acquaint himself with those commercial interests, especially those in which the welfare of Warrington was cencerned. (Applause.)
