, HERE are very few men in England who are naturally more hearty and healthy than James Braddock. He is a gamekeeper, and lives at Jepson's Clough, Adlington, near Macclesfield. He is stoutly built, and until two years ago we may say he never had a week's ill- ness in the whole sixty years of his life. One day this summer (1887) he was found at home, and in the course of the talk that sprang up, Braddock told the following story, which we print because it will interest many besides himself. Pie said: "Perhaps you have already heard about my case, and if so, it's no use my telling it all over again." "I heard it alluded to in Manchester," was the answer, "but I should like to hear it from your own lips." "Well sir," said James, "I'll run it over for you. I've told it lots of times, aald its always done good to somebody. It was two years ago this summer that I was taken very bad with indigestion. How ill I was, and how I finally got cured, is no news to the people in this part of the country, sir. Scores of them came from far and near to see me and talk to me about it. I first noticed a dull feeling all over me, and my appetite failed so I could eat nothing without just forcing it down, sir; and then it lay like a heavy weight ,C) 11 my stomach. Food used to make me feel strong for work and exercise, Put now it seemed to do me no good at all. My mouth tasted bad, and when t looked in the glass I saw my skin and eyes had a yellow colour, and People said I was dreadfully bilious, my liver was out of order, and my blood 41 full of poison. And so I believed, for my head ached and my legs and Irxns ached, as though I had some manner of fever hold of me. I took pills, 41d a hundred other medicines, but they only made me feel a little easier for clay or two, and then I was worse than ever. "After a bit, sir, I began to be short of breath, you know, and had to sit lown and rest, when once I could tramp all day without being tired or once .etching a long breath. I couldn't make out what was the matter with me Whatever had brought it on, but I kept on getting worse, and that much I 4Tas sure of. My heart would flutter and get weak and faint in my breast,

and that frightened me more than the stomach trouble, for I didn't know then that the indigestion and dyspepsia were really the cause of it all, sir. People kept telling me I had the heart complaint, and was likely to fall down dead any minute. You may fancy how this took all the courage out of me, and I thought my work was done in this world. So it went on, sir, and neither my friends nor the doctors appeared to understand what was ailing me. "One day I was taken with such a queer spell, it almost scares me to think back of it. I couldn't get my breath. I was choked as though a strong man had me by the throat, and I was sure I was going to die. The people fanned me and gave me whisky, and after a while I came out of it, weak as a cat, sir, and all in a cold sweat.,

"But my stomach got worse afterwards, and I was afraid the choking might come back, and the next time it would certainly kill me. It was about this time, one day, I picked up a North Cheshire Newspaper and read of a case like mine being cured by Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup. I thought half-a-crown would na' break me, and I bought a bottle The first few doses did me good, sir. You wouldn't 'a believed it, neither would I, but it did. In a few days, maybe two weeks, sir, my stomach began to act and my victuals stopped on it, and my strength begun to, come back." "You had no more choking then P" said the visitor. "No sir, not after that. The fluttering of the hearttrouloled me no more, and the yellow went out of my eyes and skin; and, to put it short, sir, after taking two bottles of Mother Seigel's Syrup I got as well as I ever was in my life. 'What this medicine is made of I don't know, but lam sure that it's not like anything else. If I hadn't seen that account of it in the paper, and been led to use it, as certain as I talk to you now, sir, I believe I should have been under the sod months and months ago. I tell about it to everybody, and will do so as long as I have a tongue in my head, sir." Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup is for sale by all chemists and medicine vendors, and by the proprietors, A. 3. White, Limited, 35, Farringdon- road, London, E.C., Price 2s. 6d. per bottle.

7‘ THE MORAL OF THE ELECTIONS."

Sir,—Your correspondent. " Sanitas," feasibly argues that the intercepting depots are not so black as they have been painted, or Mr. Diggle would have been returned to the Town Council as a protest to the actions of the Sanitary Committee. I am not going to discuss the point, and simply write to say that, notwithstanding what " Sanitas " may argue, the depots smell as much as ever they did, and continue to be an abominable nuisance.—Yours, Szc., Warrington, Noy. 8,1888.
SCENT.

MRS. PARTINGTON AND THE CHANNEL FLEET. Sir,—That was a good joke of yours last week about the Warrington Mrs. Partington being somewhat mixed up about "Mark Masonry in Cheshire," but I can go you. one asgood. There is ano her Mrs. P. in Warrington who is puzzling ber wise old head to find out why so many people went to Liverpool to see a flannel sheet and some blue jackets. She declares that there are as good flannel sheets in Warrington as out of it, and as for blue jackets (navy blue, I suppose) she can get them anywhere by paying for them. It should in justice be added that Mrs. Partington is a little deaf, and liable to make mistakes.—Yours Sec.,. . _
"HA! HA!"
CORPORATION EMPLOYES AND THE MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS.

Sir,—Reading an account of the results of the munici- pal elections the other day, I observed that quite a host of those hard-working and well-paid servants of the Corpora ion had been employed in the polling-booths in official capacities, far which, I suppose, they would receive the regular fees. What a happy family they appear to be, and not at all selfish! But don't you think, sir, it would be as well if struggling tradesmen and rate- payers had a little "look in" when these official crumbs are dis ributed ? It certainly appears as though these geniuses employed in the public offices of the borough were anxious to monopolise the whole loaf.—Yours, &c., Nov. 6, 1888. NORTH-WEST WARD.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S COUNCIL MEETING.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S COUNCIL MEETING.

Sir,—At the meeting of the- Town Council to-day, whilst I was speaking to an amendment proposed by CounMllor ,Monks with reference to the formation of the Watch Committee, I made a certain statement as to Councillor Bolton which led him to interrupt me with the exclamation :—" That is a deliberate falsehood !" Now, Sir, I am prepared to prove that my assertion was correct in every particular; and no one knows this better than Councillor Bolton.

It seems to me that the Mayor did not sufficiently realize the gravity and impropriety of Councillor Basil's remark, or he would at once have called upon that gentleman to withdraw it, and thus have enabled me to finish my statement. As it was, the waist of this protection left no other course open for me than to resume my seat as a protest against the discourteous treatment I was subjected to. No member of the House of Commofis is permitted to say that another member speaks falsely, and I fail to see why it should be per- mitted in the Warrington Town Council.—Yours &c. W. PIERPOINT. Warrington, Nov. 9th, 1888.

div.head: STUDY OF GRAMMAR.
div.p: THE STUDY OF GRAMMAR.

Sir —A correspondent in your columns, I think it was, stated the other day that it was impossible for some of the candidates for municipal honours to speak six con- secutive sentences without violating every rule in grammar. This remark led me to ask myself what is being done for the improvement of the rising generation in this respect. My experience tends to the conclusion "-t the rising will be no better than the risen generation. Whether it LI that gra.Mtnai I?* 1:19. taught in our ele- mentary schools, or taught in such I, nas;;;;.2 as to become irksome to young students, I cannot say. All I can say is that not one boy in a hundred can speak to you for two minutes with any degree of grammatical accuracy. As you pass along the street you repeatedly hear fromthe boys " them's um," " never no more, "there was two' style of speech ; and, if you attempt to correct the speakers with any reference to the study of grammar, you are met with a remark as to "that dry stuff." Mentioning boys reminds me also of another little matter.that may interest some of them. In the course a a somewhat lengthened experience, I have very rarely indeed come across a boy with any pretentions as to manners. Taken as a whole, the boys I have encoun- tered have been an ill-behaved, vulgar-spoken lot, -with- out the slightest shadow of respect either for their equals or superiors. Who is to blame for this state of affairs I know not; but I would advise all boys, before starting on their Monday morning rounds in search of a place, to devote a little time to the study of both grammar and politeness.—Yours, &c.,AN OBSERVER.

div.head: POPERY IN RUNCORN AND FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCHES.
div.p: POPERY IN RUNCORN AND FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCHES.

Sir,—At these places illegal processions of clergy and choir have taken place contrary to Royal injunctions of 1547. Why? In order that homage may be done to the clergy, as opposed to the scriptures (1 Cor 4c. 5v.). Why was the chancel raised after serving near two gen- erations? To elevate the clergy (alias priests) nearer heaven, as the Sacerdota,lists say, "it is the most holy place." Why do they insist on 8 a.m Communion to the exclusion of 8 p.m. in accordance with Matt. 26e., Exod. 12c. 6v.? Because it favours fasting, and is a step towards the mass, and farther it is more to the mind of Bishop Stubbs, of whom they are afraid. What kind of teaching may children and youths get when some of the teachers hold Sohn 20c 23v. to teach apostolic succession, priestly absolution, and auridular confes- sion? (most wonderful verse this), and are ignorant of the first word (but) in next verse, and of corresponding passage in Luke 24c. 33v. At confirmation (Frodsham) they were taught to meive bread in the Communion ila the palm of their hand, left under right forming a cross. -Where do they get this froth? Echo answers where? The Bible says take," Greek says " labe" i.e. grin, grasp, lay hold of ; a beautiful spiritual signification. And what teaching may they get out of "Hymns Ancient and Modern ?" The leading errors of Rome, Mary worship, image worship, transubstantiation, lying (316,394). Children are taught to bow to the table (priestly altar) and why? Because they say, not straight out yet, "that Christ is on it." Parents! Ask your children what the clergy say to them on Sunday and week "days, especially some of the curates, men of Oxford leaflet No. 24 stamp. They worship they know not what, and fail to compre- hend. Article, 19, and Canon 55 says a prayer is to be used before sermon, not Popish invention of Trinity. Nov. 7, 1888.
OBSERVER.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH SWELLS AND THE SHOP ASSISTANT. _ .
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH SWELLS AND THE SHOP ASSISTANT. _ .

Sir,—Sometime ago I was astonished to read in a shop window a public advertisement at the foot of which were the words—" No Stockton Heather need apply !" I have pondered these words considerably, wondering what peculiar trait, Stockton Heath people possessed to merit this prohibition. But at length lam beginning to find out, as the following episode will show. A young lady shop assistant who resides at Stockton Heath, and goes home to dinner, was unable to catch Connor's bus now that the driver is making up for past dilatoriness by leaving before the time. By some exer- tion, she could just catch the Carriage Lo 5. vehicle, but as the distance she had to go was only equal to the penny length, she agreed with the conductor that if he would take-her for the penny she would ride everyday. The bargain was kept, even though a new conductor was put on, but a couple of swells who were casual customers had noticed the girl pay the penny, and they evidently did net like it. So these swells; -who earned perhaps as many pounds weekly as the OOP assistant earned shillings, put their heads together, and set in motion a dog-in-the-manger policy. Sundry interviews were evidently had with the powers that be, for the poor 'bus conductor narrowly escaped instant dismissal. and the shop assistant is again compelled to walk. And all because of the extreme meanness of a couple of well-to-do young " gentlemen," who could not bear to see a young lady have a penny ride! If such be. the characteristics of Stockton Ifoath "gentlemen," it is no wonder if those lower in the social sage display like traits, and thus give force to the injunction "No Stockton Heather need apply." 1, for ore, should not care to have much to do with the people who exhibited so mean a disposition ; and it wou!,l be well if these particular ."gentlemen" would cultivate habits more in keeping with the charac- ter they p.ffect.—lam, kc.,
A PASSENGER.
THE ELECTION IN SOUTH EAST WARD. Sir,-1 gather from reading one of our local news-

papers our election contest was deemed from the first a forego•Je conclusion. It quotes for its authority the return of Messrs. Bolton and Hutchinson, and says Mr. Diggle's opposition to the Sanitary Committee and the Howley intercepting depot is nothing less than a fad of his own. By publishing the following facts I think I shall prove to the contrary—first, that Mr. Bolton canvassed I this neighbourhood himself, promising the electors that both he and his colleague would vote against the anis- 'once that he had proved existed at Howley Depot. Second, Mr. Diggle had no committee or committee room, no friends,conveyances, or posters; simply issuing a few handbills announcing his intention to contest the ward, and these he neglected to get signed by the Chair- man of the Conservative Committee of the ward, as his opponents did, asking the electors to vote true to his party, although his two opponents had placarded the, walls saying they were the nominees of the Ratepayers Association and no political party whatever. Now, sir, Mr. Diggle was pressed by a body of work- ing-men (who suffer from this nuisance) to allow himself to be nominated, they knowing at he same time that he was the only one that had spoken on their behalf against the intolerable nuisance arising from the Howley Depot. If we look at the returniug officer's figures, we shall see that Mr. Diggle was no bogus candidate; no less than 344 electors voted for him and out of that number 186 plumped for fear of his defeat and that, too, with- out one word of persuasion. Now, sir, you will see where the pressure was put on. I myself spoke to a widow lady about voting. "Yes," she says, • I am going to vote for Mr. Diggle, but the other side have been Setimes for me. I have lived in my present house for 16 years, and during the most of the time this neighbourhood has been considered the healthiest part of the borough, but that was before the erection of this Howley DepOt and the abominable nuisance that arises therefrom." _ . _

I would suggest to my neighbours that, if neither Mr. Diggle's voice nor ours be heard, we all clear out at once and leave it for the property owners to fight with the Corporation in a court of law on the question of dam- ages. One word more. I long to see the day when education will be instrumental, in conjnnction with legal combin- ation and parliamentary agitation, to teach each workingman who are his true friends, and when the day of battle comes to claim their rights as they did around Bewsey Bridge on the first day of the present month. Hoping you will insert the above in your next issue, I remain, yours &c., GEORGE BUCKLEY. 12 Wellington-st., Nov. 7th, 1888.

div.head: OTHER SIDE OF THE QUESTION.
div.p: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE QUESTION.

_ Sir,—Your correspondent," Progress," seems to think that when the clerics are in the pulpit on their own ground they can say anything they like without fear of contradiction. Probably he thinks it might bean advan- tage to the public if in every church there were two pulpits—one for the "pros" and the other for the "cons," on the principle that "one tale is good till the other is told." Well, sir, I once thought so too. I was under the impression that it would be an advantage to the congregations to hear both sides of the questipn. But now I see wfia a very awkward position the 'officia- ting clergyman might be placed in if he happened to get an opponent able and willing to hit straight from the shoulder Let us suppose the rev, gentleman to have been holding forth upon the doctrine of original sin, the fall of man, and the necessity of redemption. How if his opponent asked him to say if he knew the legends as to the creation of man, his temptation by the serpent and consequent fall were mere copies—plagiarisms from an older literature—the most ancient voitings known, the cuneiform inscriptions of the Shumiro-Accadians. So that these idolaters were in possession of this so- called "inspired account "long ages before the "chosen people" who were fain to " cabbage " it from these poor heathens, thus affording us the earliest known instance of the infringement of copyright, or literary piracy. And he might well ask what credit can be given to such accounts coming from such a source? And if the rev, gentleman insisted upon the special creation of organised beinas his hard-hitting friend in the other box might ask him for his proof, or any tittle of evidence in support of such a view, and on the other hand refer him to the savants and well ascertained facts of natural history to disprove it. Following up his advantage, he might question the .logic—nay the morality—of any man who asks for faith in legends derived from such a questionable source and found in such suspicious company. And if this Assyrian legend of the fall of man be discredited, what would become of its immediate offspring the doctrine of redemption ? As a belief in the original innocence and fall of man is the only logical basis of a belief in the necessity of redemp ion, so both must stand or fall together. You may quite iina.gine the bad half-hour the rev. gentleman would have if confronted by such an awkward customer. On this, and some other grounds, I do not now advocate the- multiplication' of pulpits. Indeed I regard the school desk as the better and more efficient agent in civiliiing and humanizing the world. I regard clergymen who are engaged in the task of asking rational men to believe fantastic tales as wasting the time and energy both of themselves and their hearers. lam anxious to see such of them as are not befooled themselves or trying to befool others to cast aw--• +his shibboleth of bli;'"' and employ his energies and talents upon imèSubject more likely to advantage his hearers. Let some preacher—who te, in a position guifieiently independent to do so—boldly, throw off the trammels of tradition, and preach the doctrine of righteousness and right doing, and denounce in Scathing tones the undoubted ills he finds around him. To such a man who could thus sacrifice his sacerdotalism upon the altar of truth a great and useful future would be open. Are there no giant-evils—universally acknowledged to be such—stalking abroad in our midst and denta.nding their tithes of th people ? Are drunkenness, vice, and imniorality quite unknown among us? Or are these of so little moment that they may be left to care for them- selves, while the preacher expounds the traditions with his millinery and posturing ? But, sir. I am hapny to say that a very evident change for the better has taken place within the last/quarter of a century. We now seldom hear the sulphureous sermons so common some years ago. Educated men have dropped them,for educated men would not listen to them. And so it is all along the line. Objectionable doctrines are quietly dropped and ignored. So it has been with witchcraft. Who dare say the belief in witches and witchcraft is not as scriptural as ever it was? But who now dare preach a crusade against , witches and their craft ? But the warrant is still there Or it as much as and as strong as ever. In another quarter of a century, he will be a bold man who, in the face of the facts of evolution,would maintain the figment of specific generation. The rejection of suchlegends would leave more time and- energy for the denunciation of the prevalent sins against humanity.—l am, &c. JOHN PEERS Penketh, Nov. sth, 1888.

div.head: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON MUSICAL SOCIETY.

Sir,—l h;;; read the-letter under this heading signed " A member of the late Orchestral Society," but seeing that it is decidedly petsonal and anonymous, it is clearly unworthy of notice. In writing my letter I had certain definite objects in view ; it is hardly possible that it can have failed entirely in effecting these objects. It stands as written, for I have nothing to add or to retract. JOHN P. REYNOLDS.

Sir,-1 read the letter, signed "J. P. Reynolds "in yours of the 20th inst., part of which was a reply to mine, signed "An Amateur." I congratulate Mr. Reynolds upon the fairness of his remarks. If I was "dogmatic" in my mode of expression I must apologise, for it was not my desire to exhibit any such characteristic. Ido not forget how much the family of which Mr. Reynolds is a member has contributed to the extension of musical knowledge in Warrington. Had there been more such families, the town would have benefitted by their influence. _ _ _

Mr. Reynolds, speaking of the Committee, says "That Dr. Hiles has made suggestions, and that his suggestions have been listened to, is true—and that no conductor, worthy of the name, would act unless this were so." I cannot dissent from this proposition; but there is a wide difference, between an arbitrary and a representative authority. I never was a member of the Committee. Then what grounds had I for my assertions? Some years ago, I asked a friend, a musician and a member of the Committee, how' the Society was progressing? He replied "I have resigned my place on the Committee. At every meeting the business was brought forward cut and dried, the oratorios to be performed, the singers to be engaged &c., and any suggestions were heard, but never discussed. We were told that Dr. Hiles desires this and that be done. This always being the theme, the Committee to my mind was useless lumber; so I resigned." This incident occurred eight or nine years ago. My authority is above suspicion. He is a man, who, privately, has helped forward the development of music, in no half-hearted way. He has spent money freely. I would ask is there any other gentleman, whose experience, as a member of the Committee, tends to prove the truth of my assertions? Your columns, I presume are open for his reply. , Mr. Reynolds acknowledges that there may be "some truth "in my remarks, "as to the utility of the Society, and as to the time of rehearsals." I should be pleased to know wherein a single suggestion that I made, was impracticable, and not pertinent to the subject under discussion. The suggestions referred to, form the sub- stance of my letter; and to suggest that they were the vapourings of an "inexperienced youth" was a ready way of disposing of substantial evidence to the con- trary. Withreferenee to Dr. Hiles as a conductor, no one has ever breathed a word detrimental to him professionally. His position, is unassailable. But as to his sarcastic manner of speaking, if I have erred on the side of exaggeration, I am sorry for it, and perhaps some mein- lirr or ex-member may be able to put me right. I can- not however, take the evidence of Mr. Reynolds as impartial, and this I say respectfully. I was" drawn "to making the remark in reference to the President, by a remark of "An old Subscriber." rregret that Mr. Reynolds has enlarged upon it, for if I must defend my statement, the truth of it will only become more apparent. Talk about "50 years experi-
THE MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL. MOORE AND ACTON GRANGE.

' Along the first of these sections very little work is being done at present. The cutting made by the German navvy is deserted and is being drained of the water which had accumulated in it by a powerful pump on the Runcorn side of the level crossing. Where the huge exca,vator lately worked.a temporary wooden bridge has been erected alongside the road which separates the two cuttings, so that they, may now be connected without injuring the highway communication. In the cutting at the further end of the Acton Grange section the sleepers and rails, with the exception of one line, have been taken up. Nearer to the offices the 'sides of the cutting are being levelled, and rock excavation is being tarried on. All along the cutting the spoil banks are increasing at an extremely rapid rate, a large number of men being employed there. The cold east winds are a great hindrance to the men employed in the open cutting. 'STOCKTON HEATH AND WALTON.

The former sub-section is now busy through all its length. The German excavator which has been removed from the Moore section, has been erected a little to the left of the Northwich-road, near Twenty Step Bridge, where it is commencing a cutting. A large number of men are also employed there laying down rails. The new road is being perfected, and will soon be iTt use. The twd American navvies near the Chester-road are making good headway and at Morley Common, a third Is commencing a second lift, in rather hard soil. The railway embankment near Walton Arches is increasing rapidly in height and length. LATCHFORD AND THELWALL. Activity appears to increase on this portion of the canal. The two American navvies at the head of the cutting, remove an enormous quantity of soil, and are, now within a very few yards of the new road. On the opposi,e side of Cross-lane another cutting is being com- menced by a large gang of men. Here although the depth reached is very slight, it has been found necess- ary to erect a hand pump which is kept constantly working. Cedar Lawn is now completely razed to the ground, and there is no trace of it remaining. Further along the cutting the rock is being rapidly removed. MR. LEADER 'WILLIAMS AT BALLINASLOE.

Mr. Leader Williams, engineer of the Manchester Ship Canal, and a party of English engineers and surveyors visited Ballinasloe on Saturday, and inspected the new bridge and Sluices, with the view of constructing similar works on the Manchester Ship

THE FATAL ACCIDENT. AT ACTON GRANGE. An inquest was held at the Ship Canal Hospital, Latchford, on Saturday, touching the death of William Hall, navvy, who died on the previous Wednesday, from injuries received in being thrown off a train of waggons at Acton Grange. After hearing evidence, the jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death." ACCIDENT DURING BLASTING AT WARBURTON. On Monday during the blasting operations at Warbur- ton, a man named Henry Watts had his hand seriously injured by a discharge, his thumb being nearly blown off. He was removed to Latchford, where the hospital. surgeon dressed' the injured limb. On inquiry yester- day we learn that he is progressing as favourably as can be expected. A STRONG LIMB.

"On Tuesday morning, Charles Glastonbury, a navvy employed at Acton Grange, was swinging face down- wards upon the "buffer" of a train in motion, when he was jolted off and three wagons passed over his leg, which, strange to say, was not broken, owing to its strength and the great thickness of his boot. The limb is, however, extremely stiff, and he will not be able to use it for a considerable time. He is being treated at the Latchford Hospital. TERRIBLE PALL AT WILDERSPOOL.

- ....... _ On Monday, two men, named Pevis Roberts and Edward Carter, were working at Wilderspool at a "sump" or hole forty-two feet in depth. Roberts was at the bottom when Carter slipped and fell from the top upon him. Roberts had his leg broken and his arm dis- located. while Carter escaped with bruises on the head and body. The men were conveyed to the hospital at Latchford, where they are progressing favourably, having had a most wonderful escape. WAGGON ACCIDENT AT ACTON GRANGE.

On Wednesday, at Acton Grange section, a train of loaded waggons was going past a :group of three or four navvies when a jolt broke the catch of one of the waggons, and it being a side-tipping waggon it emptied its load upon the men. One of them, named Wm. Clarke, had his leg broken in April last, and it being still rather weak it was again broken. lie was removed to the Latchford hospital where he is in a favourable condition. The other men escaped with bruises and a shaking. MR. GLADSTONE AND THE CANAL.

Messrs. Lewis and Co., of Market-st., Manchester, have received the following letter from Mr. Gladstone: —" October I9,lBBB.—Gentlemen,—l thank you for a copy of the prize essays received to-day, and I have at once read the very clever and interesting paper on the great question of the Manchester Ship Canal. It is not for me to enter upon the controverted matters. I think, however, that the trade of the Mersey will be increased, the trade and business of Liverpool not diminished, the public will very argely profit, and the railway com- panies will find it expedient to develop instead of repres- sing direct trade between Liverpool and North Wales. There will probably be many other consequences on which I do not enter.—Your very faithful and obedient signed), W. E. GLADSTONE." THE RUNCORN RATING APPEAL.

• At Chester Castle on Friday, before his Honor Jtfdge Horatio Lloyd, animportant appeal case was opened, in which the Manchester Ship Canal Co. appealed against the rating by the Runcorn Union with respect to the Bridgewater. Mersey, and Irwell Canal, which had been taken over by the Ship Canal Co. Mr. Balfour Browne and Mr. E. H. Lloyd were for the appellants, and Mr. Marshall and Mr. J. E. Bankes for the respondents.— Mr. •Balfour Browne, on behalf of the appellants, said that the Ship Canal Company appealed in this case against the assessment of property in the township of Runcorn. The last valuation of the property was made on the 20th June, 1882, and nothing seemed to have been done by the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Union until the 13th October, 1885, when they began to consider whether a new valuation should be made. On the 16th February, 1886, they passed a resolution to appoint persons to value the -docks and canals of the company, and on the 2nd March last, Messrs. Rabx, of Manchester, were appointed, and set to work to make a re-valuation. They made a re-vahltion, which was confirmed by the Assessment Committee, and it was against that re-valuation that the Canal Company now appealed. Messrs. Baby came to the conclusion that the gross value of the property:was £16,677, and the whole of that valuation in the existing rate book Was £7,325, so that Messrs Raby's valuation was an increase of the

ence" ;of what? Why for nearly 25 out of the 50 years, the Society was literally defunct, dead as a door nail," for the want of an active, enthusiastic and munificent leader. lam writing from memory; I have no data to guide me, but, in 1834 the Society was started. It was choral and instrumental. It continued to be such for about 15 years, when it became a quiet Society for giving Subscription Concerts, of second-class quality, Braham Philips, Mario, Grise, Sze., were never heard, the fact being there was no place to hear them in. Dur- ing these years the gentleman who infused more life into the society more than any other, was Mr. Henry White, father of Mr. John White. In 1856, or thereabout, Mr. Joseph Bancroft came to the town. The fruits of his labours are still visible. His spare hours, for years,were occupied in teaching elementary singing, and when he had made a number of recruits of both sexes, he. with others, founded the Philharmonic Society. Mr. Henry WhiLe was an active supporter, and was often at re- hearsals; his son, Mr. White' was the organist, Mr. James Rimmer was the conductor, and when he died his place was taken by Mr. Thomas Eaude. By sheer force of character and pluck, Joseph Bancroft kept the society alive for several years. No concert was ever given in which the choral parts were not accompanied by both organ and orchestra. The society "departed this life" Nthat year I cannot for certain say ; but the 'Musical Society had been dead and forgotten years ago, and was only resurrected a few years after the present Public Hall was built. From the year of its resurrec- tion until now, it has continued to perform oratories with organ accompaniments only; what any village of 2,000 souls could only be expected to do. Here we are in the year of grace 1888, with a population of 50,000, plenty of able amateur instrumentalists amongst us, and unable to have ora orbs occasionally performed as the authors of them intended. If the President of the Musical Society had been a man of experience and an enthusiast, such a condition of management would never have been tolerated.

lam not an instrumentalist; but Mr. Reynolds refers to some overtures having been made to some instrumen- talists, with the object of forming a band, as part of the society. Were not a number once brought together for this object? And because some "brew a little too flat," or "a little too sharp," or that they did not play togethqr with the ptecision of professional men, was not something said by, somebody, which gave offence to the players, and sothey disbanded themselves? "Ringers, singers, and' fiddlers "are funny mortals; I grant they are often bumptious, and as often happens they who know least are often the most consequential. Like rare old china they require handling "gingerly." This is common knowledge; but only handle them with tact and patience, always "comb their hair" in the natural direction, and good can be got out of them. But tact must never be wanting. Even in "the Militia," there are Commanders, and there are Commanders.

Here Mr. Reynolds is hard upon me. He says, I am "dogmatic," but for his failing I have apologiSed ; and then he suggests, that if I am "so clever," I ought to join the Society, and become appointed one , of the Committee. Now this is ingenious, but I am not so ingenuous as to avail myself of the -invitation. Who would appoint such a revolutionist as I am as one of the Committee? I should just as soon think of going to Cork, and addressing a host of rabid Home Rulers on "The advantages of the Union ! " No; your executive is too ossified or fossilized, whichever is most correct. I have not one word of disparagement for the Choral Society; but, that its public performances are not supplemented by an orchestra, is a discredit to the musical intelligence of the town.—Yours truly, "AN AMATEUR."

estimated value by £9,353. - The old rateable value was £7,097; the new rateable value, according to this valuation, was £13,890. Although the rateable value. according to the Assessment Committee, had doubled since 1682, the company's receipts had been falling off all the time. Roughly speaking, between 1882 and 1836 there was a falling off in the gross receipts of £56.000, and, notwithstanding this the Assessment Committee seemed to think that the tenants from year to year, in order to got a profit, would give double the amount of rent than what they would have given in 1882. There was a difficulty of applying the Act of Parliament to an undertaking such as this, because the property was not confined to one parish. The question to be considered would be what amount hypothetical tenants would give for these premises, having a right to use the canal and river. Mr. Browne then proceeded to deal minutely with thereteipts and expenditure of the company. The company, he said, had tried to arrive at the rateable value of the whole undertaking as if itwere in oneparish, and therefore they had taken the rates and haulage for the year 1836, and the tolls and dockage for the same year. The business was falling off, and in taking the figures of 1866, lie did the very best for his opponents. After dealing at length with this part of the case, Mr. Browne proceeded to show what the portion of the canal which was in the Runcorn township was worth. The gross receipts, he said, were a very difficult mat er to arrive at. From freight upon the Bridgewaterin Runcorn the compamy received £5,516. From the tolls and dockage they received in 1886 £8,339, and for carriage, wharfage, and sundry receipts theyreceived £2,749. These figures showed the gross receipts upon the Bridgewater Canal of £16,604. Deduct from that the sum of £1,420, which had to be paid to another company, made the gross receipts in that township, upon the Bridgewater Canal alone, £15,185. After dealing with other figures show- ing profits and losses, Mr. Browne remarked that the company's valuation brought out the rateable value considerably below what was arrived at in 1882. After hearing evidence the Court adjourned till half-past ten on Saturday morning.
The 47th anniversary of the birth of the Prince of Wales was celebrated at Windsor on Friday.

A Rochdale telegram states that rii:f *John Bright passed a very good night, and it is now believed that he is steadily improving. Lloyd's Dover agent says a barque, supposed to be foreign, went ashore on Friday morning abreast of the Lydden Spont coastguard station. _

-The Parnell Cominission was engaged yesterday in hearing further evidence as to outrages and boycotting. The court adjourned until Tuesday. Naw MAYORS. - The following new Mayors were elected on Friday :—Liverpool, Mr. Cookson (C) ; Bir- kenhead, Mr. Smith; Bootle, Mr. Dungwell (C) ; St. Helens, Mr. Gamble (L) ; Southport, Mr. Wilkinson (C) ; Preston, Mr. Barrow (C) ; Wrexham, Mr. Morris (C) ; Crewe, Mr. Knott (C). •

THE LORD MAYOR'S PROCESSION.—The Lord Mayor's show on Friday was witnessed by a far smaller crowd than is usually the case. The weather was dull, but no rain fell, and the small attendance was probably due to the procession being curtailed of much of the tawdry pomp which previously characterised it. SHOCKING ACCIDENT AT A COLLIERY.—Henry Booth, miner, met with a frightful death, and another collier, named Cramp, was badly injured by a shocking accident on Thursday afternoon, at Craven Colliery, near Coventry. While some tubs were ascending an incline one of them, from some cause or other, broke awarand ran back, coming in contact with Booth, who was killed instantaneously. Cramp was trtjured while endeavour- big to get clear.
FALL OF A HOUSE-MANY KILLED AND INJURED.

The corner building of a row of shops now being erected in Great Titchfield-st. adjoining Great Portland- St.. London, suddenly collapsed at a quarter to four on Friday afternoon burying a number of workmen, four of these have been brought out from the ruins dead. Seven others more or less dangerously injured, have been taken to the Middbisex Hospital.
ANOTHER HORRIBLE MURDER IN LONDON. INTENSE EXCITEMENT. _ _

At half-past ten on Friday morning the dead body of a woman, horribly mutilated and with her head almost severed from the body, was found in a room in Dorset-court, Dorset-st., Spita'fields.' It must have lairs there some hours, and was quite cold. An alarm was raised, and an inspector of police and tome constables were immediately on the spot. The greatest excitement was soon raised in the locality, and crowds flocked to the scene. A correspondent, in a later despatch, says the victim was an unfortunate,about 30 years of age, and the crime was first discovered by a man named McCarthy. who went to the house where the deceased lived to collect rent, and on opening the front door he saw the body in the room. Deceased has been identified by a man with whobi she for- merly lived. She was seen to leave the house at about eight o'clock on Friday morning, and return with milk. No clue has heed obtained as to the murderer.

The "Star "gives currency to the following:— Another Whitechapel murder has been done. This I time the tragedy was carried out even more openly than the mnrder in Mitre-square. A woman, early on Friday morning, was found murdered and muti- lated in the room of a house in a court in Dorset- street, Spitalflelds. The details to hand are meagre enough. There seems to be no doubt that the sickening details of the crimes that shocked London a short time ago were repeated. A man who saw the body said it was cut up something awful. Dorset-street is only a few minutes' walk from ilanbury-street and Osborne-street. The woman's name is Mary Jane Kelly, and the man she lived with sell oranges in the s,treets. The mutilations of the body were of a most shocking kind, the head hanging merely by a thread. Both the ears and nose were cis off; all the flesh was stripped off the thighs, and the woman was not only disembowelled, but various parts are missing Dr. Gabe said he never saw such a sight as the murdered woman presented. LATEST DETAILS.

The Central News says :—Present indications go to show that the woman fell a victim to the man who has already made himself a terror to the East end of London. On this occasion, however, the fiend has departed from his usual method, inasmuch as the crime was committed, not in the open streets, but in. a room in a lodging-house.

The scene of the murder is— Miller-court, Dorset- street, Commercial-street, within a quarter of a mile of Mitre-square, Hanbury-street, Buck's-row, and Berners-street The entrance to Miller-court, is not More than three feet wide, and the court itself is only about 30 feet by 10. The murdered woman, whose name has not yet been ascertained, is a tall, fair female, about thirty years of age. She has for some time past hired the furnished room in which her mutilated body was found. On Thursday night she was heard coming in with a companion, and the couple retired immediately to the woman's room. Nothing more was heard ot the man, and for all the people in the place know he may have left any time between one and five without fear of attract- ing attention. Shortly before ten o'clock a man , who keeps a general shop at the corner of the court, went to the room, and not hearing the woman stirring, knocked at the door. He received no answer and, becoming suspicious, pushed open the door and then rushed shouting from the house. The body lay partly on the bed, the throat cut, Etna the breasts and other parts pf Ow body hacked about in a fearful manner. The police arrived on the spot by quarter-past ten, and at once drew a cordon at each end of the street. Sir C. Warren arrived at a quarter to two in a hansom cab. A man who lives in Dorset-st., opposite Miller's- court, states that soon after eleven o'clock three bloodhounds were brought in a hansom cab by a private individual, and were put on the scent, but they did not appear to be of any use, not having been properly trained. Morris Lewis, a tailor, states that he was playing pitch and toss in the court at nine o'clock on Friday I morning, and an hour before that pe 11.1 d seen the woman leave the house and return with some milk. There is no evidence as to who was in the house with her.

div.head: SATURDAY.
div.p: SATURDAY.

The hearing was resumed on Saturday, where important statistics were given by Mr. W. H. Collier, manager of the Bridgewater Canal, as to the working of the concern. He estimated that the amount earned by that canal company in the township of Runcorn last year was £15,185, out of £268,087, the gross receipts. In cross-examination he said there had been a considerable falling off in the receipts since 1882, but admitted that.the expenditure of the undertaking had decreased in a corresponding, ratio, so that the pro- fits, remained about the same. They had entertained the project of deepening the Runcorn and Weston Canal. so as to allow of the passage of vessels of 14 feet draught, whereas at present vessels over 11 feet draught cannot WIC the canal; but they had been obliged to abandon the idea *owing to the expense. Although their trade had .decreased greatly, they had been forced by competition to incur a large expenditure in order to retain what trade they had.—The examination of this witness occu- pied the whole day, and the Court again adjourned.

div.head: MONDAY.
div.p: MONDAY.

The case was continued on Monday.—Mr. F. Marshall, addressing the Court on behalf of the respondents, dealt at length with the various points in regard to receipts and expenditure upon which the appellants claimed for a reduction in the rates. The company had spent £120,000 fornew works since they came in possession of the concern, and they contended that this outlay was unproductive. inasmuch as it was for trade purposes and not for profitable purposes that they had to make' this outlay. They stated that there Lad been a decrease in their trade, but as a matter of fact there had been; upon the whole, an increase, and to the eye apparently of everybody the concern seemed to become busier and busi2r from year to year. Undoubtedly Runcorn was better adapted for traffic and was more occupied by trading vessels, and there seemed to be a great deal more going on than was the case some years ago. He wished to point out that the shares of the company went up considerably from the time the Bridgewater Navigation Company parted possession. There was ample material for suggesting that the concern in general terms was a prosperous, and probably an im- proving one. The respondents • challenged the system adapted by the company's valuers of finding out the valuation of the concern. He submitted that the test was a wrong one to estimate the value of the company's property in Runcorn with the value of other property belonging to the company outside of Ruacorn. He con- tended that no deductions should be made in the rate- able value of the company's property in Runcorn,because of the company's enormous structural outlay la other townships. The respondents argued that thore ought to be an inquiry on the spot, and that the rateable value should be determined according to market value. They challenged the whole principle of arriving at the valua- tion both with regard to the docks and the canal.—Mr. John Newton, valuer, of Manchester, was called as a witness on behalf of the Assessment, Committee, and, after hearing further evidence, the Court adjourned.

TUESDAY. Tuesday morning was occupied by the addresses of Mr. Marshall for the respondents, and Mr. Balfour Browne for the appellants. The former argued that the figures placed before the Court for the Assessment Committee were moderate, and were such as it would be safe for the Court to act upon. The Committee had taken the usual course in their estimate, and he thought the Court would confirm the rate.—Mr. Browne urged that the principle the Ship Canal Company had adopted was the right principle, and that the valuation made by the other side was absurd.—After a few minutes' private consideration, his Honor Judge Lloyd stated that, following the usual practice, so far as he knew, at Quarter Sessinns, he did not propose to give the pro- cess by which the Bench had arrived at the rateable value of the undertaking. It was, therefore, only nec- cessary for him to announce the result, and that was that what they considered a fair rateable value of the company's property in Runcorn was £7,050. These figures very nearly coincided with the old rate, and after having considered the question they thought that there was no adequate reason for increasing the original rate, and, therefore, costs would follow the result.

div.head: GAIN_ FOR TAR RUNCORN UNION.
div.p: A GAIN_ FOR TAR RUNCORN UNION.

At the fortnightly -meeting- of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, held at Dutton Workhouse on Thursday afternoon, Mr. W. H. Lina.ker (the deputy-clerk) made a statement having reference to the appeal of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company against the assessment of 'their undertaking in the Runcorn Union Mr. Baby's valuation to the Assessment Committee at the beginning of this year was £13,736 10s. The Ship Canal Company appealed against four items in that assessment amounting to £13,343, leaving a balance of agreed items amounting to £393 10s. Taking the Assess- ment not appealed against, £393 10s.' plus the amount awarded by the chairman of Quarter Sessions, £7050. them was remaining a total assessment of £7,443 10s. The total amount of the assessment under the old valuation list was £6,943 us. 8a... so that by this appeal the assessment committee had in reality gained an increased value of £449 18s. 4d. Taking the award of the Court of £7.050, and the Company's contention that the validation should stand at £3,500, the decision of the court gave £3,550 in favour of the Union. In giving his decision the chairman ruled that the Union should pay the taxed costs of the other side. The increased assessment during the next two or three years would re-imburse them that expendi- twe, and afterwards the Union would have a clear ,gain.

FRIGHTFUL EXPLOSION NEAR LIVERPOOL.—A fearful explosion is reported from Seacombe. Three boys, the sons of Mr. Stevenson. grocer, went to their bedroom on Tuesday bight, and the two eldest were soon asleep. The youngest brother, however, was curious about a tin canister that contained dynamite or some other explo- sive. He endeavoured to open the canister by striking the lid with a stone. The room WAS immediately wrecked by an explosion, and the boys were seriously injured, the eldest having a part of the ear blown off.

div.p: A MEDICAL OPINION.

Dr. Gabe, who resides in the locality, was called in to view the remains. In an interview with a London reporter he stated that the body was dread- fully mutilated. The ears and node were cut off, the liver was lying between the legs, and the bead was hanging by a thread. A certain organ, he added, is missing. Deteetive-inspector.Ticke stated that both breasts were cut off,v and were lying on the table. '

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. _ HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. _ HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tne Speaker took the chair at 3 p.m. QUESTIONS.—Lord GEORGE HAMILTON, replying to Mr. Danbury, said the Agamemnon had been sent .to Zan- zibar, which would make seven war ships at that place. —Mr. W. Smmt, replying to Dr. Cameron, said it was intended to propose a vote for Crofter emigration this session. Mr. CONYBEARE asked, in view ,of another horrible murder, if the time had not come for replacing Sir C. Warren.—The SPEAKER said notice must be given of the question. SUPPLY. The House then went in Committee of Supply. On the vote for over three •million and a half for Public Education in England and Wales, Sir W. DYKE gave a detailed explanation of the progress of Education and school attendance during last year, which he considered highly satisfactory. It was not inteaded by the Government to make an onslaught on the present system of Education, or make any movement which would disturb the settlement arrived at with regard to the Act of 1870.---Sir J. Lubbock was glad that no attempt waste be made to upset the existing compromise. —Sir R. Temple defended the system of comimision as applied in Metropolis, which he believed was gentle and gradual. [LEFT SITTING].

The picture is a fine piece of artistic work, showing an Italian maiden returning from the reaping field and decending a quaintly formed staircase beside the water-mill.

WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB.—The annual meet- ing of the members of this club was held on Mon- day evening. The President, Councillor Wm. Pierpoint, occupied the chair. The chairman, as retiring president, was pressed to continue in that office for another ensuing year, but declined. Councillor Fleming was therefore unanimously elected to the office. Councillor Wm'. Pierpoint, Dr. Gornall, and Mr. Thomas Morris were elected vice-presidents. Mr. T. Pemberton was re-elected secretary, and Mr. Jno. Crosfield was re-electbd treasurer for the year. The following gentlemen were elected for the committee:—Messrs. P. A,. Roberts, A. Browne, J. Garner, J. Albinson, W. Gilbert, E. Warren, W. Bibby, H. Highley, S. Kenyon, and J. R. Calvert. The balance sheet was discussed and • passed. A vote of thanks was accorded'to the president for his services during the past year. This was all the business. . . _

div.p: WARRINGTON.

SUDDEN' DEATlM—Yesterday morning the infant daughter of a navvy named James Flintham, of l. 131ackhurst-st., was found dead in bed, under circumstances that lead to the supposition that it had been overlain. Mrs. Elizabeth Isherwood, wife of Mr. Robert Isherwood, contractor, was also found dead in bed yesterday morning. The deceased, who had lived at 43 Factory-lane, had been living Wart from her husband for so,me years. She had not been in good health for about twelve months, and had been medically attended, 18T ( WARRINGTON) BATT AtION PRINCE OF WALES, VOLUNTERIIB.—The annual prize meeting of the First Volunteer Battalion, Prince of Wales' Volun- teers, was held on the Widnes range on Saturday and Monday last, and will be continued to-day. (Saturday). Prizes to the value of over p5O, are to be competed for. On Saturday the field officers, sergeant-instructors, and pioneers prizes were shot for and the general competition was also begun. The latter competition is seven shots each, at 200 and 300yds. respectively. To-day, the effic its, recruits, consolation, class-firing, and drill prizes

are to be competed for. FATAL SCALDING OF A CHILD.-OD. Thursday afternoon, Mr. W. T. Husband, deputy coroner for South-west Lancashire, held an inquest at the Police Station, touching the death of a child named Victoria Green, aged, two years, the daughter of Wm. Green, a wiredrawer and shopkeeper, living in Battersby-lane, who died on Tuesday morning from injuries sustained on the 30th October. Mrs. Green, the child's mother, said that on Tuesday, the 30th ult., she poured out a cup of tea and, leaviit; it on the kitchen table, went into the shop. She had not been away many nainutes.when she heard the deceased cry, and went to see what was the matter. She found the cup on the floor, and the child scalded on the neck, arms, and face. She ;immediately applied oil and limewater to the iniured parts, and the deceased appeared to be getting better until Sunday morning. Dr. Geary was then sent for, but despite what could be done, the child died on Tues- day morning. Sarah Cooper gave corroborative evidence.—The jury returned a verdict of "Acciden- tal death."

ALLEGED WIFE DESERTION.--At the• Borough Court, yesterday morning, a man named Thordas Helsby was summoned for having on the 27th ult., deserted his wife. Mr. Arthur Browne appeared for the comPlainant, and the defendant was repre- sented by Mr. Swift, barrister. The statement of Mr. Browne was to the effect that the parties were married at Manchester in 1871. Since then the defendant, who was a signal repairer, had lived unhappily with his wife A year after marriage defendant went to America, and was away six months. Afterwards he again lived with his wife. but a few years .ago the two separated, the wife going to live with her mother at Wilmslow. It was then arranged that he should pay her Bs. a week. He did so for some time, but in March last he reduced the amount to os a week, On the 27th October the wife went to see her husband, offered to live with him again, and make him a good wife. He, however, turned her out of the home, and had not since paid anything towards her maintenance. This, Mr. Browne contended, was a desertion.—Mr. Swift quoted law at length to chew that under the circumstances Piero was no desertion, and said that if the magistrates made an order, it would be over- ruling the decision of a high legal authority. There had mply been a mutual separation, and if the husband had ceased to pay his wife anything at all it would not have amounted to legal desertion. It would be impossible to make an order without over- ruling the decisiOns of Justices Smith and Stephen. The wife must either be content with what the husband gave her, or sue under the agreement for Bs. a week, or obtain an order through the parish officers. In giving the decision of the Bench, Mr. Join White,who presided, said that the sympathies of the Bench were entirely with the complainant, but there was no alternative but to dismiss the case. If they could have made an order they would have made one for more than Bs. a week. He thought this was a shameful proceeding on the part of the part of the defendant, and it the case was brought by the Guardians and he was on the Bench he should be in favour of making a larger order tban Bs. a week.
